Three panics within 10 minutes mark the subsystem Failed. Shutdown runs in reverse order within a budget, and subsystems that miss their deadline are aborted.
  • lifecycle: the agent states (Starting, Running, Degraded, SafeMode, Updating, Stopping, Stopped, FailSafe) and the legal transitions between them. A permanently failed critical subsystem forces FailSafe, and only stopping leaves it.
  • host: the tokio runtime (ADR 0009), logging to standard error, the panic hook and the console run loop.
  • service (Windows): the service control manager integration. It handles STOP (20 s budget) and PRESHUTDOWN/SHUTDOWN (10 s budget).

Platform layer

The agent reads the OS only through the palisade_core::platform traits (#29), so its logic can be tested on any OS against the mocks in palisade_core::test_util. palisade_agent::platform holds the real implementations:

TraitImplementationStatus
ClockSystemClockDone. The one place that reads the wall clock (clippy.toml bans SystemTime::now elsewhere)
FileSystemStdFileSystemReads, size and times on every OS, opened so other processes can keep writing and deleting. Owner SID, security descriptor, streams, file ID and USN report Unsupported until they are read through palisade_fileid::win (#54) for the file inventory (#60)
EnvironmentStdEnvironmentVariables, architecture and interface addresses everywhere; host name, domain and OS version from the OS on Windows. The connection type is Unknown until network location (#38) defines it
Registrywindows::WindowsRegistryDone, on Windows
IdentityProvider, ProcessInfo, SignatureVerifierWith the process tracker (#59), which reads tokens and resolves each image's identity

Each implementation passes the same contract checks as the mocks (palisade_core::test_util::contract), in tests/platform.rs, on every CI runner. The Windows registry and environment tests run on the Windows runners.

The fake agent

palisade-agent --simulate, in a build with the test-util feature, replays a scripted scenario on the mock platform and writes the agent's events to standard output, one canonical JSON event per line. It runs on any OS, so server and console work needs no Windows machine (docs/dev/unix.md).

cargo run -p palisade-agent --features test-util -- --simulate [--scenario <path>]

It emits agent.started, one exec.decision per step, then agent.stopped. The events are built only through the platform traits: process, parent and grandparent (from the process-ID-reuse-safe ancestry), user and session, image hash and signer, and the host. Every event passes Event::validate, is numbered (seq) and linked to the previous one (prev_hash; a plain SHA-256 placeholder until the keyed chain in #220 and #202), and the same scenario always gives the same events. Decisions are scripted, not evaluated (evaluation comes with the policy cache, #61). Sending the events to a server needs the agent endpoints and enrolment (#62, #126, #223).

A scenario is strict TOML (unknown keys are errors, at most 1 MiB and 10,000 steps). The built-in one is scenarios/default.toml.

start = "2026-01-05T09:00:00.000000Z"   # the simulated wall clock at start
mode = "audit"                          # audit | monitor | learning | enforce

[device]
hostname = "SIM-0001"
domain = "example.test"                 # optional
os_version = "10.0.26100.2314"          # major.minor.build.revision
architecture = "x64"                    # x64 | arm64 | x86
tenant_id = "01936b2e-8c4a-7b3d-9f21-0a1b2c3d4e61"   # UUIDv7
host_id = "01936b2e-8c4a-7b3d-9f21-0a1b2c3d4e60"     # UUIDv7

[[user]]                                # every SID a process runs as
sid = "S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1001"
name = "alice"
domain = "EXAMPLE"                      # optional
session = "console"                     # console | remote_desktop | services
elevated = false                        # optional; elevated users hold Administrators

[[running]]                             # processes running before the first step
pid = 5120
parent = 744                            # optional
image = 'C:\Windows\explorer.exe'
user = "S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1001"

[[step]]                                # one process start each
after_ms = 1500                         # time since the previous step, at most a day
exited = []                             # process IDs that exit first (to reuse an ID)
pid = 6200
parent = 5120
image = 'C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe'
command_line = "cmd.exe /c ver"         # optional
user = "S-1-5-21-1111111111-2222222222-3333333333-1001"
outcome = "allowed"                     # allowed | blocked | audited
signer = "Example OS Publisher"         # optional: the image's signature publisher

Allowed dependencies

palisade-core, palisade-fileid, palisade-policy, palisade-proto. Must never depend on palisade-server or any HTTP server or database stack. The rules are enforced by cargo xtask check-deps.

Third-party: tokio (the only async runtime, ADR 0009), tracing and tracing-subscriber (logging), serde and toml (configuration), if-addrs (interface addresses, as in the server), and, on Windows only, windows-service (the safe service control manager API), windows-registry (safe registry reads) and windows-version (the running OS version). With test-util only: palisade-proto (the event schema) and sha2 (the simulator's placeholder chain).

Unsafe code

None. The crate root is #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. The service entry point is written by hand, not with the wrapper crate's macro, which expands to unsafe. The registry and OS version are read through safe wrapper crates. FFI that needs unsafe will go in palisade_agent::ffi (ADR 0011).

Platform support

The service host is platform-independent and builds and tests on Linux, other desktop OS and Windows. --console and --simulate work everywhere. --service and the registry backend are Windows only; elsewhere --service exits with an error.

Feature flags

  • test-util: the fake agent (--simulate) and the simulate module, built on palisade-core's platform mocks. For development builds only, never a release build (docs/workspace.md). Without it, --simulate exits with a message saying how to build it.

Stability

Unstable and not published. Anything may change.

Source: crates/palisade-agent/README.md on GitHub.

palisade-server

The central management server: policy distribution, approvals, inventory and event storage.

Status: process skeleton with a database foundation. The binary starts, loads and validates its configuration, serves TLS on separate admin, agent and metrics listeners, answers liveness and readiness probes, and shuts down gracefully. It connects to Postgres, applies its embedded migrations, and isolates tenants with row-level security (see Database). It has no agent or API functionality yet. Work is tracked in #126 and #127 (epic #10).

Commands

palisade-server serve         --config <PATH>   # run until SIGTERM or Ctrl-C
palisade-server check-config  --config <PATH>   # validate, then print the effective config
palisade-server migrate up      --config <PATH> # apply pending migrations, then verify
palisade-server migrate status  --config <PATH> # applied vs embedded migrations, as JSON
palisade-server migrate verify  --config <PATH> # checksums and row-level security checks
palisade-server version

--config can also come from PALISADE_CONFIG. Exit codes: 0 success (including a completed shutdown), 1 runtime failure, 2 invalid configuration or command line. migrate status exits 3 when migrations are pending.

check-config runs every check serve runs before it binds a socket: the TOML and environment overrides, value ranges, the certificate chain and private key, the agent CA bundle, the TLS policy, the database password files and CA file, the refused PG* variables (see Database), and that each public_url host is a subject alternative name (DNS or IP) of the server certificate. It reports every problem at once, prints placement warnings (see Overlay deployments), and prints the effective configuration as JSON with secret files shown by path only.

Configuration

A TOML file; config/server.example.toml documents every key. Unknown keys are errors. Relative paths resolve against the directory of the file.

Every key can be overridden by an environment variable: PALISADE_ plus the key path in upper case, with __ (two underscores) between levels. For example PALISADE_LISTEN__ADMIN__PORT=9443 or PALISADE_TLS__KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/server.key. Unknown PALISADE_* variables are reported as warnings and ignored, so variables meant for other Palisade components do not stop the server.

KeyDefaultNotes
deployment.profilestandardstandard or overlay
tls.cert_filerequiredPEM chain, leaf first
tls.key_filerequiredPEM key (PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1). A secret file, see below
tls.min_version1.21.2 or 1.3. TLS 1.3 is always preferred
tls.profiledefaultdefault or asd-strict, see TLS
listen.<name>.bindrequired (127.0.0.1 for metrics)An IP address, or a network interface name
listen.<name>.portrequired (9464 for metrics)
listen.<name>.public_urlnonehttps URL clients use; checked against the certificate. Not on metrics
listen.<name>.body_limit_bytesadmin 16 MiB, agent 8 MiB, metrics 64 KiBUp to 1 GiB
listen.<name>.request_timeout_secs301 to 3600
listen.<name>.max_connectionsadmin and agent 4096, metrics 64
listen.agent.client_ca_filerequiredCA bundle that agent client certificates must chain to
shutdown.grace_secs30Up to 3600
log.levelinfoerror, warn, info, debug, trace
database.hostrequired if [database] is presentHost name or IP address
database.port5432
database.namerequiredDatabase name
database.userrequiredThe runtime role. Must not own the schema or bypass RLS
database.password_filerequiredA secret file holding the runtime role's password
database.tlsverify-fullverify-full, verify-ca, require or disable. The last two warn
database.ca_filenoneExtra trusted CA certificates (PEM). Only with verify-*
database.max_connections16Runtime pool size, 1 to 1000
database.connect_timeout_secs51 to 300
database.auto_migrateon if [database.migration] is setApply pending migrations at start
database.migration.usernoneThe migration role, which owns the schema
database.migration.password_filenoneA secret file holding its password

<name> is admin (console, REST API, SSO callbacks), agent (agent traffic) or metrics (probes with full detail, and later the metrics exposition). admin and agent are required. metrics is optional; it is enabled by its section or by any PALISADE_LISTEN__METRICS__* variable. Two listeners may not share a port on the same address (or on a wildcard of the same address family); serving every surface on one port with path routing is not supported yet.

Secret files

Secrets are only ever given as file paths, never as values, so the configuration file, the environment, check-config output and the logs never contain them. The secrets are tls.key_file and the database password files. It must be a regular file of at most 64 KiB, and on Unix it must not grant any access to the group or others (chmod 600 or stricter); otherwise the server refuses to start. The database password files (database.password_file, database.migration.password_file) follow the same rules, with a limit of 4 KiB; a trailing newline is not part of the password. Its contents are held in zeroising buffers while loading, and error messages name the path and the problem, never any content. Windows ACL checks, a redaction layer for log fields, and other secret kinds are part of #227.

TLS

Every listener is TLS only; there is no plaintext listener and no option to add one. TLS is provided by rustls with the ring provider (ADR 0008), cut down to an explicit allowlist so a future default change in rustls cannot widen it:

ProfileTLS 1.3 suitesTLS 1.2 suitesKey exchange
defaultAES-256-GCM-SHA384, AES-128-GCM-SHA256ECDHE-ECDSA and ECDHE-RSA with AES-256-GCM-SHA384 or AES-128-GCM-SHA256X25519, P-256, P-384
asd-strictAES-256-GCM-SHA384ECDHE-ECDSA and ECDHE-RSA with AES-256-GCM-SHA384P-384

ChaCha20-Poly1305 is excluded. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are not implemented by rustls. TLS 1.2 requires the extended master secret extension, and the server's suite order is used. ALPN offers h2 and http/1.1.

The agent listener requires a client certificate that chains to listen.agent.client_ca_file; a handshake without one fails. Matching the certificate to an enrolled device and checking revocation is enrolment work (#223).

The certificate and key are read once at start. Hot reload is part of #224.

Listeners and binding

bind takes an IP address (127.0.0.1, 100.64.0.7, ::1, [fd7a::7], or 0.0.0.0 / :: for every interface) or the name of a network interface (for example overlay0; on Windows the interface's friendly name). An interface binds every address it has. IPv6 sockets are always IPv6-only, so :: never silently covers IPv4 too.

Each listener has a supervisor that keeps it bound:

  • An address that cannot be bound yet (an interface that is not up, an address not assigned yet, a port in use) is retried with exponential backoff from 1 s to 30 s. Readiness reports listener_unbound:<name> until every address is bound. This covers an overlay interface that comes up after the server at boot.
  • A named interface is re-resolved every 5 s. New addresses are bound; addresses that vanish stop accepting.

Connections: the TLS handshake must finish within 10 s. The protocol follows ALPN: a connection that negotiated h2 is served as HTTP/2 only, and any other (including one with no ALPN) as HTTP/1.1 only, so a client cannot switch protocols by sending another preface. The first request must arrive within 30 s of the handshake, whatever the protocol, and each later HTTP/1.1 request head within 30 s of the previous response; otherwise the connection is closed, so an idle or stalled client cannot hold a connection slot. HTTP/1.1 request heads are limited to 64 KiB. HTTP/2 allows 128 concurrent streams and 64 KiB of headers per request, with keep-alive pings. A listener serves at most max_connections connections; a connection is accepted before it takes a slot, so a socket with no clients never holds one, and while every slot is taken further clients wait in the TCP backlog.

HTTP stack

Every listener's router runs inside this middleware stack (outermost first):

  1. Request ID. A client-supplied Palisade-Request-Id of 1 to 64 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : - is kept; anything else is replaced by 128 random bits in hex. The ID is echoed on every response.
  2. Errors as problem details. Every 4xx and 5xx response is an RFC 9457 application/problem+json document with type (https://palisade.dev/problems/<slug>), title, status, detail, instance (urn:palisade:request:<id>) and request_id. Error bodies from inside the stack are replaced, so they cannot leak internals; only the Allow, Retry-After and WWW-Authenticate headers are kept. A 5xx detail tells the client to re-read before retrying a change. Errors that hyper produces before a request reaches the router (a malformed request line, oversized headers) are hyper's own minimal responses.
  3. Trace. One span per request with request_id, listener, method, the matched route template (never the raw path or query) and peer, and one log line per response with status and latency_ms.
  4. Panic guard. A panicking handler becomes a 500 problem. The panic message goes to the log.
  5. Timeout. A handler still running after request_timeout_secs is cancelled with a 503 problem.
  6. Body limit. A body over body_limit_bytes gets a 413 problem, whether the size is declared in Content-Length or discovered while streaming.

Every response also carries X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

Probes

Every listener serves:

  • GET /healthz: liveness. 200 {"status":"alive"} while the process can serve requests.
  • GET /readyz: readiness. 200 when every listener is bound on every wanted address and the server is not shutting down; otherwise a 503 problem (type ending not-ready). On the admin and agent listeners the body carries only the overall status. On the metrics listener (loopback by default) it also lists the indicators:
IndicatorMeaningReadiness
listener_unbound:<name>An address of the listener is not bound yet503
public_exposure:<name>deployment.profile = "overlay" and the listener is reachable on a public address200, status degraded
shutting_downShutdown has started503
database_down[database] is configured and the runtime role cannot reach it (also before the first check)503
database_schema:<verdict>The schema is behind (pending migrations), newer than this binary, or damaged503
database_role_unsafeThe runtime role, or any role it is a member of, is a superuser, has BYPASSRLS, or owns or can create objects in the schema; or it is not in palisade_runtime503

The database is checked every 5 seconds. Job-runner readiness joins this list with #126.

Database

Postgres 16 or later, through sqlx (ADR 0006). Without a [database] section the server runs without one, as before, and logs a warning.

Roles. Two logins, never the same role:

  • The migration role owns the database, the palisade schema and every table. Only migrate up and auto_migrate use it.
  • The runtime role serves every request. It owns nothing, is NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS, and gets its table privileges through the palisade_runtime group role, which the migrations grant to. These properties are checked through role membership too, because a role can SET ROLE to any role it is a member of: no role the runtime login can reach may be a superuser, have BYPASSRLS, or own the schema or any table, function or type in it (an owner of palisade.current_tenant_ids() could replace it). serve refuses to start, and readiness reports database_role_unsafe, if any check fails.

sql/bootstrap.sql creates the three roles and the database; run it once as a database administrator with psql (the file shows the command), then set the two passwords with \password. palisade-server never needs a superuser.

Migrations. Forward-only numbered SQL files in migrations/, embedded in the binary with sqlx::migrate!. Each runs in a transaction, as the migration role. Before anything is created, migrate up checks that role: not a superuser, not linked to palisade_runtime by membership in either direction, and the owner of the palisade schema once it exists. A run as the wrong role changes nothing. The history lives in palisade._sqlx_migrations with a SHA-384 checksum per file, so an edited migration is a hard error. At start, serve refuses a database whose schema is newer than the binary, and with auto_migrate applies pending migrations first; otherwise it starts not ready until someone runs migrate up. serve also refuses a damaged schema. migrate verify also checks the structure that ADR 0006 requires: every table with a tenant_id column (and the tenant table) has row-level security enabled and forced and has a policy and tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, every foreign key between tenant-owned tables includes tenant_id, and no role a palisade_runtime login can act as owns anything in the schema or is a superuser or BYPASSRLS. New migrations must stay forward-only and avoid long table rewrites (expand/contract).

Tables so far. tenant (a tree with one root, organisation and template kinds, a settings object) and computer_group (a tree per tenant). Each has created_at, updated_at and revision, maintained by a trigger: inserts start at revision 1 and every update adds 1, so a client can use the revision for optimistic concurrency (#185). A row's id and tenant_id never change. The rest of the schema arrives with the issues that use it.

Tenant isolation. Every tenant-owned table has tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (the policies apply to the table owner too), and a policy tenant_id = ANY (palisade.current_tenant_ids()), for reads and writes. The function reads the palisade.tenant_ids setting; when it is unset or empty, no rows match. The only way the server code runs a tenant-scoped query is Database::tenant_tx(scope), which begins a transaction and sets the scope with set_config(..., true), the function form of SET LOCAL. The scope ends with the transaction, so a pooled connection never carries it to the next request. Foreign keys between tenant-owned tables include tenant_id, so a row can never reference another tenant's row.

What row-level security does and does not protect. It stops a bug in a handler (a missing WHERE, a wrong ID) from reading or changing another tenant's rows: the database filters every query, whatever the code asks. The runtime role cannot turn it off: it does not own the tables, so it cannot DISABLE or NO FORCE row-level security or change the policies, and with row_security = off a filtered query fails rather than returning everything. It does not protect against a compromised server process. That process holds the runtime role and chooses the scope itself, so it can ask for any tenant (threat model AC-08). The integration tests demonstrate both sides.

Environment. The Postgres client library reads some PG* environment variables. The server refuses to start, and migrate refuses to run, while PGPASSWORD, PGPASSFILE, PGOPTIONS, PGSSLKEY, PGSSLCERT, PGSSLMODE, PGSSLROOTCERT or PGHOSTADDR is set, because these would override the configuration (a password outside a *_file, or a session setting such as row_security).

Queries. Fixed SQL strings with typed bind parameters only. Compile-time-checked queries (query!) need a live database or committed offline metadata; they are not used yet, and adopting them, with a lint against string-built SQL, is part of #229.

Overlay deployments

For a fleet reachable only through a private overlay network (#239), bind the admin and agent listeners to the overlay interface or address, keep metrics on loopback, and set deployment.profile = "overlay":

[deployment]
profile = "overlay"

[listen.admin]
bind = "overlay0"              # or the overlay address, e.g. "100.64.0.7"
port = 8443
public_url = "https://palisade-server.overlay.example:8443"

[listen.agent]
bind = "overlay0"
port = 8444
public_url = "https://palisade-server.overlay.example:8444"
client_ca_file = "tls/agent-ca.crt"

[listen.metrics]
bind = "127.0.0.1"

Under the overlay profile, check-config and serve warn when a listener binds every interface, is reachable on a public address, or (for metrics) is not on loopback. While the server runs, public reachability is also reported as public_exposure:<name> in readiness. "Public" means anything outside loopback, RFC 1918, the RFC 6598 shared space 100.64.0.0/10, link-local, IPv6 unique-local fc00::/7, and the documentation, benchmarking and reserved ranges.

The certificate must name every public_url host (the overlay DNS name or overlay IP) as a SAN; check-config fails otherwise. The overlay is transport only: TLS and client certificates stay mandatory over it.

Logs

serve writes one JSON object per line to standard error: timestamp, level, target, fields (including message), span (the current span) and spans (every enclosing span, so the request span's fields stay on the line when a handler opens a child span). The level comes from log.level. No secret value is passed to the logger: the configuration holds only secret paths, and the secret reader's errors never contain file contents. Tenant and principal fields join the request span with the API work.

Shutdown

On SIGTERM or SIGINT (Ctrl-C), or on Windows Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break and the console close, logoff and shutdown events (the handlers are registered before any socket is bound, so an early signal is never lost): readiness fails, every listener stops accepting, and open connections are asked to finish their in-flight requests and close (HTTP/1.1 after the current response, HTTP/2 with GOAWAY). If any remain after shutdown.grace_secs, they are dropped. The process exits 0 either way. A second signal during the drain exits 1 immediately.

Not here yet

Tracked in #126 unless noted: create-admin, backup and restore subcommands (also #138); /version with git SHA and schema version; single-port mode; compression, CORS, rate-limit, auth and tenant layers; the metrics exposition and OTLP; runtime log-level changes; clock-skew health; the job runner and scheduler; relay role. Elsewhere: the rest of the schema, secrets at rest, soft delete, retention and partitioning (#127 and the issues that own each table), the audit log (#132), enrolment and device certificate checks (#223), agent RPCs (#62), REST conventions (#185), certificate hot reload (#224), secrets hardening (#227), server hardening (#229).

xtask

Repository automation for Palisade, run as cargo xtask <command> (the alias is in .cargo/config.toml). It is a normal workspace crate, so it builds with the pinned toolchain and needs no other tools.

CommandWhat it does
ci [--fast]Runs every check in .github/workflows/ci.yml locally, with the same commands. --fast skips coverage, fuzz, docs, the book build, feature-powerset, msrv and the package, signing and server-image builds. A unit test keeps its step list identical to ci.yml. Steps: src/ci.rs.
check-banned-terms [--digest <term>]No commercial vendor or product name in any file or path, matched as whole words in any letter case (docs/NAMING.md). The list, docs/banned-terms.txt, holds SHA-256 digests only; --digest prints the line for a new term. Rules: src/banned_terms.rs.
docs generate, docs check, docs build, docs assembleThe documentation site (#27): generates the reference pages, checks that they are current and that every page is in the book and accessible, builds the book with mdBook and checks its links, and assembles the GitHub Pages tree. Code: src/docs/; see docs/ci.md.
check-depsThe allowed dependency directions between workspace crates, and crates banned from the palisade-policy and palisade-agent dependency trees. Rules: src/deps.rs.
check-manifestsEvery member crate inherits version, edition, MSRV, licence, repository, authors, publish and lints from the workspace, and takes every dependency from [workspace.dependencies]. test-util is never on by default and only dev-dependencies may enable it (an explicit --features test-util on the command line still can). Every crate README has no HTML comments, opens with a purpose paragraph, has the required sections and documents every feature. Rules: src/manifests.rs.
adr new "<title>", adr index, adr lintThe ADR tooling from docs/adr/PROCESS.md: scaffold the next ADR from the template, regenerate the index in docs/adr/README.md, and check every ADR's file name, number, title, Status, Date and Deciders lines, sections (present, in order, not empty), supersession links and the index. Rules: src/adr.rs.
auditRuns cargo-audit with exactly the advisory ignores from deny.toml.
check-supply-chainAt most 10 duplicated crates, deny.toml ignores with an ID, a reason and an unexpired date, reasons on skips and licence exceptions, the cargo-vet criteria and exemption notes, and no audit.toml. Rules: src/supply_chain.rs; see docs/dependencies.md.
check-unsafeOnly files listed in unsafe-allowlist.txt, in the locations ADR 0011 allows, may relax the unsafe_code lint. Crates without an allowlisted module keep #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at their roots. Rules: src/unsafe_code.rs.
check-workflowsGitHub-hosted runners only, allowlisted and SHA-pinned actions, least-privilege permissions, and no cloud-managed build service named anywhere under .github/. Rules: src/workflows.rs; see docs/ci.md.
threat-coverageThe threat model (docs/security/threat-model.md): STRIDE rows well formed, every component considers all six categories, one mitigation row per threat in order with the same issues, every implemented or verified threat cites a check on main, every cited test function, fuzz target and workflow command exists, the status summary matches, and no file names an undefined threat ID. Rules: src/threat_coverage.rs.
dist [--target <triple>] [--msi] [--sign <signer>] [--out <dir>] [--bump-patch] [--compare-sizes <file>] [--from <dir>] [--no-timestamp]Release-builds the Windows executables (static CRT, version resource, manifest, /Brepro), checks them, writes the symbols archive and size report, and with --msi builds and validates the installer package with the pinned WiX; on Linux, the server binary. dist driver explains the local-only driver package (#8). Code: src/dist/; see docs/packaging.md.
sign --signer <none|test-ca|pfx|cloud-hsm> [--verify] [--no-timestamp] <file>...Authenticode-signs PE files and packages with a SHA-256 digest and an RFC 3161 timestamp, then verifies them; secrets come from the environment and are scrubbed from output. Code: src/release/sign.rs; see docs/releasing.md#code-signing.
release <prepare|check-tag|notes|checksums|verify-checksums|verify|provenance> ...The release pipeline's steps: version bump and changelog, tag checks, release notes, SHA256SUMS, signature verification inside packages, and the provenance hook. Code: src/release/; see docs/releasing.md.
deps-report [--base <commit>]The dependency report on the CI job summary: duplicates, cargo tree -d, third-party crates per crate, third-party unsafe counts and their change, build scripts and proc-macros. Code: src/report.rs.
sbomReserved for #226; prints where the CycloneDX files will go (target/dist/sbom/) and fails.
test-summary <label> <junit.xml>Turns a nextest JUnit report into the CI job summary and one annotation per failed test. Code: src/junit.rs.
coverage-summary <label> <coverage.json>Turns a cargo llvm-cov --json --summary-only report into a per-crate coverage table on the job summary, with a warning for each crate below its target. Code: src/coverage.rs.
fixturesBuilds palisade-fileid's generated fixture corpus into target/fixtures/, with a MANIFEST of hashes (release build: the RSA-3072 test keys are slow in debug). Code: src/testdata.rs, crates/palisade-fileid/tests/corpus/.
golden [--update]Rebuilds the corpus and compares every fixture's SHA-256 with testdata/golden/fixtures.txt, or rewrites it. Code: src/testdata.rs.
check-testdataFails if any file in the repository starts like an executable (MZ) and is not allowlisted, by SHA-256 with a reason, in testdata/manifest.txt. Code: src/testdata.rs.
check-fuzz-locksRuns cargo metadata --locked on every crates/*/fuzz/Cargo.toml and fails, with the minimal re-lock command, if a fuzz workspace's committed lockfile is out of date. Code: src/fuzz_locks.rs.
coverage-gate --base <commit>Measures palisade-policy line coverage at <commit> (in a temporary worktree) and at the working tree, and fails if it decreased. Needs cargo-llvm-cov and cargo-nextest. Code: src/coverage_gate.rs.
bench-compare --base <commit>Runs every criterion bench at <commit> and at the working tree (twice each, alternating, keeping the faster), writes a comparison table to the job summary, and fails if a median is more than 10% slower with non-overlapping confidence intervals. Code: src/bench_compare.rs.
fuzz [--seconds N] [--target NAME]Builds every cargo-fuzz target, seeds its corpus from the test fixtures, runs it for N seconds (default 60) and writes the results, with a base64 reproducer for each finding, to the job summary. Needs the pinned nightly and cargo-fuzz. Its tests keep the target list in step with each fuzz Cargo.toml and fuzz.yml. Code: src/fuzz.rs; see docs/testing.md.

Each command prints one line per violation and exits non-zero if there are any. Each rule set has unit tests with passing and failing fixtures: cargo test -p xtask. The workspace rules themselves are described in docs/workspace.md.

More commands are planned in #29; sbom is filled in by #226.

Allowed dependencies

No workspace crates: no product crate may depend on xtask, and xtask reads the workspace through cargo metadata instead of linking it. Third-party: serde_json, toml and yaml-rust2, to read cargo metadata output, manifests, workflow files and JSON Schemas; proc-macro2, to tokenise Rust source; and sha2, for the term digests in check-workflows and check-banned-terms, and the WiX package checksum in dist.

Platform support

All platforms. It runs on every CI runner and every contributor machine. dist builds Windows targets only on Windows and the server only on Linux x64, each with the platform's own linker.

Feature flags

None.

Stability

Internal tool, not published. Commands and messages may change.

Source: xtask/README.md on GitHub.

Workspace rules

How the Cargo workspace is laid out, and the rules every crate follows. The decisions behind them are in ADR 0003 (crate layout), ADR 0011 (MSRV and unsafe code) and ADR 0012 (panic strategy). Each rule says which check enforces it. All the checks run in CI (ci.md).

Crates

The members are the ten crates under crates/ plus xtask. palisade-driver is left out of default-members, so a plain cargo build at the root does not build it. --workspace still includes it. Every crate has a README with its purpose, allowed dependencies, platform support, feature flags and stability level. cargo xtask check-manifests fails if the purpose paragraph (text before the first ## section) or one of those sections is missing. A crate README may not contain an HTML comment (<!--): the rendered page hides it, and a line-based check cannot tell where one ends, so a section or feature inside it could be counted. Write &lt;!-- to show the characters.

Shared settings

[workspace.package] sets the version, edition (2024), MSRV (rust-version), licence (Apache-2.0 OR MIT), repository, authors and publish = false. Every crate inherits all of them and the workspace [lints], and takes every dependency from [workspace.dependencies] with { workspace = true }. Enforced by cargo xtask check-manifests.

Dependency directions

core ← fileid ← policy ← proto ← {agent, server, cli, tray}. console may use only proto, and driver only core without std. policy never reaches tokio, reqwest, windows or windows-sys, and agent never reaches a server or database stack. Enforced by cargo xtask check-deps.

Unsafe code

The workspace sets unsafe_code = "deny" (ADR 0011 lowered it from forbid when the first FFI module, palisade_fileid::win::trust, landed), so any unsafe fails to compile unless the file relaxes the lint. Every crate root without an allowlisted module keeps #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. Only these locations may relax the lint:

  • palisade_agent::ffi and its submodules (crates/palisade-agent/src/ffi.rs or ffi/)
  • palisade_tray::ffi and its submodules
  • palisade_fileid::win and its submodules
  • the whole palisade-driver crate

Every file that relaxes the lint (allow, expect or warn naming unsafe_code in the same attribute, as an inner or outer attribute, including inside cfg_attr and macro bodies) must be listed in unsafe-allowlist.txt, which needs code owner review. cargo xtask check-unsafe fails if:

  • a file relaxes the lint and is not listed;
  • a listed file no longer relaxes it, does not exist, is listed twice, or is outside the locations above;
  • the library or binary root of palisade-core, -policy, -proto, -server, -console, -cli or xtask does not start with #![forbid(unsafe_code)] (a forbid inside a nested module or function does not count, and neither does a tool path such as forbid(clippy::unsafe_code));
  • the workspace level is anything but forbid or deny, or the lint is set twice under both spellings (unsafe_code and unsafe-code);
  • a Cargo config file in the repository (.cargo/config.toml, or the legacy .cargo/config, in any letter case) sets anything but [alias], or an alias passes --config, a response file (@file), a rustflags setting (a word naming rustflags with an =), --cap-lints, any -Z unstable option, or a lint option (-A, --allow and the rest, also grouped after other short flags as in -gA) whose operand names the lint. Other arguments may mention either, such as a unsafe_code::tests or rustflags test filter. Rustflags, compiler and wrapper overrides and [env] can all switch lints off, so a repository config may not set them;
  • a file is a symbolic link, in the working tree or as recorded in the git index (which catches a link that core.symlinks=false checked out as a regular file), a listed file cannot be inspected (only a tracked file deleted from the working tree is skipped), or a Rust file (.rs in any letter case) cannot be tokenised. That includes a first line starting with #! that is not an inner attribute: rustc strips such a shebang line and the tokeniser does not, so the check fails rather than guess.

The files scanned are the ones git tracks or would track (ignored build output is skipped), and each is tokenised with proc-macro2, the tokeniser procedural macros use, so comments and literals are never mistaken for attributes. What text scanning cannot see is left to review: an attribute a macro builds from its parameters (#[$a($b)]), a module loaded through #[path] or include! from a file that is untracked or not named .rs, and code a build script generates. The workspace forbid still applies to all of these. Every unsafe block also needs a // SAFETY: comment (clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks = "deny").

Feature flags

  • Additive only. Turning a feature on adds code or output. It never changes how a policy decides, so a build with more features makes the same decisions.
  • Documented. Every feature, including optional dependencies that act as features, is listed in the ## Feature flags section of the crate README. Enforced by cargo xtask check-manifests.
  • Each feature builds on its own. CI runs cargo hack check --each-feature --all-targets on the portable crates, core, fileid, policy, proto, server, cli and console, and on agent, which builds on every OS (the feature-powerset job).
  • No ordinary build turns test-util on. It may hold fixtures and mocks. It is never in default, no other feature of the crate turns it on (so default cannot reach it indirectly), and only [dev-dependencies] may enable it on another crate. No [workspace.dependencies] entry may enable it, because members inherit those features in every table. Enforced by cargo xtask check-manifests. The check reads manifests, not build commands, so cargo build --release --features test-util or --all-features would still turn it on. palisade-policy (builders, #25), palisade-core (platform mocks) and palisade-agent (the fake agent) have it. The release build (cargo xtask dist) builds named binaries with their default features only, and must never pass --all-features. CI's --all-features jobs only check and test.

The planned flag names, each added with the code that needs it:

FlagMeaningLands with
stdStandard library support. Off for no_std users such as the driver.palisade-core (now)
serdeSerialize/Deserialize for public types.palisade-core (now)
schemaJSON Schema descriptions (schemars). #19 calls this flag schemars; it landed in palisade-core as schema (#30), and palisade-policy depends on that name.palisade-core (now)
test-utilFixtures and mocks for other crates' tests.palisade-policy (#25), palisade-core and palisade-agent (#29) (now)
etwEvent Tracing for Windows collection in the agent.#59
minifilterAgent support for the optional kernel driver.#110
os-native-compilerCompiling policies with the operating system's own tooling, on a Windows build host.#84
os-trustOS signature and catalog checks in palisade-fileid (ADR 0003).#3
content-rulesContent tagging in palisade-fileid: the built-in tag set and organisation pattern rules.palisade-fileid (now, #44)

Profiles

  • [profile.dev] keeps overflow checks.
  • [profile.release]: lto = "thin", codegen-units = 1, debug = "line-tables-only" with split-debuginfo = "packed" (PDB files on Windows, which the release pipeline publishes as symbols in #22), and strip = "none".
  • panic = "unwind" in release. #19 suggested abort for agent binaries, subject to an ADR. ADR 0012 decided unwind, so that the agent can catch a parser panic on one crafted file and treat that file as unknown, instead of crashing the whole service. That recovery is planned, not built: the agent is still a stub (#4), and the catch_unwind boundaries land with its service host (#56). Cargo applies panic to a whole profile, so every release binary unwinds. The no_std driver is built separately and sets its own strategy (#8).
  • palisade-policy, palisade-fileid and palisade-proto keep overflow checks in release builds too: decision logic, and the parsers of untrusted input.

Toolchain and MSRV

rust-toolchain.toml pins one stable release with rustfmt, clippy and llvm-tools-preview, and the Windows x64, Windows ARM64 and Linux x64 targets. rust-version in [workspace.package] is the MSRV, never newer than stable minus 2. Every bump is recorded in the changelog, or in an ADR if it drops a platform (ADR 0011). The msrv CI job checks the workspace on exactly that version.

There is no changelog yet, so MSRV bumps are recorded here:

  • 2026-11-24: 1.85 → 1.94. sqlx 0.9, the Postgres layer for #127, needs 1.94. sqlx 0.8 still builds on 1.85, but it brings older versions of the hashing, random-number and Windows binding crates and takes the tree over the duplicate budget in cargo xtask check-supply-chain. At 1.94 Clippy also applies collapsible_if, manual_is_multiple_of and chunks_exact_to_as_chunks to existing code. They are allowed in [workspace.lints.clippy] until a follow-up under #19 rewrites that code.

Source: docs/workspace.md on GitHub.

Architecture decision records

This directory holds Palisade's architecture decision records (ADRs). Each ADR records one significant design decision: its context, the options considered, the choice and its consequences, including its security impact.

  • How to write, number, accept and supersede an ADR: PROCESS.md
  • Template for new ADRs: 0000-template.md

Index

0003Crate boundaries and dependency directionaccepted

Source: docs/adr/README.md on GitHub.

ADR process

Palisade records significant design decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) in this directory. An ADR is a short document that captures one decision: its context, the options that were considered, the choice made and its consequences. ADRs stop settled questions from being reopened by accident, and they explain to a learner why Palisade works the way it does.

ADR 0001 adopts this process.

When to write an ADR

Write one when a change:

  • picks between design forks that are expensive to reverse (protocols, storage, crypto, enforcement mechanisms, crate boundaries, default security behaviour);
  • changes a default that affects whether something is blocked or allowed;
  • adds a dependency on a new privileged component (driver, service, signing key); or
  • contradicts an accepted ADR. That requires a new, superseding ADR (see below).

Routine choices inside one crate do not need an ADR. Put those in code comments or the crate README.

Format

  • Location: docs/adr/.

  • File name: NNNN-kebab-title.md, for example 0002-enforcement-strategy.md.

  • NNNN is a 4-digit number. 0000 is reserved for the template.

  • Start from 0000-template.md. The sections and their order are fixed: Title, Status, Date, Deciders, Context, Decision drivers, Considered options, Decision, Consequences (Positive and Negative), Security impact, Links.

  • The first line is # NNNN. Title. The next three lines are a list, so that tooling can parse them:

    - Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-11-23
- Deciders: Palisade maintainer

  • Status is exactly one of proposed, accepted, superseded by NNNN, deprecated or rejected.

  • Date is the date of the most recent status change.

  • Security impact must say something real. If a decision truly has no security effect, the section explains why.

  • Keep an ADR to one or two pages. Put long research in docs/design/ and link to it.

  • Never name commercial products or vendors. Describe approaches generically (naming guide).

Numbering

  • Numbers increase monotonically. The next ADR takes the highest existing number plus one, counting every file in the directory, including rejected and superseded ADRs.
  • Numbers are never reused. A rejected ADR stays in the repository with status rejected, so its number and reasoning are not lost.
  • If two open PRs pick the same number, the PR that merges second renumbers its ADR before it merges. That is allowed because the ADR is not yet accepted.

Lifecycle

proposed ──▶ accepted ──▶ superseded by NNNN
    │            └───────▶ deprecated
    └──▶ rejected
  1. Propose. Open a PR that adds the ADR with status proposed (or accepted, if the PR is meant to accept it on merge). Label the PR area:infra.
  2. Discuss. While an ADR is proposed, its content may change freely in follow-up PRs.
  3. Accept. An ADR becomes accepted when a PR that sets that status is merged. The PR needs:
    • approval from at least one maintainer, and
    • at least 3 days open since the PR was created, unless the maintainer marks it urgent. To mark it urgent, the maintainer adds a line ADR-Urgent: <reason> to the PR description, and the reason is copied into the ADR's Links section.
  4. Reject. A proposal that is declined is merged with status rejected, with a sentence in Decision explaining why, so the reasoning is kept.

Accepted ADRs are immutable

Once accepted, an ADR's text does not change. The only edits allowed are:

  • the Status line and the Date line (to superseded by NNNN or deprecated), and
  • the Links section (to add links to later ADRs, issues or docs).

Typos may be fixed if the meaning does not change.

Changing direction

To change an accepted decision:

  1. Write a new ADR that explains what changed, links the old one with a Supersedes: NNNN bullet in its Links section, and is accepted through the normal process.
  2. In the same PR, set the old ADR's status to superseded by NNNN and add a link back.

A PR that contradicts an accepted ADR must link the superseding ADR (an existing one, or one proposed in the same PR). Reviewers reject PRs that contradict an accepted ADR without one. deprecated is for decisions that no longer apply because the thing they governed was removed, with nothing to replace them.

Index and tooling

README.md holds the index of all ADRs. Three commands do the mechanical work:

  • cargo xtask adr new "<title>" copies the template to the next number, with the title, today's date and status proposed. It never overwrites a file.
  • cargo xtask adr index regenerates the table between the adr-index markers in README.md from the ADR files.
  • cargo xtask adr lint runs in CI (the runner-guard job, behind the required ci-ok check). It fails on:
    • a file name that is not NNNN-kebab-title.md, a reused number, a gap in the numbering, or 0000 used for anything but the template;
    • a first line that is not # NNNN. Title with the file's number;
    • a missing or invalid Status, Date or Deciders line;
    • a template section that is missing, repeated, out of order or empty (Security impact included), judged as the Markdown renders: a heading or text inside an HTML comment does not count, and neither does a ## line inside a fenced code block. A ## section's ### subsections are part of its content;
    • in the template, a title other than # NNNN. ..., a status other than proposed, or a date other than YYYY-MM-DD, because adr new relies on all three;
    • a date that is not a real calendar date;
    • superseded by NNNN naming an ADR that does not exist, is not later, or is not accepted or proposed, or whose Links section has no visible - Supersedes: NNNN bullet for it (the number may be a Markdown link);
    • a symbolic link, subdirectory or file other than an ADR, README.md or PROCESS.md in docs/adr/ (dotfiles such as .gitattributes are allowed);
    • an index in README.md that differs from what adr index would write.

The lint cannot see history, so it cannot tell whether an accepted ADR's text was changed. Reviewers check that, and the rest of the checklist below, by hand.

Review checklist for ADR PRs

  • The file name and number follow the numbering rules.
  • All template sections are present, in order, and none is empty.
  • Every considered option has its trade-offs against the decision drivers.
  • The Decision can be checked against later PRs.
  • A proposed ADR says what evidence would decide it.
  • Security impact is specific.
  • No commercial product or vendor names.
  • The index in README.md is updated.
  • Any superseded ADR has its status and links updated in the same PR.

Source: docs/adr/PROCESS.md on GitHub.

0001. Record architecture decisions

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Application control has several design forks where the options exclude each other and are expensive to reverse: how enforcement happens, how conflicting rules resolve, what is trusted, and what happens when a component fails. Palisade is also a learning project, so the reasons behind each choice matter as much as the choice itself. Without a written record, later contributors (including the maintainer, months later) reopen settled questions, or change a security default without seeing why it was set.

Issue #20 asks for a lightweight decision record process under docs/adr/ and an initial set of decisions that the other epics depend on.

Decision drivers

  • Decisions and their trade-offs must be findable next to the code, in version control.
  • Low ceremony: one maintainer has to be able to run the process.
  • A changed decision must leave the old reasoning readable, not overwrite it.
  • Security consequences must be stated for every decision, because Palisade is security software.

Considered options

  1. No formal record. Decisions live in issue threads and commit messages. No overhead, but the reasoning is scattered, issue threads mix proposals with outcomes, and nothing marks a decision as settled.
  2. A single living design document. One place to read, but edits overwrite history, a reader cannot tell when a decision was made, and the document grows past what anyone reads.
  3. Markdown ADRs in the repository, one decision per file, in a MADR-style format. Small, reviewable in PRs, immutable once accepted, superseded rather than edited. Costs a short document per decision.

Decision

Option 3. Palisade keeps ADRs in docs/adr/, using the template in 0000-template.md and the rules in PROCESS.md. In summary:

  • Files are NNNN-kebab-title.md, with 4-digit, monotonic numbers that are never reused.
  • Status is one of proposed, accepted, superseded by NNNN, deprecated, rejected.
  • ADR PRs are labelled area:infra. Acceptance needs one maintainer approval and at least 3 days open, unless the maintainer marks the PR urgent.
  • An accepted ADR is immutable except for its Status, Date and Links lines. A change of direction is a new ADR that supersedes the old one. A PR that contradicts an accepted ADR must link the superseding ADR.
  • Every ADR has a non-empty Security impact section.

Bootstrap. A process cannot govern its own adoption. The ADRs marked accepted in the PR that introduces this directory are accepted when that PR merges, which needs maintainer approval like any other PR. The 3-day rule applies to every later ADR PR. ADRs in that first PR that still need evidence are marked proposed.

Consequences

Positive

  • Each fork has one place that records what was chosen, what was rejected and why.
  • Reviewers can reject a PR by pointing at an accepted ADR, instead of arguing again.
  • The superseded chain shows how the design changed over time, which helps learners.

Negative

  • Each significant decision costs a short document and, for acceptance, a 3-day wait.
  • Until the cargo xtask adr tooling lands (#29, #21), the index and the format checks are manual, and reviewers have to check them.

Security impact

ADRs make security defaults (enforcement mode, failure behaviour, crypto, trust rules) explicit and reviewable. A PR that silently weakens a default can be rejected against a named ADR. The immutability rule stops an accepted security decision from being edited to mean something else without a visible superseding record. The required Security impact section means no architectural change can merge without its security effect being stated.

Links

  • Issue #20 (this process), epic #1.
  • Tooling: cargo xtask adr new|index|lint in #29, CI enforcement in #21, ADR table in the docs site in #27, PR template checklist in #28.
  • The tooling was delivered under #20 (xtask/src/adr.rs); cargo xtask adr lint runs in the runner-guard CI job (PROCESS.md).

Source: docs/adr/0001-record-architecture-decisions.md on GitHub.

0002. Enforcement strategy: OS-native policy first, optional own driver

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade's rules (#2) have to stop code before it runs. Windows has two built-in application control policy formats:

  • the OS-native code integrity policy (XML compiled to binary, with base and supplemental policies). It is enforced by the kernel for drivers, executables, DLLs, packaged apps, installers and scripts run by enlightened hosts; and
  • the OS-native legacy rule-collection policy (exe, dll, script, msi and packaged-app collections), enforced through the Application Identity service. It can target users and groups by SID.

Neither format can express every Palisade condition. The code integrity format has no notion of the user, the parent process or the command line. The alternative is Palisade's own kernel minifilter with process-creation callbacks (#8), which can see all of those, but which needs kernel code, driver signing and a careful boot story.

Some products enforce from user mode by terminating a process after it has started. The first execution still happens, so an assessment treats that approach as ineffective. Epic #8 (#113) already rules it out as a default.

Decision drivers

  1. Pre-execution blocking. Kill-after-start is not acceptable.
  2. Boot safety. A bad policy or driver must not leave a machine unbootable without a recovery path.
  3. Expressiveness: per-user rules, parent process, command line, file owner.
  4. Cost and feasibility for an open-source educational project: driver signing needs an EV certificate and attestation signing, and server SKUs need hardware certification (#112).
  5. Robustness against a local administrator, and survival when the Palisade agent is not running.

Considered options

  1. (a) OS-native only. Compile Palisade policy to both OS-native formats. The agent only collects audit events and inventory.
    • Pro: kernel-enforced and pre-execution, with no Palisade kernel code. It keeps enforcing when the agent is stopped or has crashed. Signed code integrity policies, with Secure Boot, resist removal by administrators. Recovery tooling for bad policies is built into the OS.
    • Con: no parent-process, command-line or owner-based conditions. Per-user rules only exist in the rule-collection format, which depends on a service. Format limits apply.
  2. (b) Own driver only. A Palisade minifilter decides on section creation, and process-creation callbacks decide on process start.
    • Pro: full expressiveness, one decision engine everywhere.
    • Con: a kernel bug can stop the machine. Production signing needs an EV certificate and attestation signing (client SKUs only without hardware certification). Nothing enforces when the driver is absent, unsigned or fails to load. That is the largest attack and failure surface.
  3. (c) Hybrid. OS-native compile for the baseline, plus the optional Palisade driver for the conditions the native formats cannot express (user, parent, command line, owner). A file must pass both layers.
    • Pro: the native layer gives a robust, boot-safe baseline that keeps working without the driver. The driver only adds restrictions on top.
    • Con: two compilers and two sets of events to keep consistent. Each rule needs a "requires driver" flag so that gaps are reported, not hidden.

Decision

Option (c), delivered in stages:

  • M2 default: (a) OS-native only. The enforcement_strategy is native_only. The OS-native compiler (#6) is the first enforcement path. The agent (#4) collects events and inventory and deploys the compiled policies.
  • When the driver exists (#8): layered becomes the recommended default. The native base expresses everything it can, and the driver enforces the rest. The two intersect. driver_only stays available for experiments but is not recommended.
  • Kill-after-start is never a default. It is only an opt-in post_start_terminate mode for endpoints with neither the driver nor native support, with a warning that it does not meet pre-execution requirements (#113).
  • Rules the active layers cannot enforce are reported per endpoint as "not enforced" (#81, #113). They are never silently dropped.

Consequences

Positive

  • Pre-execution enforcement is available from M2 without any Palisade kernel code.
  • Losing the driver degrades to the native column of the capability matrix, not to nothing.
  • The project can ship and test enforcement without a production driver signature. Driver work can proceed on test-signed lab VMs.

Negative

  • Until the driver ships, parent-process, command-line and owner-based rules can only audit (through ETW). The console must show this.
  • Per-user enforcement relies on the rule-collection format, which an administrator can disable by stopping its service. The tamper work in #220 has to account for that.
  • Two compilers (code integrity and rule-collection) plus the driver protocol must stay consistent. The compile report and golden tests in #6 carry that cost.

Security impact

This choice decides what an attacker has to defeat. With (a) and (c), stopping the Palisade agent does not stop enforcement, because the kernel keeps enforcing the native policy, and signed native policies on Secure Boot devices resist removal by an administrator (#85). With (c), the driver only adds restrictions, so a driver fault cannot widen what is allowed beyond the OS-native baseline. It can narrow the gap back to that baseline: a rule such as "allow this tool only when its parent is the installer" needs a native allow for the tool (the layers intersect), with the driver enforcing the parent condition. If the driver fails open (fail_safe, ADR 0012), that rule degrades to the broader native allow. The compile report (#81) marks every such rule as requires_driver and names the broader native allow it falls back to, so the risk is visible and can be removed with fail_secure. The residual risks are the conditions only the driver can enforce (open until #8 ships) and the service dependency of the rule-collection format. Both are recorded in the threat model (#219). Rejecting kill-after-start removes a false sense of protection.

Links

  • Issue #20. Epics #4, #6, #8. Issues #81, #85, #112, #113, #219, #220.
  • Failure behaviour of each layer: ADR 0012, superseded by ADR 0018.

Source: docs/adr/0002-enforcement-strategy.md on GitHub.

0003. Crate boundaries and dependency direction

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade has a portable decision engine, a privileged Windows endpoint, a management server and tooling. If they mix, a privileged service ends up linking a web framework, Windows-only code leaks into logic that should be testable anywhere, and the trusted computing base grows. Issue #19 defines the workspace layout. This ADR records it as a decision, together with the rule for which crate may depend on which, and settles the open question #19 left for this ADR: whether palisade-fileid should be split.

Decision drivers

  • The evaluation core (palisade-policy) stays small, deterministic and portable, so it can be unit-tested and fuzzed on any OS.
  • All Windows FFI lives in a few named places.
  • The agent never links server-side stacks.
  • The kernel driver can share types without pulling in std.
  • Rules can be checked mechanically from cargo metadata.

Considered options

  1. One large crate with feature flags. Simple to start, but features leak, and the dependency rules cannot be checked.
  2. Many fine-grained crates. Strong isolation, but heavy to maintain for one maintainer.
  3. The ten #19 crates plus xtask, in strict layers. Matches the component boundaries (core types, file identity, policy, wire protocol, and one crate per binary).

For palisade-fileid:

  • Split into palisade-fileid (pure) and palisade-fileid-win (OS trust APIs). This gives a clean crate boundary, but an eleventh crate and a more complex graph.
  • Keep one crate with a win module gated by #[cfg(all(windows, feature = "os-trust"))], where the feature is off by default. Fewer crates. The cfg and feature gate keep Windows dependencies out of every crate that does not opt in.

Decision

Option 3. The workspace has exactly these members:

CrateRole
palisade-coreShared types (IDs, hashes, timestamps, errors, Decision, Mode). No I/O. no_std with alloc, and std behind a feature.
palisade-fileidPE parsing, hashing, signatures, certificate chains, version metadata (#3).
palisade-policyPolicy model, conditions, precedence, evaluation, decision trace (#2). Pure and deterministic.
palisade-protoAgent-server wire types, event schema, schema versioning.
palisade-agentWindows service: ETW and code integrity collection, policy cache, enforcement glue (#4).
palisade-trayPer-session user notifier and request UI.
palisade-serverManagement server (#10).
palisade-consoleWeb console frontend and asset embedding.
palisade-cliThe pal binary (#15).
palisade-driverOptional kernel minifilter (#8). Built separately and excluded from default-members.
xtaskBuild and automation commands (#29).

Dependency direction. In A ← B, B may depend on A:

  • core ← fileid ← policy ← proto ← {agent, server, cli, tray}
  • A crate may depend on any crate to its left, never on one to its right. The four crates in braces are siblings and never depend on each other (in particular, agent never depends on server). They talk over IPC or the network using proto types.
  • console may depend only on proto (generated types).
  • Among workspace crates, driver may depend only on core, built no_std.
  • agent never depends on server, axum, sqlx or any HTTP server stack.
  • policy never depends on tokio, reqwest, windows or windows-sys.
  • No product crate depends on xtask.

These rules are enforced by cargo xtask check-deps (#19) for edges inside the workspace, and by cargo-deny bans (#23) for third-party crates. A ban such as "policy never depends on windows" applies to the crate's own resolved graph: its declared dependencies and the features it enables on them, for every supported target, as cargo tree -p palisade-policy --target <t> reports. Cargo's feature unification in a combined workspace build can compile extra code into a shared dependency. That does not count as a dependency of policy, and it cannot be relied on: CI also builds and tests each portable crate on its own (-p), where unified features are absent.

palisade-fileid stays one crate. The OS trust API backend (signature verification and catalog lookups) lives in a module palisade_fileid::win that is compiled only when both the target is Windows and the off-by-default Cargo feature os-trust is enabled (#[cfg(all(windows, feature = "os-trust"))]). The windows dependency is optional and is enabled only by that feature. The pure-Rust parser is always built and is what every other consumer uses.

  • Only palisade-agent enables os-trust, for cross-checking its pure-Rust results against the OS (#3). palisade-cli may enable it for local diagnostics on Windows.
  • palisade-policy, palisade-proto and palisade-server never enable it, so their own graphs contain no windows crate on any target, and policy code cannot call fileid::win (it does not compile when policy is built on its own).
  • The feature is additive: enabling it adds cross-check results, and never changes what the pure-Rust parser reports or how policy decides. It joins the feature flags listed in #19 and follows the same conventions (documented in the crate README, covered by cargo hack --each-feature). This keeps the crate list as #19 defines it, and matches the unsafe allowlist in ADR 0011. A split is reconsidered, through a superseding ADR, if the win module's dependencies start reaching non-Windows builds or the module grows its own release cadence.

Consequences

Positive

  • palisade-policy and its dependencies build and test on Linux and other desktop OS, and can be fuzzed there.
  • The privileged agent's dependency tree has no web server stack, which keeps it smaller.
  • Violations fail CI mechanically. They are not left to reviewer memory.

Negative

  • Sharing code between sibling binaries means moving it down a layer (usually into proto or core). Sometimes that feels heavier than a direct dependency.
  • palisade-fileid carries Windows-only code behind a cfg and feature gate, so bugs in that module are only caught by a Windows CI job that enables os-trust.

Security impact

The layering keeps the trusted computing base small. The code that decides "may this run" (policy, plus the pure-Rust parts of fileid and core that it uses) has no network or OS-specific dependencies in its own graph, so it can be audited and fuzzed in isolation. The only OS trust code in fileid is opt-in, compiled only for the agent (and optionally the CLI) on Windows, and is one of the allowlisted unsafe modules in ADR 0011. Banning server stacks from the agent removes a whole class of remotely reachable code from the privileged endpoint service. The no_std core lets the kernel driver share decision types without duplicating them, which avoids drift between user mode and kernel mode decision encodings.

Links

  • Issues #19 (workspace), #20, #23 (cargo-deny bans), #29 (xtask).
  • Unsafe allowlist: ADR 0011.

Source: docs/adr/0003-crate-boundaries-and-dependency-direction.md on GitHub.

0004. Default rule precedence model

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

A file often matches more than one rule: a publisher allow and a path deny, or a hash allow inside a blocked folder. The precedence model decides which rule wins. Products in this space use incompatible models, and a policy written for one model can mean the opposite under another:

  • Deny-wins. Explicit deny beats explicit allow, and anything unmatched is implicitly denied. This is how the OS-native formats work.
  • Allow-wins. Any matching allow beats any deny. Some products also let a more specific item beat a less specific one within a rule.
  • Specificity ladder. A fixed ranking such as hash, then signer with file and version, then publisher, then path, with deny and allow alternating at each level.
  • First-match ordered. Rules are numbered, the first match decides, and a catch-all sits at the bottom, as in a firewall.

Every model in practice also needs blocklists (recommended block rules, the vulnerable driver blocklist) that override every kind of trust, including temporary overrides. Issue #35 specifies the full evaluation pipeline. This ADR fixes the default and the safety rules every model must keep.

Decision drivers

  1. Safety by default: a mistaken allow must not defeat a deliberate deny.
  2. Compatibility with the OS-native compile target (#6), so a policy means the same thing in both enforcement layers (ADR 0002).
  3. Predictability: the result must not depend on rule order unless the model says it does.
  4. Migration: people bring policies written for other models.
  5. Essential Eight: recommended blocklists must override allow rules (ISM-1544, ISM-1659).

Considered options

  1. Deny-wins (explicit deny > explicit allow > implicit deny). Order-independent and safe by default, and it compiles directly to the OS-native formats. A broad deny can hide a narrow allow. Exceptions have to be written as exceptions on the deny rule.
  2. Allow-wins. Convenient for permissive environments, but one over-broad allow defeats every deny. That is unsafe as a default, and it does not map to the native formats.
  3. Specificity ladder. Intuitive ("the more exact rule wins"), but the tier of a multi-condition rule needs a definition, and native compilation needs extra work.
  4. First-match ordered. Very explicit, but order-dependent. Inserting one rule can change decisions far away, and it does not compile cleanly to the unordered native formats.

Decision

  1. Deny-wins is the default precedence_model for every new policy.
  2. The other models are selectable per policy: allow_wins, specificity, first_match and priority, as specified in #35. Selecting allow_wins produces a validation warning that it is not recommended for Essential Eight.
  3. Fixed safety tiers apply under every model. The model only decides among ordinary rules. It never touches:
    • the mandatory-deny tier (recommended block rules, the vulnerable driver blocklist and tenant "never run" lists), which is evaluated first and blocks regardless of any allow, trust source, exception, offline override, override session, elevation or exclusion. Only a rule-specific, scoped, expiring mandatory_exception (#35) can override it; and
    • the implicit deny for unmatched files in enforce mode (#39).

Consequences

Positive

  • The default matches the OS-native formats, so the native compiler (#6) does not need to reorder or rewrite rules for default policies.
  • Decisions under the default do not depend on rule order, which property tests can check (#2).
  • Blocklists cannot be bypassed through override codes or self-service, which removes a whole class of support-desk social engineering.

Negative

  • Five models means five code paths to test, and the decision trace must name the model used.
  • Policies using a non-default model may not compile one-to-one to native formats. The compile report has to flag rules whose meaning changes (#81).
  • People used to allow-wins need to rewrite "allow this file in a denied folder" as an exception on the deny.

Security impact

Deny-wins fails towards blocking. A mistaken or malicious broad allow rule cannot undo a specific deny, which limits the damage from a compromised policy author or a typo. The non-overridable mandatory-deny tier means known bypass binaries and vulnerable drivers stay blocked even during an override session, which is when an attacker with a stolen override code would try to use them. Allowing other models per policy reintroduces risk, so validation warns, and the policy's model is recorded in every decision trace (#41) for audit.

Links

  • Issues #20, #35 (precedence pipeline), #39 (unknown applications), #41 (decision trace), #81 (compile report). Epic #2.

Source: docs/adr/0004-default-rule-precedence-model.md on GitHub.

0005. Agent-server protocol

  • Status: superseded by 0015
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

The agent (#4) talks to the server (#10) to check in, fetch policy and deltas, upload events and inventory, and receive near-real-time nudges such as "policy available" or "rapid check-in". Agents often sit behind corporate proxies, some of which break HTTP/2 or inspect TLS. All agent-server traffic must use mutual TLS with a device certificate (#223). The wire types live in palisade-proto (ADR 0003).

Decision drivers

  1. Mutual TLS with a device key that never leaves its key store (#223).
  2. Works through restrictive proxies, including ones that break HTTP/2.
  3. Efficient, diff-based policy delivery and batched event upload.
  4. Offline queueing and replay, which happen on the agent whatever the transport.
  5. Generated, typed clients for the agent, the CLI and the console.
  6. A small, auditable dependency set in the privileged agent.

Considered options

  1. gRPC over HTTP/2 (tonic). Typed services from protobuf, server streaming for push, compact binary framing, and mTLS through rustls. Some proxies break HTTP/2 or gRPC trailers. Browsers need a separate API (the console uses REST, #15).
  2. HTTPS with JSON or CBOR, plus long-poll or WebSocket for push. Works through almost any proxy and is easy to debug. But it is hand-written or OpenAPI-generated, has no service-level schema shared with the agent, and long-poll adds latency and server load.
  3. MQTT over TLS. Good for push to many devices, but it needs a broker. Request/response and bulk transfer fit it poorly, and topic ACLs become a second authorisation system.

Decision

Option 1, gRPC over HTTP/2 with tonic and rustls, as the primary transport, plus an HTTPS + JSON fallback for check-in:

  • palisade-proto defines the AgentService RPCs listed in #62. The server push channel (StreamPush) only carries nudges, never payloads. The agent then pulls through the normal RPCs.
  • The fallback is used after 3 consecutive gRPC handshake failures. It carries the same protobuf messages, encoded as JSON (the standard protobuf JSON mapping), over HTTP/1.1. It covers check-in, policy fetch and event upload. Push falls back to polling at the check-in interval.
  • Both paths use the same mTLS identity, the same server pinning, and the same signed payloads. Policy bundles and commands are signed end to end (ADR 0008), so their trust never depends on which transport delivered them.
  • The console and external integrations use the REST API (#15). That is a separate surface, not an agent transport.

Consequences

Positive

  • One schema (.proto) generates the agent, server and CLI types, and schema changes are reviewable in one place.
  • Server streaming gives near-real-time nudges without a broker.
  • The JSON fallback keeps agents manageable behind proxies that break HTTP/2.

Negative

  • Two encodings of the same messages must stay in step. Contract tests are needed for both.
  • tonic and hyper add to the agent's dependency tree. That is accepted, but they are reviewed under the supply-chain policy (#23).
  • TLS-inspecting proxies break mTLS by design. The docs must say the agent endpoints need an inspection bypass (#62). Palisade never disables verification to work around this.

Security impact

mTLS with a non-exportable device key authenticates every agent, and server pinning defeats interception, including by an inspecting proxy that presents its own CA. The fallback is not a downgrade: it uses the same TLS and identity requirements, and the selection logic must never fall back to plaintext or to unauthenticated TLS. Push messages carry no payloads, so a compromised or spoofed push channel can at worst cause extra check-ins. Message parsers in palisade-proto handle data from the network and are fuzz targets (#230).

Links

  • Issues #20, #62 (check-in and transport), #223 (enrolment and mTLS), #15 (REST API), #23 (supply chain), #230 (fuzzing). Epics #4, #10, #18.
  • Superseded by ADR 0015.

Source: docs/adr/0005-agent-server-protocol.md on GitHub.

0006. Server database and tenant isolation

  • Status: superseded by 0016
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

palisade-server (#10) stores tenants, groups, policies and their version history, approvals, RBAC, inventory and a large volume of execution events. The Essential Eight logging controls expect allowed and blocked events to stay searchable for at least 12 months and to be protected from modification. The server is multi-tenant (#128), so one tenant must never read or write another tenant's rows, whether through the API, the console or the query language. Issue #127 holds the detailed schema work.

Decision drivers

  1. Tenant isolation that holds even when application code has a bug.
  2. Relational integrity across policies, rules, groups, approvals and their history.
  3. Query safety: SQL checked at build time, no string-built queries.
  4. Forward-only, reviewable migrations that run automatically and idempotently.
  5. Event volume: time-partitioned tables with retention.
  6. One database a learner can run locally or in a container.

Considered options

Database and access layer:

  1. Postgres with sqlx (async, compile-time checked queries through query!/query_as!, with offline metadata for CI). Mature row-level security, partitioning and JSON support.
  2. Postgres with a full ORM. Less SQL to write, but the generated SQL is harder to review, and RLS and partitioning still need raw SQL.
  3. An embedded or document store. Simple to deploy, but no row-level security, weak relational integrity, and poor fit for 12-month searchable event retention.

Multi-tenancy:

  1. Shared schema, tenant_id on every row, enforced by Postgres row-level security (RLS). One schema to migrate. Isolation is enforced by the database for every query.
  2. Schema per tenant. Strong separation, but migrations run once per tenant, cross-tenant features (the tenant tree, global groups) need dynamic SQL, and the catalogue grows with the tenant count.
  3. Database per tenant. Strongest separation, but the most operational cost, and it rules out the shared tenant tree in #128.
  4. Application-only filtering (WHERE tenant_id = $1 in code). Cheapest, but one missed filter leaks data.

Decision

  • Postgres 16 or later, through sqlx, with compile-time checked queries. The SQLX_OFFLINE query metadata is committed so CI builds without a live database (#127).
  • Migrations use sqlx::migrate!, embedded in the binary, numbered and forward-only, with expand/contract for schema changes. A migration checksum mismatch is a hard error, and the server refuses to start against a schema newer than itself.
  • Tenancy is a shared schema with row-level tenant_id plus RLS.
    • Every tenant-owned table has tenant_id uuid not null and an RLS policy keyed on a per-transaction setting that the server sets from the caller's resolved scope.
    • Tenant tables use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so the policies apply even to the table owner. The policy expression fails closed: when the tenant setting is unset or empty, no rows match.
    • The server connects as a non-owner role with NOBYPASSRLS. Migrations run as a separate owner role.
    • Foreign keys include tenant_id, so a row can never reference another tenant's row.
    • Shared rows (built-in permissions, seeded content) belong to a root tenant and are exposed through explicit read-only policies.
  • High-volume event tables are partitioned by month (#127).

Consequences

Positive

  • Isolation does not depend on every query remembering a filter. A bug in the application layer still cannot cross tenants.
  • Query typos and type mismatches fail at build time.
  • One schema and one migration stream, whatever the tenant count.

Negative

  • RLS adds a per-query cost and makes query plans harder to read. Indexes must lead with tenant_id.
  • Building with compile-time checks needs either a database or up-to-date offline metadata. Stale metadata fails CI until it is regenerated.
  • Each connection must set the tenant scope at the start of every transaction. Pooling code has to make that impossible to forget (#127).

Security impact

RLS moves tenant isolation from application code into the database, so an injection or authorisation bug in one handler cannot read another tenant's policies, events or approval history. NOBYPASSRLS on the application role means a compromised server process cannot simply turn RLS off. The owner role used for migrations is a separate secret (#227). Compile-time checked, parameterised queries remove string-built SQL as an injection vector. Event tables are the evidence trail for ISM-1660, so their append-only protection and retention live in #127 and #229.

Links
