  • Issues #20, #127 (schema, migrations, isolation), #128 (multi-tenancy), #227 (secrets), #229 (server hardening). Epic #10.
  • Superseded by ADR 0016.

Source: docs/adr/0006-server-database.md on GitHub.

0007. Agent local store

  • Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

The agent keeps three kinds of local state:

  1. The policy cache: the current signed policy bundle, the previous one (last-known-good) and the anti-rollback record (#61, #225). The bundle bytes and their canonical encoding are defined by #43, and signing and encryption at rest by #225.
  2. The event queue: events buffered while offline, then replayed in order, with a size cap and back-pressure (#63). Thirty days offline must survive restarts (#4).
  3. The hash cache: file identity keyed by file ID and change stamp, so a cached lookup takes under 50 µs (#3, #46).

All three must survive power loss, resist tampering by non-SYSTEM users (#220), and support encryption at rest. Issue #20 lists the candidates: a signed, memory-mappable, versioned policy cache file, plus SQLite (through rusqlite) or an embedded pure-Rust key-value store (redb or sled) for the queue and the hash cache.

Decision drivers

  1. Crash safety: no torn writes, and no lost acknowledged events after power loss.
  2. Tamper evidence: changes made outside the agent are detected (#220, #225).
  3. Encryption at rest for the policy cache, and optionally for the event queue.
  4. Throughput and latency within the agent's resource budget (#65).
  5. Dependency footprint and auditability: C code, unsafe, maintenance status.
  6. Builds for x64 and ARM64 Windows with the GitHub-hosted toolchain.

Considered options

Policy cache:

  1. Signed file, memory-mapped in place. Zero-copy loading. But a mapping reflects later changes to the file. If anything with write access changes it after verification, the agent evaluates bytes it never verified (a time-of-check to time-of-use gap). It also does not fit AES-GCM encryption at rest (#225), which needs a decrypted copy anyway.
  2. Signed file, read whole into private memory, then verified, then parsed. One copy per activation (bundles are capped at 64 MiB by #225). What is evaluated is exactly what was verified.
  3. Policy rows in the embedded database. One store for everything, but a signature over a database is awkward, and atomic swap of a whole policy becomes a transaction design problem.

Event queue and hash cache:

  1. SQLite through rusqlite (bundled). Decades of crash-safety testing, WAL mode, and an easy query surface for diagnostics. Brings a large C library into the privileged service, and encryption needs an extension or application-level encryption.
  2. redb. Pure Rust, ACID with copy-on-write B-trees, a small API. Younger, and its power-loss behaviour on Windows has not been verified for this project.
  3. sled. Pure Rust, but it has stayed in beta for years with an unstable on-disk format. Rejected.

Decision

Policy cache: option 2, decided. The policy cache is a set of files (active, previous, pending) under the agent's SYSTEM-only store directory. Each holds one signed envelope from #225. The agent reads a file whole into private memory, verifies its signature before parsing anything beyond the envelope, and only then decodes it. Memory mapping is not used.

The anti-rollback record (#225) is kept separately from the cache files, but it is ordered against them. It holds two values:

  • the floor: the highest bundle version the agent has made active. The rule is that the floor never exceeds the version of the bundle in active, so a crash can never leave every bundle on disk below the floor;
  • the fallback: the version of the bundle in previous that the current active directly replaced, or none. Only that bundle may be loaded under the one-step N-1 exception of ADR 0018. This keeps the exception to one step even when active was already corrupt at the last activation. For example, if active (10) was corrupt when 11 arrived, previous still holds 9, and the fallback is none, so a later failure of 11 leads to the emergency policy, not to 9.

Activation follows #61, in this order:

  1. Write pending, flush, and verify it. Its version must be at or above the floor. If active is loadable (its signature verifies and its version is at or above the floor, the same test as at startup), the version must also be above active's version. Otherwise reject it and keep what is loaded (PolicyRejected). So while the agent runs previous (N-1) or the emergency policy because active (N) failed, a re-fetched copy of N is accepted, as ADR 0018 requires.
  2. If active is loadable, copy it to previous (written to a temporary file, flushed, then renamed). If active is missing, fails verification or is below the floor, leave previous untouched, so a verified last-known-good bundle is never overwritten by a bad or stale one.
  3. Set the fallback to none in every copy of the record, so that no crash from here on can leave a fallback that points at a bundle the new active did not replace.
  4. Atomically rename pending over active, with write-through, so the rename is durable before the next step.
  5. Only then, in one write per copy of the record (#225), raise the floor to the new version and set the fallback to the version copied in step 2, or leave it none if step 2 copied nothing.

A power loss before step 4 leaves the old active in place with the old floor. A power loss between steps 4 and 5 leaves the new bundle in active with a floor below it. At every point a verified active exists that the floor accepts, so a power loss mid-swap never leaves the agent without its current policy. An interrupted activation can only leave the fallback at none, which removes the N-1 exception until the next activation; it never widens it.

At startup the agent:

  • deletes any leftover pending. It was never activated, and the agent fetches it again;
  • reads the floor as the highest value among the record's intact copies;
  • reads the fallback as none unless every intact copy records the same fallback;
  • loads active if it verifies and its version is at or above the floor, then raises the floor to that version if it is lower, leaving the fallback at none (completing an interrupted step 5). If the record's copies are all intact and differ only because step 3 or step 5 updated some of them and not others, and the highest floor equals the verified active version, the agent writes the reconciled values to every copy and does not raise tamper.policy.rollback_suspected. Any other mismatch, and any missing or corrupt copy once a bundle has been activated, raises it (#225) and is not treated as an interrupted activation;
  • otherwise follows the failure rows of ADR 0018: previous may load below the floor only if it verifies and its version equals the recorded fallback (the one-step N-1 exception);
  • if no bundle on disk can load, even with that exception (for example, both files were replaced with older, validly signed bundles), treats that as both bundles failing: it loads the built-in emergency policy, raises tamper.policy.rollback_suspected, and starts a rapid check-in. It never lowers the floor to make an old bundle load.

Event queue and hash cache: proposed, leaning to redb, pending a spike. The lean is redb, because it keeps C code out of the privileged service and keeps the dependency tree pure Rust. It becomes accepted (or is replaced by SQLite through a revised proposal) once a spike on the Windows VM harness (#26) shows:

  • Crash safety: at least 1,000 forced power-offs or process kills during sustained writes, with no corruption and no loss of committed records;
  • Throughput: the #63 event rate and the #46 hash cache lookup target within the #65 CPU and memory budgets, on x64 and ARM64;
  • Size and maintenance: added binary size, unsafe count, licence and maintenance status, checked against the #23 dependency admission policy;
  • Encryption: a working design for encrypting records with a DPAPI-wrapped data key (#225), with the measured overhead.

The same spike runs against SQLite as the control. Either store keeps only data that can be rebuilt or that is already integrity-protected: the hash cache can be recomputed, and queued events carry their own hash chain (#220).

Consequences

Positive

  • Policy loading has no time-of-check to time-of-use gap, and works the same with or without encryption at rest.
  • The store decision is made on measured crash behaviour, not on reputation.

Negative

  • Reading the whole bundle costs a copy and up to 64 MiB of peak memory during activation, which #65 must budget for.
  • #60, #63 and #46 start against a storage trait until this ADR is accepted, so the backend can be swapped.

Security impact

Verify-then-parse on a private copy means a bundle that changes on disk after verification can never reach the evaluator. That closes a policy substitution route for anyone who can write to the cache directory. Raising the anti-rollback floor only after the rename means a power loss cannot leave the agent with no bundle it may load, and a floor that rejects every bundle on disk leads to the stricter emergency policy, never to a lowered floor. The store directory is SYSTEM-only (#220), and the policy cache is authenticated by signature, not by file permissions alone. The event queue and the hash cache are not trusted inputs to a decision without verification: a tampered hash cache entry must not turn a deny into an allow. Binding entries to file ID and change stamp only detects that the file changed; it does not protect the cache store. So each hash cache record is also authenticated with an agent-held key (HMAC-SHA-256 over volume ID, file ID, change stamp and hashes, ADR 0017), and a record that fails is discarded and the file re-hashed (#46). The spike measures the cost of that MAC. The choice of store also changes how much C code runs in the privileged service, which is why it is part of the spike criteria.

Links

  • Issues #20, #43 (bundle encoding), #46 (hash cache), #60, #61 (policy cache), #63 (event pipeline), #65 (budgets), #220 (tamper), #225 (signing and encryption), #26 (VM harness), #23 (dependency policy). Epics #4, #18.
  • ADR 0018 (failure behaviour when bundles fail to load).

Source: docs/adr/0007-agent-local-store.md on GitHub.

0008. Cryptographic algorithms and libraries

  • Status: superseded by 0017
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade uses cryptography in five places:

  1. File identity: hashes that rules match on (#3, #46, #47).
  2. Palisade's own signatures: policy bundles (#225), server commands (#62) and trust-set updates (#224).
  3. OS-defined signatures: Authenticode on Palisade's releases (#24, #226) and signed OS-native code integrity policies (#85). Their formats are fixed by the OS.
  4. Transport: mutual TLS between agent, relays and server (#223).
  5. At rest and short secrets: the encrypted policy cache (#225), the driver boot cache MAC (#113) and offline override codes (#222).

The project aims to align with the Australian Government ISM cryptography guidance (ASD-approved algorithms), which favours ECDSA with P-384, RSA of at least 3072 bits, SHA-2 and AES-GCM. Issue #20's summary suggests Ed25519 for bundle signing, while #225 specifies ECDSA P-384 as the default with Ed25519 as an option, and #61 mentions Ed25519 or P-256. This ADR settles that.

Decision drivers

  1. Collision-resistant identities: no allow decision may rest on a broken hash.
  2. Alignment with ASD-approved algorithms, since Essential Eight and the ISM frame the project.
  3. Exact compatibility with what the OS computes and requires (#3, #6).
  4. Algorithm agility, so a key or algorithm can be rotated without a format break (#224).
  5. A small number of well-reviewed libraries, with builds for x64 and ARM64 Windows and Linux.
  6. A path to a FIPS-validated module later, without a rewrite.

Considered options

Bundle and command signatures:

  1. Ed25519 only. Fast, deterministic, small keys, hard to misuse. Not on the ASD-approved list, so an ISM-aligned deployment could not use it.
  2. ECDSA P-384 with SHA-384 only. ASD-approved. Slower, and it needs a careful library because naive ECDSA nonce handling is dangerous.
  3. Algorithm-agile envelope supporting both, with ECDSA P-384 as the default. Each signature names its key ID and algorithm. The agent accepts only algorithms in its trust set.

Libraries:

  1. ring for signatures, AEAD and HMAC, and as the rustls crypto provider. Small API surface designed against misuse, with nonce generation handled inside the library. Builds with only a C compiler (no CMake or separate assembler). No FIPS-validated build.
  2. A FIPS-capable rustls provider. Offers a validated mode, but needs a heavier native build (CMake, and extra build tools for the validated mode) on Windows runners. Validated mode is not needed yet.
  3. Pure-Rust RustCrypto crates for everything. No C or assembly, but no single provider for rustls, and a wider set of crates to review.

Decision

Hashing (file identity)

  • SHA-256 is the primary identity. Every stored or exchanged file identity carries it.
  • SHA-1 and MD5 are compatibility-only: they are computed so Palisade can match what the OS and imported policies use, and to join with OS events. They are never the sole basis of an allow. Policy validation (#40) rejects an allow rule whose only identity is SHA-1 or MD5. A deny rule may use them, because a collision there can only cause an extra block.
  • The OS-native compiler emits whatever hash forms the target OS build requires (#81). That can include SHA-1 Authenticode values alongside SHA-256, never instead of it.
  • SHA-384 and SHA-512 are optional extras (#46).
  • Implementation: the RustCrypto sha2 crate (with sha1 and md-5 for compatibility hashes), because they are pure Rust, no_std capable and support streaming. The single-pass multi-hash design is in #46.

Palisade-native signatures (bundles, commands, trust-set updates)

  • Option 3: an algorithm-agile envelope ({kid, alg, sig} entries, #225).
  • Algorithms: ecdsa-p384-sha384 (default) and ed25519 (opt-in per tenant). Nothing else. The agent accepts only algorithms listed in its trust set, and the trust set is itself signed (#224).
  • Every signature covers a domain-separation prefix plus the canonical bytes (#43, #225), so a signature for one purpose cannot be replayed as another.

OS-defined signatures

  • Authenticode on releases and signed OS-native policies use RSA 3072-bit or larger with SHA-256, and RFC 3161 timestamps for releases. The OS fixes these formats, and Palisade only chooses the key size and digest.

Transport

  • TLS through rustls, TLS 1.3 preferred and TLS 1.2 allowed only with the restricted AEAD cipher suites in #223. Certificate verification is never disabled, in any build.

Symmetric

  • AES-256-GCM for data at rest (#225). HMAC-SHA-256 for MACs (the driver boot cache, #113) and for one-time override codes (#222).

Libraries

  • ring provides signatures, AES-GCM, HMAC and the rustls crypto provider. It replaces the wider candidate crate list in #225. Access goes through a thin crypto module, so call sites never use ring directly. This covers user-mode crates only. ring cannot link into the no_std kernel driver, so palisade-driver verifies the boot cache MAC with the kernel's own cryptography API or no_std RustCrypto crates (hmac, sha2). That choice is made in #113, using the same algorithm (HMAC-SHA-256) and the same test vectors.
  • FIPS (future work). A FIPS-validated provider can be swapped in later through rustls's provider interface and the same crypto module. Adopting one needs a superseding ADR, which must also decide whether file-identity hashing (done by sha2, outside the provider) is in FIPS scope. Palisade makes no FIPS claim until then (#18 lists certification as out of scope).

Consequences

Positive

  • No allow decision rests on SHA-1 or MD5.
  • ISM-aligned defaults, with Ed25519 available where alignment is not needed.
  • Algorithm agility means key and algorithm rotation are data changes, not format changes.
  • One provider for TLS and signatures keeps the reviewed crypto surface small.

Negative

  • P-384 verification is slower than Ed25519. Bundles are verified on activation and every 15 minutes (#225), not per decision, so the cost is acceptable.
  • Two signature algorithms means two sets of known-answer test vectors on every platform (#225).
  • Imported policies (#15) whose allow rules carry only a SHA-1 or MD5 hash cannot be imported as-is. The importer must resolve them to SHA-256 from inventory or a supplied file, or report them as rejected.
  • ring has no FIPS-validated mode, so a FIPS deployment needs the future provider swap.

Security impact

This ADR sets the strength of every trust decision Palisade makes. Banning weak hashes as the sole basis of allow rules closes collision-based bypasses in Palisade's own evaluation, where an attacker builds a malicious file with the same SHA-1 or MD5 as an allowed one. The native layer is limited by what the target OS build checks: where an older build only matches SHA-1 Authenticode values, the compile report (#81) flags the rule so the weakness is visible. Algorithm lists in a signed trust set prevent algorithm downgrade, and domain separation prevents cross-protocol signature reuse. Keeping verification always on in TLS means a misconfigured proxy fails closed rather than silently exposing traffic. A flaw in ring would affect TLS and signatures at once, so it is tracked under the supply-chain advisory scan (#23).

Links

  • Issues #20, #3, #43, #46, #47, #62, #81, #85, #113, #222, #223, #224, #225, #226. Epic #18.
  • Superseded by ADR 0017.

Source: docs/adr/0008-cryptographic-algorithms.md on GitHub.

0009. Async runtime and concurrency model

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

The agent, server and CLI all do network I/O, timers and concurrent tasks. The policy engine (#2) sits on the process-creation and image-load path, with a p99 budget under 200 µs for a cached-identity request (#61) and deterministic output (#2). Mixing async runtimes in one binary causes subtle bugs, and an enforcement decision that waits on the network turns a slow server into a hung machine.

Issue #20 requires that the agent's enforcement hot path never awaits the network. Issue #61's "lazy approval lookup" asks the server for a decision with a 2 s timeout when the local result is deny or indeterminate. Read literally, that would hold a verdict for up to 2 s. This ADR settles how the two fit together.

Decision drivers

  1. Enforcement latency and determinism: decisions must be fast, bounded and reproducible.
  2. A decision must never depend on network availability.
  3. One runtime ecosystem, compatible with the chosen protocol and server stacks (ADR 0005, ADR 0006).
  4. Testability: the engine runs in plain unit and property tests and in fuzzers without a runtime.

Considered options

  1. tokio everywhere, including the policy engine (an async evaluate). Uniform, but it forces a runtime into fuzzers and the driver-facing path, and invites awaiting I/O inside a decision.
  2. tokio for I/O-bound binaries, a synchronous policy engine. The engine is a pure function over its inputs. Callers decide how to schedule it.
  3. A smaller or different runtime, or plain threads for the agent. Fewer dependencies, but tonic, axum and sqlx all assume tokio. Running two runtimes, or bridging between them, costs more than it saves.

Decision

Option 2.

  • tokio (multi-threaded runtime) is the only async runtime in palisade-agent, palisade-server and palisade-cli. No other runtime is added to those crates.
  • palisade-policy is synchronous and deterministic. It does no I/O and reads no clock and no randomness itself. Time and other context arrive as inputs (the Clock trait in palisade-core::platform, specified by #29). It does not depend on tokio (ADR 0003). palisade-core and palisade-fileid are synchronous too.
  • The enforcement hot path never awaits the network. In the agent, decision requests (from the driver, from ETW handling, from script hosts) run synchronously against the in-memory evaluator on dedicated threads, or through spawn_blocking where they start in async code. Policy swaps are lock-free reads (ArcSwap, #61).
  • Server lookups are asynchronous follow-ups, never part of the verdict. When #61's "lazy approval lookup" applies (the 2 s timeout bounds the background request, not the verdict), the agent returns the local verdict immediately and sends the lookup in the background. If the server has an approval, it lands in the local cache and the next attempt is allowed. A verdict is never delayed waiting for the server. Lookups are de-duplicated by file identity and rate-limited, so a loop of denied executions cannot flood the server or exhaust the agent's connections.
  • Heavy file identity work (hashing a large file) runs on a bounded blocking pool and is cancellable. The CPU and I/O budgets are in #65.

Consequences

Positive

  • The engine can be property-tested, benchmarked and fuzzed with no runtime.
  • Server outages and slow links cannot stall process creation.
  • One runtime keeps the dependency tree and the mental model small.

Negative

  • A user whose file is approved on the server sees one block before the approval reaches the device. The tray message must say "approved, run it again" (#11).
  • Callers must remember to move evaluation off async worker threads. The agent wraps this in a single entry point, so the rule is applied in one place.

Security impact

Keeping decisions off the network removes a denial-of-service lever: an attacker who blocks or slows the server cannot hang endpoints or force a timeout path. It also removes a bypass lever: no verdict depends on a reply an attacker might be able to delay, spoof or race. A synchronous, I/O-free engine with injected time is deterministic, so a decision can be replayed exactly from its inputs for audit (#41), and fuzzing covers the code that makes decisions.

Links

  • Issues #20, #29 (developer environment and platform traits, including Clock), #41 (decision trace), #42 (performance budget), #56 (service host), #61 (policy cache and lazy lookup), #65 (budgets). Epics #2, #4.
  • ADR 0015 supersedes ADR 0005, and ADR 0016 supersedes ADR 0006.

Source: docs/adr/0009-async-runtime-and-concurrency.md on GitHub.

0010. Licence

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade is a public, educational Rust project. The repository already contains LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE. The licence decides who can reuse the code and on what terms, which third-party code can be pulled in, and whether kernel sample code can be reused in the driver (#8). Licence work in #28 (DCO, file headers, third-party notices) and #23 (the dependency licence allowlist) depends on this decision.

Decision drivers

  1. Maximum reuse for learners and other projects, which is the point of an educational project.
  2. Compatibility with the Rust ecosystem, where most crates are MIT or Apache-2.0.
  3. An explicit patent grant for contributors and users.
  4. No obligations that a learner reusing a small part would trip over.

Considered options

  1. MIT only. Simple and permissive, but no explicit patent grant.
  2. Apache-2.0 only. Patent grant and contributor terms, but incompatible with GPLv2-only projects that might want to reuse the code.
  3. Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual). The Rust ecosystem convention. Users pick either, so they get the patent grant when they want it and GPLv2 compatibility when they need it.
  4. A copyleft licence (GPL or MPL). Keeps derivatives open, but limits reuse, and mixing it with permissive crates complicates the release licence notices.

Decision

Option 3. Palisade is licensed under Apache-2.0 OR MIT.

  • Every crate declares license = "Apache-2.0 OR MIT", inherited from [workspace.package] (#19).
  • Contributions are accepted under the same dual licence (inbound = outbound). Whether that is confirmed by DCO sign-off is decided in a separate ADR under #28.
  • Dependencies must be compatible with distributing a binary under either licence. Strong copyleft (GPL, AGPL) and LGPL crates are not admitted into shipped binaries. File-level weak copyleft (such as MPL-2.0) needs a case-by-case review under #23. The exact allowlist is enforced by cargo-deny (#23).
  • palisade-driver is assessed separately. It is under the same dual licence by default. If kernel sample code is ever reused, its licence is checked before the code is merged: permissive sample code is kept with its notice; code under any other terms is not copied. The result is recorded in the driver crate README, and in a superseding ADR if the driver licence has to differ.

Consequences

Positive

  • Anyone can reuse any part of Palisade with minimal obligations.
  • Matches most of the dependency tree, so licence review is mostly mechanical.

Negative

  • Derivatives can be closed source. That is accepted for an educational project.
  • Release artefacts must ship third-party notices (#28), and the dependency allowlist must be kept current (#23).

Security impact

The licence has no direct effect on runtime security. It affects supply-chain security indirectly: restricting dependencies to an explicit, mechanically enforced licence allowlist (#23) means every new dependency gets reviewed when it is added, which is also when its provenance and maintenance status are checked. Keeping kernel sample code under a review gate stops unreviewed code from entering the most privileged component.

Links

  • Issues #20, #19 (workspace metadata), #23 (cargo-deny licences), #28 (DCO, headers, notices). Epic #8 (driver).
  • ADR 0019: contributor sign-off (DCO, no CLA), the decision this ADR left to #28.

Source: docs/adr/0010-licence.md on GitHub.

0011. MSRV and unsafe code policy

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade parses untrusted files (#3), runs as a privileged Windows service (#4) and may load a kernel driver (#8). Memory-safety bugs in those places are the worst kind of bug it can have. Rust prevents them only outside unsafe code, so where unsafe is allowed is a security decision. Windows APIs and the driver still need FFI, so unsafe cannot be banned outright.

The build also needs a known compiler. Contributors, CI (#21) and release builds (#24) must agree on the toolchain, and the minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) must be stated and tested. Issue #19 sets the rules. This ADR records them and fixes one detail #19 leaves implicit: how "forbidden by default" and "allowed in named modules" fit together in Rust's lint system.

Decision drivers

  1. Keep unsafe code small, named, reviewed and impossible to add by accident.
  2. Make the compiler and Clippy enforce the rules, not reviewers alone.
  3. Reproducible builds: one pinned toolchain for CI and releases.
  4. Do not leave contributors behind: a stated MSRV that CI checks.

Considered options

Unsafe code:

  1. No unsafe rules. Unacceptable for this project.
  2. forbid(unsafe_code) across the whole workspace. The strongest setting, but forbid cannot be relaxed by a later allow. The compiler rejects #![allow(unsafe_code)] inside a crate compiled with forbid (error E0453, checked with the current stable compiler). The FFI modules could not exist.
  3. deny across the workspace, forbid at the root of every crate that has no allowlisted module, allow only in allowlisted modules, and an allowlist file checked by xtask. The same strength in effect, and it compiles.

MSRV:

  1. Latest stable only. Simplest, but every stable release forces an upgrade on contributors.
  2. A pinned toolchain for builds, plus a declared MSRV no newer than stable minus 2, tested in CI. Reproducible builds and a predictable window.

Decision

Toolchain and MSRV

  • rust-toolchain.toml pins one stable release, with rustfmt, clippy and llvm-tools-preview, and the targets listed in #19. CI and releases use it.
  • rust-version (the MSRV) is declared once in [workspace.package] and inherited by every crate. A CI job builds the workspace on the MSRV toolchain (#21).
  • The MSRV is never newer than the current stable release minus 2. Every MSRV bump is recorded in the changelog, or in an ADR if it drops support for a platform.
  • edition = "2024", inherited from [workspace.package].

Unsafe code, option 3:

  • [workspace.lints] sets rust.unsafe_code = "deny". While no allowlisted module exists yet, the workspace may set forbid instead, as #19 describes. The PR that adds the first allowlisted module lowers it to deny, since forbid would reject that module.
  • Every crate that contains no allowlisted module adds #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at its crate root. That covers palisade-core, palisade-policy, palisade-proto, palisade-server, palisade-console, palisade-cli and xtask.
  • Only these modules may say #![allow(unsafe_code)]:
    • palisade_agent::ffi and its submodules,
    • palisade_tray::ffi and its submodules,
    • palisade_fileid::win and its submodules (only if the OS trust APIs are needed; ADR 0003),
    • palisade-driver, as a whole crate.
  • Every unsafe block has a // SAFETY: comment. Clippy's undocumented_unsafe_blocks lint is set to deny.
  • unsafe-allowlist.txt lists the files that allow unsafe code. An xtask check lists the actual files and fails CI if they differ from the allowlist. The check matches every way of relaxing the lint: allow(unsafe_code) and expect(unsafe_code), as inner (#![...]) or outer (#[...]) attributes, including inside cfg_attr. Changing the allowlist needs CODEOWNERS review (#28).

Related lints (from #19, in [workspace.lints]): clippy.all = "deny", rust.unused_must_use = "deny", rust.missing_docs = "warn" for library crates, clippy.unwrap_used = "deny" outside tests (with allow-unwrap-in-tests = true in clippy.toml, because workspace lints also apply to test code), clippy.expect_used = "warn", and clippy.indexing_slicing = "warn" in the parser crates.

Consequences

Positive

  • unsafe can only appear in four named places. Anywhere else, the compiler rejects it.
  • Reviewers know exactly where to look, and the allowlist diff makes a new unsafe file visible.
  • Builds are reproducible, and the MSRV is tested, not assumed.

Negative

  • The workspace-level lint is deny, not forbid. A crate that drops its root forbid could then allow unsafe locally. The allowlist check catches that, because it lists every file that allows unsafe code, whatever crate it is in.
  • The toolchain pin and the MSRV need regular bumps, which are small but recurring PRs.
  • palisade-fileid cannot forbid at its root because of the win module. Its pure-Rust parser modules each carry #![forbid(unsafe_code)] instead.

Security impact

This ADR is the main control against memory-safety bugs in Palisade. File parsers handle attacker-supplied input and, outside the win module, cannot contain unsafe code at all, so a crafted file can at worst cause a panic or an error, not memory corruption. The privileged service's FFI is confined to ffi modules, where every block has a written safety argument. The kernel driver is the one crate where unsafe is pervasive, which is why it is optional, built separately, and limited to depending on palisade-core (ADR 0003). Denying unwrap in non-test code also removes a common source of attacker-triggered panics.

Links

  • Issues #20, #19 (workspace rules), #21 (MSRV CI job), #24 (release builds), #28 (CODEOWNERS).
  • ADR 0003 (crate layout).

Source: docs/adr/0011-msrv-and-unsafe-code-policy.md on GitHub.

0012. Fail-open versus fail-closed defaults

  • Status: superseded by 0018
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Every enforcement component can fail. When one does, Palisade either fails open (allows, keeping the machine usable) or fails closed (blocks, keeping the control effective). A control that an attacker can switch off by crashing a process or corrupting a file is not a control (ISM-0846). A control that bricks machines when a cache file is damaged will be removed by the people it protects. The child issues make choices for individual cases (#56, #61, #113, #220, #225), and two of them pull in different directions:

  • #61 says that if both cached policies are corrupt, the agent runs built-in safe defaults in audit mode.
  • #225 says the agent loads a built-in emergency policy that blocks everything except OS-signed binaries and Palisade itself, and must not fail open.

#19 also defers the release profile's panic strategy for the agent to this ADR, and #56 wants to restart a panicked subsystem without restarting the whole service.

This ADR sets one rule for these cases. It relies on ADR 0002: the OS-native policy is enforced by the kernel and does not depend on the Palisade agent process.

Decision drivers

  1. Nothing an unprivileged attacker can cause (a crash, a corrupt file, a clock change) may widen what is allowed.
  2. A recoverable failure must not make the machine unbootable or unmanageable.
  3. Failure is visible: every degraded state raises an event and shows in health.
  4. Behaviour must be predictable and testable on the VM harness (#26, #230).

Considered options

  1. Fail open everywhere. Maximum availability, but any crash is a bypass.
  2. Fail closed everywhere, including the driver layer and first install. Maximum security, but a driver fault or a bad first deploy blocks everything, including recovery tools.
  3. Fail closed for anything that holds or once held policy, fail open only where another enforcing layer still covers the gap, and say which case is which. This is the option detailed below.

Decision

Option 3. Case by case:

FailureBehaviourWhy
Agent process crash or hangThe OS-native policy keeps enforcing, because the kernel holds it. The SCM restarts the service after 5 s, and the watchdog repairs it (#56, #220).Stopping the agent removes reporting, not enforcement.
Panic while parsing one fileThe agent is built with panic = "unwind". Each file parse runs inside its own catch_unwind boundary. A panic there marks that file's identity as unparseable, raises a fileid.parse_panic event (rate-limited, with the file's hash if one was computed), and the subsystem carries on with the next file. Any decision the agent itself makes treats an unparseable file as an unknown file (implicit deny in enforce mode, #39). Per-file panics do not count towards the subsystem circuit breaker below.With abort, one crafted file that triggers a parser panic would crash the whole agent on every scan, blinding it in a loop. Counting per-file panics towards the breaker would let a standard user disable a subsystem by dropping three crafted files. Treating the file as unknown keeps the decision closed.
Panic in a subsystem outside a per-file boundaryThe subsystem task is wrapped with catch_unwind and restarted (#56). After 3 such panics in 10 minutes the subsystem is marked Failed and a critical health alert is raised. If the failed subsystem is the one that answers driver verdict requests, the driver sees the agent as disconnected, and the driver row below applies. Aborts that unwinding cannot catch (stack overflow, out of memory) fall back to the first row (agent process crash).A real bug, not a crafted input, is the likely cause, so it is surfaced loudly. The native layer keeps enforcing whatever the subsystem state.
New bundle (pending) fails verification or activationKeep active. Report PolicyRejected(reason) (#61).Nothing was rolled back: the device stays on the policy it already had.
Active bundle (N) corrupt or fails verification at loadLoad previous (N-1) if it verifies, as #225 specifies. This is a bounded, one-step exception to anti-rollback: the anti-rollback record keeps N, so only bundles at N or above are accepted from the server. The agent raises a critical policy.lkg_loaded tamper event at once (not only when both bundles fail) and starts a rapid check-in to fetch a fresh bundle.Availability: disk corruption must not lock a machine down when a verified, previously approved policy exists. N-1 may be weaker than N (for example, if N added a deny), so this is recorded as an accepted risk below.
Active and previous bundles both fail, after a policy was ever acceptedLoad the built-in emergency policy from #225 in enforce mode: allow OS-signed binaries and Palisade itself, block the rest. Raise a critical event.Corruption after enrolment is a possible attack, so it must not relax anything.
No policy yet (first install, before the first bundle)Run the built-in safe defaults from #61: audit mode, with the mandatory blocklists (#87) enforced if the agent ships them. Report PolicyMissing.Nothing has been approved yet, so there is nothing to protect by locking down. Blocking everything at install time would make deployment fail.
Policy stale or past expires_atKeep enforcing the current policy. Report PolicyStale. Never relax automatically (#61, #225).Staleness is not evidence that the policy is wrong.
Driver absent, disconnected, timed out or version-mismatchedFollow driver_failure_mode (#113). Default fail_safe (pass-through with audit) for early rollout rings; fail_secure recommended once stable. The native layer keeps enforcing either way.The driver only adds restrictions on top of the native policy (ADR 0002), so failing it open loses the extra rules but keeps the baseline.
Clock skew, rollback or forward jumpTime-bounded grants (exceptions, override codes, maintenance windows, tokens) follow the rules in "Time rules" below.By default only offline override codes and tokens consult the wall clock, so changing it cannot start, extend or revive a scheduled grant. The remaining gaps are listed as accepted risks.

Time rules. The wall clock can be changed by an administrator or a spoofed time source, so by default only one decision uses it: redeeming an offline override code on an offline-started agent (rule 3). The monotonic clock only counts forwards while the agent runs. From these the agent keeps two values:

  • Anchored time: the server time from an authenticated check-in reply (mTLS with server pinning, ADR 0005), advanced by the monotonic clock. It is valid until the agent process stops or the machine resumes from a sleep that the monotonic clock did not count. The agent is anchored while it holds a valid anchored time, and offline-started otherwise (after a restart or such a resume, before its next check-in).
  • The floor: a lower bound on real time in protected storage (#220). On load it is advanced only by the monotonic time elapsed since the load, never by boot uptime, so a service restart within one boot is not counted twice. While anchored it is raised to anchored time. It is written every minute and at shutdown, in every state, and a write never lowers it. It does not count time spent powered off, so it lags real time after a shutdown.

For a scheduled grant with start s and end e (an exception or maintenance window from the policy bundle):

  1. Anchored. The grant is active when s <= anchored time < e and e > floor. The wall clock plays no part, so changing it cannot start, extend, end or revive a grant.

  2. Offline-started, default. Grants from the policy bundle do not start or continue. A grant that was active when the agent stopped stays closed until the next check-in. This is the closed direction: scheduled work waits for the device to check in. For offline maintenance, an administrator uses an override code (rule 3) instead.

  3. Offline override codes and unlock tokens (#222). A code or token is accepted only if it is authenticated by its secret, its ID is not in the redeemed-code list, its end is after the floor, and its validity window contains anchored time (when anchored) or the wall clock (when offline-started). The override session it opens is timed on the monotonic clock, not by s and e. Its remaining duration is kept in protected storage and only ever decreases, so restarts and reboots cannot lengthen it. Entries in the redeemed-code list are kept until the code's end is at or before the floor; after that, the floor check alone rejects the code.

  4. Opt-in offline scheduling. A group may set offline_scheduled_grants = allow. Then, while offline-started, rule 1 applies with session time in place of anchored time. An offline session starts each time the agent becomes offline-started: at agent start, and on resume from an uncounted sleep. Session time is the wall clock recorded when the offline session started, plus the monotonic time since, so wall-clock changes during the session do not move it. Session time is discarded when the agent becomes anchored. The console marks groups using this option.

  5. Skew. tamper.clock.skew is raised, depending on the state:

    • while anchored: when the wall clock differs from anchored time by more than 5 minutes;
    • when an offline session starts: when the wall clock is more than 60 s behind the floor;
    • during an offline session: when the wall clock drifts from session time by more than 60 s backwards or 5 minutes forwards, measured cumulatively, so small steps add up.

    The alert sets a skew latch in protected storage. Only an authenticated check-in clears it, and the offline-session checks stop once the agent is anchored, so a corrected clock does not re-set the latch. While the latch is set, rule 4 is off and rule 2 applies.

#220 implements these rules as one pure function of (wall clock, monotonic clock, stored state), with a property-test table covering anchored, offline-started, service restart, uncounted sleep, offline reboot, rollback, forward jump and slow drift.

Accepted risk. With the default rules, the wall clock only matters for offline override codes on an offline-started agent. Someone who can change the clock (administrator rights, or a spoofed time source) can redeem a genuine, unredeemed code outside its intended window: later, by setting the clock back, or earlier, by setting it forward. Each code still works only once, only while its end is after the floor, and only for its own monotonic-timed duration. They cannot forge a code or reuse a redeemed one. The same applies to unlock tokens.

With offline_scheduled_grants = allow, someone who sets the clock while the agent is not running (with physical access, administrator rights, or a spoofed time source at boot) can, until the next check-in, start a scheduled grant early or use a grant whose end the floor has not reached. An authenticated check-in ends this: from then on rule 1 uses server time, and a clock that is still wrong raises tamper.clock.skew. Check-in cannot always detect that it happened. If the clock is put back right before the device reconnects, a grant used inside the time the device was powered off looks the same as a legitimate offline run. The uploaded events still show the grant was used offline, which is why the console marks groups with this option.

"A policy was ever accepted". The device is treated as having had a policy if the anti-rollback record (#225) shows a version above zero, or an active or previous cache file exists. An unverified pending file does not count, so an interrupted first download leaves the device on the first-install path. Deleting the record alone does not unlock the first-install path. The mismatch between record copies raises tamper.policy.rollback_suspected (#225).

Consequences

Positive

  • One rule covers almost every case: if Palisade has ever enforced a policy, failures keep it enforced or make it stricter. The bounded exceptions are listed in Security impact.
  • The #61 and #225 behaviours are reconciled. Each applies to a different, testable state.
  • A crafted file cannot use a parser panic to stop the agent reporting or to trip a subsystem circuit breaker.

Negative

  • panic = "unwind" makes binaries slightly larger than abort, and code must be unwind-safe at subsystem boundaries. Because Cargo applies panic to a whole profile, the release profile uses unwind for every binary. The no_std driver crate is built separately (#8) and sets its own panic strategy.
  • The driver's default fail_safe leaves driver-only rules unenforced while the driver is down. The endpoint reports those rules as "not enforced" (#113), so it is not counted as effective for them.
  • A device whose caches are both corrupted after enrolment becomes very restrictive until it gets a new bundle. Users will notice, which is intended.
  • By default, scheduled maintenance windows and exceptions do not run on a device that has restarted and cannot check in. Offline maintenance needs an override code.
  • The time rules need protected storage for the floor, the redeemed-code list, the override session budget and the skew latch.

Security impact

This ADR decides whether crashing, corrupting or confusing Palisade is a bypass. With these defaults it is not: the kernel-enforced native layer survives agent failure, losing both cached bundles leads to the stricter emergency policy, a stale policy keeps enforcing, crafted files cannot disable a subsystem, and by default a clock change cannot start, extend or revive a scheduled grant. There are four deliberate, bounded weak points:

  1. the first-install audit window (built-in mandatory blocklists still enforce, and it ends at the first verified bundle);
  2. the one-step N-1 fallback when active is corrupt (it raises a critical tamper event at once, it never goes further back than N-1, and the agent re-fetches N or later straight away). Only SYSTEM can write the cache directory (#220), so an attacker who can trigger this already has stronger options;
  3. the driver's default fail_safe (the native layer still enforces, and it is configurable to fail_secure); and
  4. the clock risks in "Accepted risk" above: using an unredeemed override code or token outside its window, and, only for groups that opt in to offline scheduling, starting or stretching scheduled grants until the next check-in.

All four are listed in the threat model as accepted risks (#219) and are exercised by the bypass regression suite (#230).

Links

  • Issues #20, #19 (release profile), #39, #56, #61, #87, #113, #219, #220, #222, #225, #226, #230.
  • ADR 0002 (enforcement layers), ADR 0005 (authenticated server time), ADR 0007 (cache files).
  • Superseded by ADR 0018.

Source: docs/adr/0012-fail-open-vs-fail-closed-defaults.md on GitHub.

0013. Protected process light feasibility

  • Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

A Windows service can run as a protected process light (PPL) at the antimalware signer level. Then even administrators and SYSTEM cannot terminate it, inject into it or debug it, unless the caller runs at an equal or higher protection level. Some commercial application control agents use this. It needs three things:

  1. an early-launch antimalware (ELAM) driver that declares the service's signing certificate in its certificate-info resource;
  2. that ELAM driver signed through the OS vendor's antimalware partner program; and
  3. the service executable signed with the declared certificate (page hashes, SHA-256). Every DLL loaded into the service must either be signed as part of Windows, or be signed with the declared certificate, or be listed in a catalog file that is signed with the declared certificate and installed with the service. Third-party DLLs can be covered by that catalog without re-signing them.

The partner program has membership criteria that an educational open-source project probably cannot meet. Test-signing mode allows experiments, but it is not a deployable protection. The ISM's "users cannot disable or bypass" requirement (ISM-0846) allows exemptions for local administrator and break-glass accounts, and it can largely be met without PPL through the driver-backed handle protection in #220. PPL mainly raises the bar against an attacker who already has administrator or SYSTEM rights.

Issue #221 is the investigation and spike. This ADR records the options and a provisional direction now, so that #220 and #8 can design against it.

Decision drivers

  1. Feasibility for an open-source project without partner-program membership.
  2. Protection against stopping or tampering with the agent by standard users (required) and by administrators (desirable).
  3. Constraints PPL places on the agent: only correctly signed DLLs may load, Winsock layered providers are restricted, some ETW consumers and diagnostics are limited, and updates need a protected stop path.
  4. Coverage on Server Core, ARM64 and with hypervisor-enforced code integrity on.

Considered options

  • (a) Full PPL through the partner program. Strongest protection against SYSTEM, but probably unavailable to this project.
  • (b) Driver-backed handle protection only (#220 moderate/strong levels). The Palisade driver strips terminate, write and inject rights from handles to the agent processes for callers that are not Palisade. Feasible with test signing in the lab, and with an attested driver later (#112). It does not stop a SYSTEM attacker who can unload or disable drivers.
  • (c) Optional PPL for organisations that can sign their own ELAM driver. A build feature ppl and an install property PALISADE_ENABLE_PPL=0|1, default 0. The organisation supplies the signing inputs. Palisade ships the plumbing, not the signature.
  • (d) A virtualization-based-security enclave for key material only. Protects device keys from a SYSTEM attacker, but does not stop the agent being killed.
  • (e) User-mode hardening only: service and file ACLs plus the mutual watchdog (#220 minimal). Stops standard users. Does not stop administrators.

Decision

Proposed, not accepted. The provisional direction is (b) as the baseline, with (c) as an opt-in, and (e) as the floor when no driver is present. (a) is recorded as out of reach unless the eligibility criteria turn out to be met. (d) is a separate question for key custody (#224) and is not a substitute for process protection.

This ADR becomes accepted (or is revised) when the #221 spike has produced:

  • the documented eligibility criteria of the OS vendor's antimalware partner program, and a yes or no on whether an open-source project can be admitted;
  • a test-signed ELAM driver and a service launched as antimalware PPL on a test-signing VM, with captured results showing administrator taskkill /f, OpenProcess(PROCESS_TERMINATE) and debugger attach all fail with PPL on and succeed with it off;
  • confirmation that the Rust agent binaries and their dependencies load under the PPL signing rules: the agent's own binaries signed with the declared certificate, every other DLL either signed as part of Windows or listed in a signed catalog, and no DLL outside those three cases; and that the agent's tracing and ETW use still works;
  • measured startup and boot-time impact;
  • a working clean-uninstall and update path, with the service stopping itself on a signed command;
  • notes on Server Core, ARM64 and hypervisor-enforced code integrity.

Results go under docs/spikes/ppl/, and the residual-risk register in #219 is updated with the final choice.

Consequences

Positive

  • #220 and #8 can design the handle protection and the tamper levels now, without waiting for the spike.
  • Organisations that can sign an ELAM driver are not shut out, if (c) is confirmed.

Negative

  • Until the spike is done, Palisade makes no claim of protection against administrators or SYSTEM.
  • Devices without a signed native policy and Secure Boot have no protection of the baseline against an administrator, under any option here. Closing that gap is a deployment choice (#85), not something PPL or the driver can provide.
  • Option (c) adds a build flavour and a signing input that CI can only exercise with test certificates.
  • If PPL is adopted, the agent has to be split into a small protected part and an unprotected helper for heavy parsing (#221 design notes). That design work only happens if (c) is chosen.

Security impact

This decision sets how strongly the agent resists an attacker who already has administrator or SYSTEM rights. Under the provisional direction, standard users and user-level malware cannot stop the agent (through #220), but an administrator who can disable the driver can. Because of ADR 0002 and ADR 0018, stopping the agent does not stop the kernel-enforced native policy. How much of the baseline survives an administrator then depends on how the native policy is deployed:

  • Signed native policy on a Secure Boot device (#85). The administrator cannot remove or replace the code integrity policy, so the kernel-enforced code integrity baseline is kept. The residual risk is loss of reporting, of driver-only rules, and of per-user rules in the rule-collection format, which depend on a service the administrator can stop (ADR 0002). Signing does not protect that service.
  • Unsigned native policy, or Secure Boot off. An administrator can delete or replace the code integrity policy, so the residual risk also includes loss of the code integrity baseline. Palisade layers cannot prevent this, because the same administrator can disable the driver too.

Signing and Secure Boot are not required. A signed policy that is wrong can leave a device unbootable, with recovery only by turning Secure Boot off (#85), so signing stays an opt-in per deployment, recommended once a policy is stable. The unsigned case is an accepted risk. To keep it visible, the agent reports secure_boot_enabled and signed_policy_active (#85), and the console shows a device without both as "baseline removable by an administrator". Both residual risks are recorded in #219. Test signing is only ever enabled on throwaway VMs, never on runner hosts.

Links

  • Issues #20, #221 (PPL spike), #220 (tamper protection), #112 (driver signing), #85 (signed native policies), #219 (threat model), #224 (key custody). Epics #8, #18.

Source: docs/adr/0013-protected-process-light-feasibility.md on GitHub.

0014. Educational scope statement

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

Palisade is a personal learning project, built in public to understand application control end to end. The README says it is not a replacement for enterprise products or enterprise support, and should not be relied on to protect production environments. Because Palisade is security software, people will still ask whether it is production ready, file vulnerability reports, and may deploy it anyway. Unclear promises are worse than plain limits: someone who assumes a security fix will ship within days may leave an exposure in place. This ADR says precisely what "educational" and "not for production" mean, so that the README (#28), SECURITY.md (#28), SUPPORT.md (#28) and the docs site (#27) say the same thing.

Decision drivers

  1. Honesty about what one maintainer can sustain.
  2. Users must be able to make a safe decision about whether to run it.
  3. Security reports still need a clear, private path and a stated response, because the code is public and people may use it.
  4. Engineering practice stays high: the project exists to learn how to do this well.

Considered options

  1. Say nothing beyond the licence's no-warranty clause. Legally enough, but it leaves expectations about fixes and support undefined.
  2. Offer production-style commitments (an SLA, supported versions, security-fix timelines). Not sustainable for one maintainer, and it would mislead users.
  3. An explicit educational-scope statement with best-effort targets. Clear limits, a defined security reporting path, and response targets stated as best effort.

Decision

Option 3. Palisade's scope is defined as follows.

What "educational" means

  • Palisade is built to learn and to teach. Design choices are documented so others can learn from them (ADRs, the threat model, design docs).
  • The engineering bar is still high: signed releases, a threat model, tests, fuzzing and supply-chain checks. "Educational" lowers the support commitment, not the engineering quality.

What "not for production" means

  • No support commitment. Help is community best-effort, through GitHub Discussions for questions and Issues for bugs. There is no commercial support, now or planned.
  • No SLA. No guaranteed response, fix or release times for anything, including security.
  • Security fixes are best effort. Reports go through GitHub private vulnerability reporting. The targets are acknowledgement within 7 days and triage within 14 days, stated as best effort. Coordinated disclosure defaults to 90 days. Fixes land on the latest minor release only; older releases are not patched. SECURITY.md (#28) holds the full policy.
  • No certification or compliance claim. Essential Eight and ISM mappings are learning aids and evidence examples, not an assessment outcome. Palisade claims no certified status (#18).
  • No warranty, as stated in both licences (ADR 0010).
  • Anyone who runs Palisade on machines they care about does so at their own risk, and should test on disposable VMs first (#26).

Where it is stated

  • README (already present), SECURITY.md and SUPPORT.md (#28), and the docs site landing page (#27). They use the same wording, and the docs site wording is the source (#27, #28).

Consequences

Positive

  • Users know the limits before they deploy anything.
  • Security reporters know where to report and what response to expect.
  • The maintainer is not held to commitments one person cannot keep.

Negative

  • Some potential users will skip the project because it offers no support.
  • Best-effort security targets can still be missed. When that happens, the advisory should say so plainly.

Security impact

Clear scope reduces the risk of Palisade being relied on as someone's only application control in production without them knowing the fix cadence is best effort. A defined private reporting path keeps vulnerability details out of public issues until a fix or advisory is ready. "Latest minor only" means users must upgrade to receive fixes, and SECURITY.md has to state that plainly.

Links

  • Issues #20, #18, #26, #27, #28. README "About this project" and "Disclaimer".
  • Security reporting path: SECURITY.md (#28). Reports go through GitHub private vulnerability reporting for this repository, which is enabled; the setting and how to verify it are in docs/repo-settings.md. If the form cannot be used, SECURITY.md tells reporters to ask for a private channel in GitHub Discussions without giving any details.

Source: docs/adr/0014-educational-scope-statement.md on GitHub.

0015. Agent-server protocol with protocol-failure fallback

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

This ADR supersedes ADR 0005. It keeps that decision (gRPC as the primary transport, with an HTTPS + JSON fallback), but changes when the fallback is used.

ADR 0005 switched to the fallback only after 3 consecutive gRPC handshake failures. Some proxies let the TLS and HTTP/2 handshake succeed and then break gRPC itself: they strip the trailers that carry grpc-status, downgrade the response to HTTP/1.1, or reset streams. Every RPC then fails, but no handshake does, so under ADR 0005 the agent never uses the fallback and cannot check in at all. This is the case the fallback exists for (decision driver 2).

The rest of the context is unchanged. The agent (#4) talks to the server (#10) to check in, fetch policy and deltas, upload events and inventory, and receive near-real-time nudges such as "policy available" or "rapid check-in". Agents often sit behind corporate proxies, some of which break HTTP/2 or inspect TLS. All agent-server traffic must use mutual TLS with a device certificate (#223). The wire types live in palisade-proto (ADR 0003).

Decision drivers

  1. Mutual TLS with a device key that never leaves its key store (#223).
  2. Works through restrictive proxies, including ones that break HTTP/2 or gRPC.
  3. Efficient, diff-based policy delivery and batched event upload.
  4. Offline queueing and replay, which happen on the agent whatever the transport.
  5. Generated, typed clients for the agent, the CLI and the console.
  6. A small, auditable dependency set in the privileged agent.

Considered options

Transport (unchanged from ADR 0005):

  1. gRPC over HTTP/2 (tonic). Typed services from protobuf, server streaming for push, compact binary framing, and mTLS through rustls. Some proxies break HTTP/2 or gRPC trailers. Browsers need a separate API (the console uses REST, #15).
  2. HTTPS with JSON or CBOR, plus long-poll or WebSocket for push. Works through almost any proxy and is easy to debug. But it is hand-written or OpenAPI-generated, has no service-level schema shared with the agent, and long-poll adds latency and server load.
  3. MQTT over TLS. Good for push to many devices, but it needs a broker. Request/response and bulk transfer fit it poorly, and topic ACLs become a second authorisation system.

Fallback trigger (new):

  1. Handshake failures only (ADR 0005). Simple, but misses proxies that pass the handshake and then break gRPC framing, so the agent stays unmanaged behind them.
  2. Any RPC error. Catches every proxy fault, but also fires on ordinary server answers such as PERMISSION_DENIED or UNAVAILABLE during a server restart. Agents would then leave gRPC for reasons the fallback cannot fix.
  3. Handshake failures plus gRPC protocol failures, counted separately from errors the server itself returns. Catches the proxy case without reacting to valid server replies.

Decision

Transport option 1, gRPC over HTTP/2 with tonic and rustls, as the primary transport, plus an HTTPS + JSON fallback for check-in. Fallback trigger option 3.

  • palisade-proto defines the AgentService RPCs listed in #62. The server push channel (StreamPush) only carries nudges, never payloads. The agent then pulls through the normal RPCs.

  • Fallback triggers. The agent switches to the fallback after either:

    • 3 consecutive gRPC handshake failures (TCP connect, TLS or HTTP/2 negotiation); or
    • 3 consecutive calls to the same unary RPC method that the fallback carries (check-in, policy fetch, event upload) that fail with a gRPC protocol failure after a successful handshake. A protocol failure is a response without a valid grpc-status (missing or stripped trailers), a response that is not HTTP/2 or not application/grpc, or an HTTP/2 stream reset or connection close before the call completes.

    Counters. The handshake counter resets only on a successful handshake. Each unary RPC method has its own protocol-failure counter, which resets only when a call to that method returns a complete gRPC response. A success on another method does not reset it, so a proxy that breaks GetPolicy but lets CheckIn through still triggers the fallback. A complete response with a non-OK grpc-status from the server (for example PERMISSION_DENIED, INVALID_ARGUMENT or UNAVAILABLE) is an application error, not a protocol failure. It does not count towards any trigger, and it resets that method's counter, because the framing worked. When a trigger fires, the agent moves every call the fallback carries to the fallback and raises a comms.grpc.protocol_failure health alert naming the method. A unary method the fallback does not carry (for example UploadInventory) cannot trigger the switch, because switching would not help it. Three consecutive protocol failures on such a method raise the same alert, and the method keeps retrying on gRPC with the normal backoff (#62).

  • Server streaming (StreamPush) is never a fallback trigger. A healthy push stream stays open and has no trailers until it ends, so a network drop, a sleep or an idle timeout closes it in a way that looks like a protocol failure. Stream closes therefore count for nothing towards the transport triggers. The agent reopens a closed stream with backoff, capped at the retry interval below. If the stream closes 3 times in a row within 60 s of opening, push is marked degraded (comms.push.degraded) and the agent polls at the check-in interval, while unary RPCs stay on gRPC. Push is restored once a stream stays open for more than 60 s or delivers a message.

  • TLS failures never trigger anything weaker. A certificate, pinning or client-identity failure is a handshake failure. It may move the agent to the fallback, but the fallback applies the same checks and fails in the same way. No trigger relaxes TLS.

  • The fallback. It carries the same protobuf messages, encoded as JSON (the standard protobuf JSON mapping), over HTTP/1.1. It covers check-in, policy fetch and event upload. Push falls back to polling at the check-in interval. While on the fallback, the agent probes gRPC at agent start and then every 15 minutes (comms.grpc_retry_interval_s, default 900, range 300 to 86,400, delivered by policy and implemented in #62). The probe calls the unary method that tripped the trigger (CheckIn for a handshake trigger), so it always completes against a healthy server. The agent returns to gRPC after one probe completes with a valid gRPC response, and resets all counters when it does.

  • Both paths use the same mTLS identity, the same server pinning, and the same signed payloads. Policy bundles and commands are signed end to end (ADR 0017), so their trust never depends on which transport delivered them.

  • The console and external integrations use the REST API (#15). That is a separate surface, not an agent transport.

Consequences

Positive

  • One schema (.proto) generates the agent, server and CLI types, and schema changes are reviewable in one place.
  • Server streaming gives near-real-time nudges without a broker.
  • The JSON fallback keeps agents manageable behind proxies that break HTTP/2, including proxies that pass the handshake but break gRPC framing.

Negative

  • Two encodings of the same messages must stay in step. Contract tests are needed for both.
  • The agent must classify failures (handshake, protocol, application), keep a counter per unary RPC method, and handle push-stream health separately. #62 needs tests that simulate each kind, including a proxy that strips trailers on one method only, and repeated push-stream drops that must not move unary RPCs off gRPC.
  • A broken proxy is only noticed after the next probe, so returning to gRPC can take up to the retry interval.
  • tonic and hyper add to the agent's dependency tree. That is accepted, but they are reviewed under the supply-chain policy (#23).
  • TLS-inspecting proxies break mTLS by design. The docs must say the agent endpoints need an inspection bypass (#62). Palisade never disables verification to work around this.

Security impact

mTLS with a non-exportable device key authenticates every agent, and server pinning defeats interception, including by an inspecting proxy that presents its own CA. The fallback is not a downgrade: it uses the same TLS and identity requirements, and the selection logic must never fall back to plaintext or to unauthenticated TLS. An on-path attacker who breaks gRPC framing can force the fallback. That costs only push latency (polling instead of nudges), because both paths carry the same authenticated, signed messages. Push messages carry no payloads, so a compromised or spoofed push channel can at worst cause extra check-ins. Message parsers in palisade-proto handle data from the network and are fuzz targets (#230).

Links

  • Supersedes: 0005
  • Issues #20, #62 (check-in and transport), #223 (enrolment and mTLS), #15 (REST API), #23 (supply chain), #230 (fuzzing). Epics #4, #10, #18.
  • ADR 0017 (signatures).

Source: docs/adr/0015-agent-server-protocol-fallback-triggers.md on GitHub.

0016. Server database, tenant isolation and tenant scope binding

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

This ADR supersedes ADR 0006. It keeps that decision (Postgres through sqlx, a shared schema with row-level security), but corrects what the decision guarantees.

ADR 0006 said that RLS means "a bug in the application layer still cannot cross tenants". That is too strong. RLS compares each row with the tenant scope the server sets for the transaction. It does not check that the scope is the right one for the caller. If an authorisation bug resolves a tenant A request to tenant B, the server sets scope B, and RLS returns B's rows. The same holds for SQL injection: injected SQL runs in the same session and could change the scope setting. RLS protects against a query that forgets or gets wrong its tenant filter. It does not protect against a wrong scope.

The rest of the context is unchanged. palisade-server (#10) stores tenants, groups, policies and their version history, approvals, RBAC, inventory and a large volume of execution events. The Essential Eight logging controls expect allowed and blocked events to stay searchable for at least 12 months and to be protected from modification. The server is multi-tenant (#128), so one tenant must never read or write another tenant's rows, whether through the API, the console or the query language. Issue #127 holds the detailed schema work.

Decision drivers

  1. Tenant isolation that holds even when a query omits or mistypes its tenant filter.
  2. Relational integrity across policies, rules, groups, approvals and their history.
  3. Query safety: SQL checked at build time, no string-built queries.
  4. Forward-only, reviewable migrations that run automatically and idempotently.
  5. Event volume: time-partitioned tables with retention.
  6. One database a learner can run locally or in a container.

Considered options

Database and access layer:

  1. Postgres with sqlx (async, compile-time checked queries through query!/query_as!, with offline metadata for CI). Mature row-level security, partitioning and JSON support.
  2. Postgres with a full ORM. Less SQL to write, but the generated SQL is harder to review, and RLS and partitioning still need raw SQL.
  3. An embedded or document store. Simple to deploy, but no row-level security, weak relational integrity, and poor fit for 12-month searchable event retention.

Multi-tenancy:

  1. Shared schema, tenant_id on every row, enforced by Postgres row-level security (RLS). One schema to migrate. Isolation is enforced by the database for every query.
  2. Schema per tenant. Strong separation, but migrations run once per tenant, cross-tenant features (the tenant tree, global groups) need dynamic SQL, and the catalogue grows with the tenant count.
  3. Database per tenant. Strongest separation, but the most operational cost, and it rules out the shared tenant tree in #128.
  4. Application-only filtering (WHERE tenant_id = $1 in code). Cheapest, but one missed filter leaks data.

Binding the scope to the caller (new):

  1. A database-enforced binding, for example one database role per tenant selected with SET ROLE, or a signed scope token that a database function verifies. The database only ever talks to the server, never to the end caller. So the server still chooses the role or holds the signing key, and the same server bug that picks the wrong tenant picks the wrong role or signs the wrong token. Per-tenant roles also grow the catalogue with the tenant count, like option 2 above. This adds cost without adding an independent check.
  2. One audited scope-resolution point in the server, and a narrower stated guarantee. RLS covers query mistakes. Scope resolution is kept small, in one place, and tested on its own.

Decision

  • Postgres 16 or later, through sqlx, with compile-time checked queries. The SQLX_OFFLINE query metadata is committed so CI builds without a live database (#127).
  • Migrations use sqlx::migrate!, embedded in the binary, numbered and forward-only, with expand/contract for schema changes. A migration checksum mismatch is a hard error, and the server refuses to start against a schema newer than itself.
  • Tenancy is a shared schema with row-level tenant_id plus RLS.
    • Every tenant-owned table has tenant_id uuid not null and an RLS policy keyed on a per-transaction setting that the server sets from the caller's resolved scope.
    • Tenant tables use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so the policies apply even to the table owner. The policy expression fails closed: when the tenant setting is unset or empty, no rows match.
    • The server connects as a non-owner application role with NOSUPERUSER, NOBYPASSRLS and NOCREATEROLE. NOBYPASSRLS alone is not enough, because a superuser bypasses RLS whatever that attribute says. The application role is not a member of any role that is a superuser, has BYPASSRLS or owns tenant tables, so SET ROLE cannot leave RLS behind. At startup the server checks these attributes and memberships for its own role, and refuses to start if any is wrong. Migrations run as a separate owner role.
    • Foreign keys include tenant_id, so a row can never reference another tenant's row.
    • Shared rows (built-in permissions, seeded content) belong to a root tenant and are exposed through explicit read-only policies.
  • Scope binding: option 2.
    • The scope is resolved in one function, from the authenticated principal only: the tenant bound to the device certificate (#223) for agents, and the RBAC grants of the signed-in user for the console and API (#128). It is never taken from a request path, parameter or body. A request that names a tenant is checked against the resolved scope, not used to set it.
    • The same function is the only code that writes the tenant setting, at the start of each transaction (#127). A CI check rejects any other code that writes it.
    • #127 has a cross-tenant test suite: two tenants, every API route, and each principal type, asserting that no response contains the other tenant's rows. For every attempted cross-tenant insert, update and delete, the suite also reads the stored rows directly and asserts that the other tenant's data is unchanged, because an empty response does not prove that nothing was written. The verifier uses a test-only role with BYPASSRLS, never the application role or the owner role, because FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY would otherwise hide a wrongly written row from it too.
  • High-volume event tables are partitioned by month (#127).

Consequences

Positive

  • Isolation does not depend on every query remembering a filter. A missing or wrong WHERE clause in a handler still cannot cross tenants.
  • The code that can cross tenants is one small function, so review and tests can focus on it.
  • Query typos and type mismatches fail at build time.
  • One schema and one migration stream, whatever the tenant count.

Negative

  • A bug in scope resolution, or SQL injection, can still cross tenants. RLS does not catch either. The resolver and the parameterised-query rule carry that risk instead.
  • RLS adds a per-query cost and makes query plans harder to read. Indexes must lead with tenant_id.
  • Building with compile-time checks needs either a database or up-to-date offline metadata. Stale metadata fails CI until it is regenerated.
  • Each connection must set the tenant scope at the start of every transaction. Pooling code has to make that impossible to forget (#127).

Security impact

RLS moves the per-query tenant filter from handler code into the database, so a handler that omits or mistypes its filter cannot read another tenant's policies, events or approval history. RLS trusts the scope the server sets. The trust boundary for tenant isolation is therefore the scope resolver, and the threat model (#219) records it as such. A resolver bug that maps a caller to the wrong tenant crosses tenants, and RLS does not stop it. SQL injection is countered by compile-time checked, parameterised queries, not by RLS, because injected SQL could change the session's tenant setting. NOSUPERUSER and NOBYPASSRLS on the application role, with no route to a role that bypasses RLS, mean a compromised server process cannot simply turn RLS off, but it can set any scope, so a compromised server is not contained by RLS either. The owner role used for migrations is a separate secret (#227). Event tables are the evidence trail for ISM-1660, so their append-only protection and retention live in #127 and #229.

Links

  • Supersedes: 0006
  • Issues #20, #127 (schema, migrations, isolation), #128 (multi-tenancy), #219 (threat model), #223 (device identity), #227 (secrets), #229 (server hardening). Epic #10.

Source: docs/adr/0016-server-database-and-tenant-scope.md on GitHub.

0017. Cryptographic algorithms, libraries and AEAD nonces

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

This ADR supersedes ADR 0008. The algorithms and libraries are unchanged. It corrects one wrong statement and adds the rule that replaces it. ADR 0008 said that ring handles AEAD nonce generation inside the library. It does not. ring's AEAD API takes a nonce, or a caller-supplied nonce sequence, for every seal operation. Reusing a nonce under the same AES-GCM key reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge authentication tags for that key. So Palisade's own code must keep nonces unique under each key, including across agent restarts and reboots. With random nonces that is a probability bound, not an absolute guarantee, and this ADR states the bound.

Palisade uses cryptography in five places:

  1. File identity: hashes that rules match on (#3, #46, #47).
  2. Palisade's own signatures: policy bundles (#225), server commands (#62) and trust-set updates (#224).
  3. OS-defined signatures: Authenticode on Palisade's releases (#24, #226) and signed OS-native code integrity policies (#85). Their formats are fixed by the OS.
  4. Transport: mutual TLS between agent, relays and server (#223).
  5. At rest and short secrets: the encrypted policy cache (#225), the driver boot cache MAC (#113) and offline override codes (#222).

The project aims to align with the Australian Government ISM cryptography guidance (ASD-approved algorithms), which favours ECDSA with P-384, RSA of at least 3072 bits, SHA-2 and AES-GCM. Issue #20's summary suggests Ed25519 for bundle signing, while #225 specifies ECDSA P-384 as the default with Ed25519 as an option, and #61 mentions Ed25519 or P-256. This ADR settles that.

Decision drivers

  1. Collision-resistant identities: no allow decision may rest on a broken hash.
  2. Alignment with ASD-approved algorithms, since Essential Eight and the ISM frame the project.
  3. Exact compatibility with what the OS computes and requires (#3, #6).
  4. Algorithm agility, so a key or algorithm can be rotated without a format break (#224).
  5. A small number of well-reviewed libraries, with builds for x64 and ARM64 Windows and Linux.
  6. A path to a FIPS-validated module later, without a rewrite.

Considered options

Bundle and command signatures:

  1. Ed25519 only. Fast, deterministic, small keys, hard to misuse. Not on the ASD-approved list, so an ISM-aligned deployment could not use it.
  2. ECDSA P-384 with SHA-384 only. ASD-approved. Slower, and it needs a careful library because naive ECDSA nonce handling is dangerous.
  3. Algorithm-agile envelope supporting both, with ECDSA P-384 as the default. Each signature names its key ID and algorithm. The agent accepts only algorithms in its trust set.

Libraries:
