  1. ring for signatures, AEAD and HMAC, and as the rustls crypto provider. Small API surface designed against misuse. The caller supplies every AEAD nonce, so nonce uniqueness is Palisade's job, not the library's. Builds with only a C compiler (no CMake or separate assembler). No FIPS-validated build.
  2. A FIPS-capable rustls provider. Offers a validated mode, but needs a heavier native build (CMake, and extra build tools for the validated mode) on Windows runners. Validated mode is not needed yet.
  3. Pure-Rust RustCrypto crates for everything. No C or assembly, but no single provider for rustls, and a wider set of crates to review.

Decision

Hashing (file identity)

  • SHA-256 is the primary identity. Every stored or exchanged file identity carries it.
  • SHA-1 and MD5 are compatibility-only: they are computed so Palisade can match what the OS and imported policies use, and to join with OS events. They are never the sole basis of an allow. Policy validation (#40) rejects an allow rule whose only identity is SHA-1 or MD5. A deny rule may use them, because a collision there can only cause an extra block.
  • The OS-native compiler emits whatever hash forms the target OS build requires (#81). That can include SHA-1 Authenticode values alongside SHA-256, never instead of it.
  • SHA-384 and SHA-512 are optional extras (#46).
  • Implementation: the RustCrypto sha2 crate (with sha1 and md-5 for compatibility hashes), because they are pure Rust, no_std capable and support streaming. The single-pass multi-hash design is in #46.

Palisade-native signatures (bundles, commands, trust-set updates)

  • Option 3: an algorithm-agile envelope ({kid, alg, sig} entries, #225).
  • Algorithms: ecdsa-p384-sha384 (default) and ed25519 (opt-in per tenant). Nothing else. The agent accepts only algorithms listed in its trust set, and the trust set is itself signed (#224).
  • Every signature covers a domain-separation prefix plus the canonical bytes (#43, #225), so a signature for one purpose cannot be replayed as another.

OS-defined signatures

  • Authenticode on releases and signed OS-native policies use RSA 3072-bit or larger with SHA-256, and RFC 3161 timestamps for releases. The OS fixes these formats, and Palisade only chooses the key size and digest.

Transport

  • TLS through rustls, TLS 1.3 preferred and TLS 1.2 allowed only with the restricted AEAD cipher suites in #223. Certificate verification is never disabled, in any build.

Symmetric

  • AES-256-GCM for data at rest (#225). HMAC-SHA-256 for MACs (the driver boot cache, #113) and for one-time override codes (#222).
  • AES-GCM nonces are the crypto module's responsibility. ring takes the nonce from the caller, so the crypto module keeps the chance that any 96-bit nonce repeats under one key at or below 2^-33, including across restarts, reboots and crashes. Two random draws can collide, so this is a bound, not a guarantee. With q seals under one key the chance of any repeat is at most about q^2 / 2^97, which is 2^-33 at the 2^32 seal limit. That is the limit NIST SP 800-38D sets for random 96-bit nonces:
    • It generates each nonce from the OS cryptographically secure random number generator and never accepts a nonce from call sites. The seal API takes no nonce parameter.
    • Each data key seals at most 2^32 messages, which is what keeps the bound above. The module counts seals per key and rotates the data key before the limit. The persisted count must never be below the number of seals actually made: the module may reserve a block of K seals by persisting count + K before using them, so a high-rate store (such as an encrypted event queue) does not need a synchronous write per record. A crash wastes at most the rest of the block. On load, an unknown or missing count is treated as "rotate now".
    • No counter-based nonce scheme is used, because a counter restored from an older copy of protected storage would repeat nonces.
    • A known-answer test and a test that seals many records and checks for repeated nonces run on every platform (#225).

Libraries

  • ring provides signatures, AES-GCM, HMAC and the rustls crypto provider. It replaces the wider candidate crate list in #225. Access goes through a thin crypto module, so call sites never use ring directly. This covers user-mode crates only. ring cannot link into the no_std kernel driver, so palisade-driver verifies the boot cache MAC with the kernel's own cryptography API or no_std RustCrypto crates (hmac, sha2). That choice is made in #113, using the same algorithm (HMAC-SHA-256) and the same test vectors.
  • FIPS (future work). A FIPS-validated provider can be swapped in later through rustls's provider interface and the same crypto module. Adopting one needs a superseding ADR, which must also decide whether file-identity hashing (done by sha2, outside the provider) is in FIPS scope. Palisade makes no FIPS claim until then (#18 lists certification as out of scope).

Consequences

Positive

  • No allow decision rests on SHA-1 or MD5.
  • ISM-aligned defaults, with Ed25519 available where alignment is not needed.
  • Algorithm agility means key and algorithm rotation are data changes, not format changes.
  • One provider for TLS and signatures keeps the reviewed crypto surface small.
  • Nonce handling lives in one module, so no call site can choose or reuse a nonce.

Negative

  • P-384 verification is slower than Ed25519. Bundles are verified on activation and every 15 minutes (#225), not per decision, so the cost is acceptable.
  • Two signature algorithms means two sets of known-answer test vectors on every platform (#225).
  • Imported policies (#15) whose allow rules carry only a SHA-1 or MD5 hash cannot be imported as-is. The importer must resolve them to SHA-256 from inventory or a supplied file, or report them as rejected.
  • ring has no FIPS-validated mode, so a FIPS deployment needs the future provider swap.
  • The crypto module must persist a per-key seal count and rotate data keys, which adds state to protected storage (#220, #225).

Security impact

This ADR sets the strength of every trust decision Palisade makes. Banning weak hashes as the sole basis of allow rules closes collision-based bypasses in Palisade's own evaluation, where an attacker builds a malicious file with the same SHA-1 or MD5 as an allowed one. The native layer is limited by what the target OS build checks: where an older build only matches SHA-1 Authenticode values, the compile report (#81) flags the rule so the weakness is visible. Algorithm lists in a signed trust set prevent algorithm downgrade, and domain separation prevents cross-protocol signature reuse. Keeping verification always on in TLS means a misconfigured proxy fails closed rather than silently exposing traffic. AES-GCM fails badly on nonce reuse: two records sealed with the same key and nonce leak the XOR of their plaintexts and allow forged tags under that key. Random nonces from the OS generator, a per-key seal limit of 2^32 with rotation, and no caller-supplied nonces keep the probability of any repeat under one key at or below 2^-33, including after a restart or a restored backup of protected storage. A deterministic counter could make repeats impossible in principle, but restoring an old counter would repeat nonces in practice, so it is not used. A flaw in ring would affect TLS and signatures at once, so it is tracked under the supply-chain advisory scan (#23).

Links

  • Supersedes: 0008
  • Issues #20, #3, #43, #46, #47, #62, #81, #85, #113, #222, #223, #224, #225, #226. Epic #18.

Source: docs/adr/0017-cryptographic-algorithms-and-nonces.md on GitHub.

0018. Fail-open versus fail-closed defaults, revised

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-23
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

This ADR supersedes ADR 0012. It keeps that decision and its failure table, and closes three gaps found in review:

  • Emergency policy and the native policy. ADR 0012 loads a built-in emergency policy that allows OS-signed binaries, but did not say what happens to the OS-native code integrity policy already installed on the device. If loading the emergency policy replaced or relaxed the native policy, a native deny (including a deny on an OS-signed binary) could be lost.
  • Sleep and reboot during an override session. ADR 0012 kept an override session's remaining duration across restarts and reboots. Time that the agent does not count (powered off, or a sleep the monotonic clock did not count) was not deducted, so a session with ten minutes left could resume ten minutes of access after a day.
  • Crash order of the redeemed-code list. ADR 0012 dropped a redeemed code's ID once the live floor passed the code's end. The floor is only written every minute. A crash before that write restores an older floor that no longer covers the code, while the ID is already gone. With the clock set back on an offline-started agent, the same code could then be redeemed again. The same gap exists if the agent crashes after opening a session but before the ID is written.

A later review found two more gaps, also closed here: the one-step N-1 fallback could reach further back than one step after a corrupt active was replaced (fixed in ADR 0007, and referenced in the table below), and in native_only mode nothing enforced the emergency policy.

The rest of the context is unchanged.

Every enforcement component can fail. When one does, Palisade either fails open (allows, keeping the machine usable) or fails closed (blocks, keeping the control effective). A control that an attacker can switch off by crashing a process or corrupting a file is not a control (ISM-0846). A control that bricks machines when a cache file is damaged will be removed by the people it protects. The child issues make choices for individual cases (#56, #61, #113, #220, #225), and two of them pull in different directions:

  • #61 says that if both cached policies are corrupt, the agent runs built-in safe defaults in audit mode.
  • #225 says the agent loads a built-in emergency policy that blocks everything except OS-signed binaries and Palisade itself, and must not fail open.

#19 also defers the release profile's panic strategy for the agent to this ADR, and #56 wants to restart a panicked subsystem without restarting the whole service.

This ADR sets one rule for these cases. It relies on ADR 0002: the OS-native policy is enforced by the kernel and does not depend on the Palisade agent process.

Decision drivers

  1. Nothing an unprivileged attacker can cause (a crash, a corrupt file, a clock change) may widen what is allowed.
  2. A recoverable failure must not make the machine unbootable or unmanageable.
  3. Failure is visible: every degraded state raises an event and shows in health.
  4. Behaviour must be predictable and testable on the VM harness (#26, #230).

Considered options

  1. Fail open everywhere. Maximum availability, but any crash is a bypass.
  2. Fail closed everywhere, including the driver layer and first install. Maximum security, but a driver fault or a bad first deploy blocks everything, including recovery tools.
  3. Fail closed for anything that holds or once held policy, fail open only where another enforcing layer still covers the gap, and say which case is which. This is the option detailed below.

Decision

Option 3. Case by case:

FailureBehaviourWhy
Agent process crash or hangThe OS-native policy keeps enforcing, because the kernel holds it. The SCM restarts the service after 5 s, and the watchdog repairs it (#56, #220).Stopping the agent removes reporting, not enforcement.
Panic while parsing one fileThe agent is built with panic = "unwind". Each file parse runs inside its own catch_unwind boundary. A panic there marks that file's identity as unparseable, raises a fileid.parse_panic event (rate-limited, with the file's hash if one was computed), and the subsystem carries on with the next file. Any decision the agent itself makes treats an unparseable file as an unknown file (implicit deny in enforce mode, #39). Per-file panics do not count towards the subsystem circuit breaker below.With abort, one crafted file that triggers a parser panic would crash the whole agent on every scan, blinding it in a loop. Counting per-file panics towards the breaker would let a standard user disable a subsystem by dropping three crafted files. Treating the file as unknown keeps the decision closed.
Panic in a subsystem outside a per-file boundaryThe subsystem task is wrapped with catch_unwind and restarted (#56). After 3 such panics in 10 minutes the subsystem is marked Failed and a critical health alert is raised. If the failed subsystem is the one that answers driver verdict requests, the driver sees the agent as disconnected, and the driver row below applies. Aborts that unwinding cannot catch (stack overflow, out of memory) fall back to the first row (agent process crash).A real bug, not a crafted input, is the likely cause, so it is surfaced loudly. The native layer keeps enforcing whatever the subsystem state.
New bundle (pending) fails verification or activationKeep active. Report PolicyRejected(reason) (#61).Nothing was rolled back: the device stays on the policy it already had.
Active bundle (N) corrupt or fails verification at loadLoad previous (N-1) if it verifies and the anti-rollback record names it as the bundle N directly replaced (ADR 0007), as #225 specifies. Otherwise the next row applies. This is a bounded, one-step exception to anti-rollback: the anti-rollback record keeps N, so only bundles at N or above are accepted from the server. The agent raises a critical policy.lkg_loaded tamper event at once (not only when both bundles fail) and starts a rapid check-in to fetch a fresh bundle.Availability: disk corruption must not lock a machine down when a verified, previously approved policy exists. N-1 may be weaker than N (for example, if N added a deny), so this is recorded as an accepted risk below.
Active and previous bundles both fail, after a policy was ever accepted (including when the anti-rollback floor rejects every bundle on disk, ADR 0007)Load the built-in emergency policy from #225 in enforce mode: allow OS-signed binaries and Palisade itself, block the rest. Raise a critical event. The emergency policy is an extra restriction in Palisade's own layer. It never removes, replaces or relaxes the installed OS-native policies: see "Emergency policy and the native layer" below. In native_only mode it is audit-only: see "Who enforces the emergency policy" below.Corruption after enrolment is a possible attack, so it must not relax anything.
No policy yet (first install, before the first bundle)Run the built-in safe defaults from #61: audit mode, with the mandatory blocklists (#87) enforced if the agent ships them. Report PolicyMissing.Nothing has been approved yet, so there is nothing to protect by locking down. Blocking everything at install time would make deployment fail.
Policy stale or past expires_atKeep enforcing the current policy. Report PolicyStale. Never relax automatically (#61, #225).Staleness is not evidence that the policy is wrong.
Driver absent, disconnected, timed out or version-mismatchedFollow driver_failure_mode (#113). Default fail_safe (pass-through with audit) for early rollout rings; fail_secure recommended once stable. The native layer keeps enforcing either way.The driver only adds restrictions on top of the native policy (ADR 0002), so failing it open loses the extra rules but keeps the baseline.
Clock skew, rollback or forward jumpTime-bounded grants (exceptions, override codes, maintenance windows, tokens) follow the rules in "Time rules" below.By default only offline override codes and tokens consult the wall clock, so changing it cannot start, extend or revive a scheduled grant. The remaining gaps are listed as accepted risks.

Emergency policy and the native layer. The installed OS-native code integrity policies are enforced by the kernel and do not depend on the agent's bundle cache (ADR 0002). Loading the emergency policy:

  • leaves every installed native base and supplemental policy in place and active. While in emergency mode the agent makes no change to native policy files at all: it does not remove, replace, refresh, downgrade or stage any of them. A native deny, including a deny on an OS-signed binary, therefore stays enforced. A native policy that was already staged from an earlier verified bundle (for example, one waiting for a reboot) is left as it is;
  • does not compile the emergency policy to a native policy. Native deployment and activation stay governed by the activation contract in #6, which only deploys policies compiled from a verified bundle;
  • applies the emergency policy only to the decisions Palisade itself makes (the driver layer when present, and the agent's own evaluation and reporting). A file must pass both layers, so the effective result is the native policy and the emergency policy. The emergency policy's "allow OS-signed binaries" can never override a native deny.

Who enforces the emergency policy. It depends on the enforcement_strategy (ADR 0002):

  • layered or driver_only: the Palisade driver enforces it before execution. If the driver is absent or failing, the driver row of the table applies (driver_failure_mode).
  • native_only (the M2 default): there is no Palisade pre-execution enforcer, so the emergency policy is not enforced. Enforcement stays at the installed native policy, which was compiled from the last verified bundle the device activated, so it is no weaker than a policy that was already approved. Rules that only the agent or driver could enforce were already reported as "not enforced" in this mode, and stay so. The agent applies the emergency policy to its own audit evaluation, so events show what it would block. It reports the degraded state as PolicyEmergencyUnenforced in health, with a critical policy.emergency_loaded event that says the emergency policy has no enforcer. The console shows the device as degraded until a verified bundle arrives.

A native emergency policy for native_only devices (a separate, pre-built base policy that allows only OS-signed binaries and Palisade, and intersects with the installed one) is not part of this decision. It would need signing inputs and possibly a reboot, so it is left to #225 and #6.

The emergency policy itself is defined in #225. When the agent next receives a verified bundle, it leaves emergency mode and normal activation (#61, #6) resumes.

Time rules. The wall clock can be changed by an administrator or a spoofed time source, so by default only one decision uses it: redeeming an offline override code on an offline-started agent (rule 3). The monotonic clock only counts forwards while the agent runs. From these the agent keeps two values:

  • Anchored time: the server time from an authenticated check-in reply (mTLS with server pinning, ADR 0015), advanced by the monotonic clock. It is valid until the agent process stops or the machine resumes from a sleep that the monotonic clock did not count. The agent is anchored while it holds a valid anchored time, and offline-started otherwise (after a restart or such a resume, before its next check-in).
  • The floor: a lower bound on real time in protected storage (#220). On load it is advanced only by the monotonic time elapsed since the load, never by boot uptime, so a service restart within one boot is not counted twice. While anchored it is raised to anchored time. It is written every minute and at shutdown, in every state, and a write never lowers it. It does not count time spent powered off, so it lags real time after a shutdown.

For a scheduled grant with start s and end e (an exception or maintenance window from the policy bundle):

  1. Anchored. The grant is active when s <= anchored time < e and e > floor. The wall clock plays no part, so changing it cannot start, extend, end or revive a grant.

  2. Offline-started, default. Grants from the policy bundle do not start or continue. A grant that was active when the agent stopped stays closed until the next check-in. This is the closed direction: scheduled work waits for the device to check in. For offline maintenance, an administrator uses an override code (rule 3) instead.

  3. Offline override codes and unlock tokens (#222). A code or token is accepted only if it is authenticated by its secret, its ID is not in the redeemed-code list, its end is after the floor, and its validity window contains anchored time (when anchored) or the wall clock (when offline-started).

    • Redeem before use. The ID is written durably to the redeemed-code list, together with the open-session marker below, before the session takes effect. A crash after redemption therefore leaves the code redeemed, never reusable, and the session is still reported as ended at the next start.
    • Session timing. The session is timed on the monotonic clock, not by s and e, and it lasts at most the code's duration. It ends at the first event after which the agent can no longer count elapsed time itself: the agent process stopping (service stop, crash or restart), a reboot, or a resume from a sleep the monotonic clock did not count (the same events that end anchored time). A session is never resumed after such an event. The agent marks the session open in protected storage (written with the redeemed ID, before the session takes effect), and if it finds an open session at start it records it as ended and raises an event, so the end is reported even after a crash. Time the agent cannot count is therefore never credited to a session, and the access period can only be shorter than the code's duration, never longer. Work that needs a restart or reboot uses a new code after it.
    • Pruning. An entry in the redeemed-code list is kept until the code's end is at or before the floor as stored in protected storage. The ID is removed only after a floor write that covers the code's end has completed. After a crash the stored floor still covers the code, so the floor check alone rejects it, whatever the clock shows.

  4. Opt-in offline scheduling. A group may set offline_scheduled_grants = allow. Then, while offline-started, rule 1 applies with session time in place of anchored time. An offline session starts each time the agent becomes offline-started: at agent start, and on resume from an uncounted sleep. Session time is the wall clock recorded when the offline session started, plus the monotonic time since, so wall-clock changes during the session do not move it. Session time is discarded when the agent becomes anchored. The console marks groups using this option.

  5. Skew. tamper.clock.skew is raised, depending on the state:

    • while anchored: when the wall clock differs from anchored time by more than 5 minutes;
    • when an offline session starts: when the wall clock is more than 60 s behind the floor;
    • during an offline session: when the wall clock drifts from session time by more than 60 s backwards or 5 minutes forwards, measured cumulatively, so small steps add up.

    The alert sets a skew latch in protected storage. Only an authenticated check-in clears it, and the offline-session checks stop once the agent is anchored, so a corrected clock does not re-set the latch. While the latch is set, rule 4 is off and rule 2 applies.

#220 implements these rules as one pure function of (wall clock, monotonic clock, stored state), with a property-test table covering anchored, offline-started, service restart, uncounted sleep, offline reboot, rollback, forward jump and slow drift. The table also covers an override session across a service restart, a crash, a reboot and an uncounted sleep, and a crash at each write point: between redeeming a code and opening its session, and between a floor write and pruning an ID.

Accepted risk. With the default rules, the wall clock only matters for offline override codes on an offline-started agent. Someone who can change the clock (administrator rights, or a spoofed time source) can redeem a genuine, unredeemed code outside its intended window: later, by setting the clock back, or earlier, by setting it forward. Each code still works only once, only while its end is after the floor, and only for its own monotonic-timed duration, which ends at the next agent restart, reboot or uncounted sleep. They cannot forge a code or reuse a redeemed one: the ID is recorded before the session opens, and it is only dropped once the stored floor alone rejects the code. The same applies to unlock tokens.

With offline_scheduled_grants = allow, someone who sets the clock while the agent is not running (with physical access, administrator rights, or a spoofed time source at boot) can, until the next check-in, start a scheduled grant early or use a grant whose end the floor has not reached. An authenticated check-in ends this: from then on rule 1 uses server time, and a clock that is still wrong raises tamper.clock.skew. Check-in cannot always detect that it happened. If the clock is put back right before the device reconnects, a grant used inside the time the device was powered off looks the same as a legitimate offline run. The uploaded events still show the grant was used offline, which is why the console marks groups with this option.

"A policy was ever accepted". The device is treated as having had a policy if the anti-rollback record (#225) shows a version above zero, or an active or previous cache file exists. An unverified pending file does not count, so an interrupted first download leaves the device on the first-install path. Deleting the record alone does not unlock the first-install path. The mismatch between record copies raises tamper.policy.rollback_suspected (#225).

Consequences

Positive

  • One rule covers almost every case: if Palisade has ever enforced a policy, failures keep it enforced or make it stricter. The bounded exceptions are listed in Security impact.
  • The #61 and #225 behaviours are reconciled. Each applies to a different, testable state.
  • A crafted file cannot use a parser panic to stop the agent reporting or to trip a subsystem circuit breaker.

Negative

  • panic = "unwind" makes binaries slightly larger than abort, and code must be unwind-safe at subsystem boundaries. Because Cargo applies panic to a whole profile, the release profile uses unwind for every binary. The no_std driver crate is built separately (#8) and sets its own panic strategy.
  • The driver's default fail_safe leaves driver-only rules unenforced while the driver is down. The endpoint reports those rules as "not enforced" (#113), so it is not counted as effective for them.
  • A device whose caches are both corrupted after enrolment becomes very restrictive until it gets a new bundle. Users will notice, which is intended.
  • By default, scheduled maintenance windows and exceptions do not run on a device that has restarted and cannot check in. Offline maintenance needs an override code.
  • The time rules need protected storage for the floor, the redeemed-code list, the open-session marker and the skew latch. Writes to them are ordered: the redeemed ID before the session opens, and the stored floor before an ID is pruned.
  • An override session ends when the agent restarts, the machine reboots, or it resumes from a sleep the agent could not count. Offline work that needs a restart or reboot needs a second code.
  • While in emergency mode, no native policy change reaches the device, including one that would have added a deny. The device keeps its last installed native policy until a verified bundle arrives.
  • On native_only devices the emergency policy has no pre-execution enforcer. Losing both caches leaves the device on its last installed native policy, reported as degraded, not on the stricter emergency policy.

Security impact

This ADR decides whether crashing, corrupting or confusing Palisade is a bypass. With these defaults it is not: the kernel-enforced native layer survives agent failure, losing both cached bundles leads to the stricter emergency policy where a Palisade driver can enforce it (it only adds restrictions on top of the installed native policy, never replacing it) and to the unchanged, last-approved native policy on native_only devices, a stale policy keeps enforcing, crafted files cannot disable a subsystem, and by default a clock change cannot start, extend or revive a scheduled grant. There are five deliberate, bounded weak points:

  1. the first-install audit window (built-in mandatory blocklists still enforce, and it ends at the first verified bundle);
  2. the one-step N-1 fallback when active is corrupt (it raises a critical tamper event at once, it never goes further back than N-1, and the agent re-fetches N or later straight away). Only SYSTEM can write the cache directory (#220), so an attacker who can trigger this already has stronger options;
  3. the driver's default fail_safe (the native layer still enforces, and it is configurable to fail_secure);
  4. on native_only devices, no enforcement of the emergency policy when both caches fail (the last installed native policy, compiled from a verified bundle, keeps enforcing, and the device is reported as degraded); and
  5. the clock risks in "Accepted risk" above: using an unredeemed override code or token outside its window (each code still opens one session, which ends at the next agent restart, reboot or uncounted sleep), and, only for groups that opt in to offline scheduling, starting or stretching scheduled grants until the next check-in.

All five are listed in the threat model as accepted risks (#219) and are exercised by the bypass regression suite (#230).

Links

  • Supersedes: 0012
  • Issues #20, #6 (native policy deployment and activation), #19 (release profile), #39, #56, #61, #87, #113, #219, #220, #222, #225 (emergency policy, anti-rollback), #226, #230.
  • ADR 0002 (enforcement layers), ADR 0015 (authenticated server time), ADR 0007 (cache files and anti-rollback ordering).

0019. Contributor sign-off: DCO, no CLA

  • Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Deciders: Palisade maintainer

Context

ADR 0010 licenses Palisade as Apache-2.0 OR MIT and accepts contributions under the same terms (inbound = outbound). It leaves open whether contributors must also confirm, on each commit, that they have the right to submit their change, and points to #28 for that decision. This ADR makes it.

Palisade is security software that runs as a privileged Windows service. Its history should show, for every change, who submitted it and on what terms, so that a disputed or tainted contribution can be traced and removed. It has one maintainer, no legal entity and no budget, so whatever is chosen must cost nothing to run and must not put off a first-time contributor.

Two common mechanisms exist. A Contributor Licence Agreement (CLA) is a separate legal agreement, signed once per contributor, that grants the project rights to the contribution, sometimes including the right to relicense it. The Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO, version 1.1, https://developercertificate.org) is a short statement that a contributor certifies per commit by adding a Signed-off-by: Name <email> trailer, usually with git commit -s.

Decision drivers

  1. A clear, per-change record of who submitted what, under the project licence.
  2. Nothing that stops a first-time contributor: no account on another service, no legal review.
  3. No infrastructure, secrets or services for one maintainer to run. CI may use only the allowlisted, SHA-pinned actions (docs/ci.md).
  4. No extra rights for the maintainer beyond the project licence, so contributors give up nothing by contributing.
  5. Checkable by a machine on every pull request.

Considered options

  1. Inbound = outbound only (the current state). The Apache-2.0 contribution clause already says contributions are licensed under the project licence. Costs nothing, but leaves no explicit, per-commit statement that the contributor had the right to submit the change, and nothing to check. Weak on driver 1 and 5.
  2. A CLA. Gives the strongest legal record and can allow relicensing. But it needs a signing service, a stored record of signatures, a legal text the maintainer cannot have reviewed, and a hosted bot or third-party action that is not on the allowlist. Contributors must sign before their first pull request, and a relicensing right asks them to trust the maintainer with more than the licence grants. Fails drivers 2, 3 and 4.
  3. DCO sign-off, checked by a script in the repository. Each non-merge commit in a pull request that is not exempt (see Decision) carries Signed-off-by:, and a short shell script (.github/scripts/check-dco.sh), run by a workflow that uses only actions/checkout, checks them. No service, no secret, no extra rights. The DCO certifies the contributor's right to submit, which is what driver 1 asks for; it does not allow relicensing, which driver 4 rules out anyway.
  4. DCO sign-off, checked by a hosted app or a third-party action. Same record as option 3, but adds an external integration or an action outside the allowlist, and with it a supply-chain dependency with access to pull requests. Fails driver 3 for no gain over option 3.

Decision

Option 3. Every non-merge commit in a pull request carries a DCO 1.1 sign-off, except in a pull request the repository owner opened. There is no CLA.

  • A sign-off is a Signed-off-by: Name <email> trailer in the commit message, with a non-empty name and an email that matches the commit's author email, ignoring case. git commit -s adds one.
  • A DCO check, added in #244 as the workflow .github/workflows/dco.yml and the script .github/scripts/check-dco.sh with its tests, runs on every pull request. It fails if any non-merge commit lacks a matching sign-off, with the Dependabot rule and the owner exemption below as the only exceptions. The script lives in the repository and changes only through review (CODEOWNERS).
  • Merge commits are skipped. They are not free of content: a merge that resolves a conflict, or that is edited before it is committed, can add changes found in neither parent. They are skipped because the hosting platform's "update branch" button creates them, usually without a sign-off, and failing those would punish contributors for keeping a branch current. Changes made inside a merge commit are therefore not covered by the check (see Negative and Security impact). Contributors who must change code while resolving a conflict should rebase instead.
  • Once this ADR is accepted, DCO becomes a required status check on main. Changing the ruleset is a repository setting, tracked with the other required checks in #21. The steps are in docs/repo-settings.md (from #244). Until then the check reports but does not block.
  • Pull requests are squash-merged, and the squashed commit on main is not itself checked. The record is the pull request's own commits, which GitHub keeps with the closed pull request.
  • Dependabot signs off its own commits, but with a different email from the one it authors them with. The check accepts that sign-off only when GitHub reports Dependabot as the pull request's author, and only for commits authored at the bot's address. The pull request author comes from GitHub, not from the commit, so copying the bot's address into a commit gains nothing.
  • Owner-opened pull requests are exempt (#249). When GitHub reports the pull request's author_association as OWNER, the check passes with a notice and does not inspect the commits. The owner holds the copyright and the right to license their own changes, so a sign-off adds nothing; this covers changes prepared for the owner by tools or AI agents, which never sign off in the owner's name. The exemption is decided by GitHub's record of who opened the pull request, not by anything in the commits, so it cannot be claimed by copying the owner's name or email. It covers every commit in such a pull request, so when the owner carries someone else's commit, the owner checks that commit's sign-off by hand. CONTRIBUTING.md states the same rule.
  • No other exemptions exist.
  • The licence terms do not change: contributions remain inbound = outbound under Apache-2.0 OR MIT (ADR 0010).

A later PR can be checked against this decision: no CLA text, signing service or CLA bot is added, and the DCO check stays a script in the repository run with allowlisted actions only.

Consequences

Positive

  • Every non-merge commit in a pull request that someone other than the owner opened has a signed statement from its author that they may submit it. The owner's own pull requests are recorded by GitHub's account history instead (see Decision).
  • Nothing to sign up for or sign in advance; git commit -s is enough.
  • No service, secret or third-party action to run or trust. The checker is under 100 lines of shell, with tests.
  • Contributors keep every right the project licence gives them; nobody can relicense their work.

Negative

  • First-time contributors will forget to sign off and must amend or rebase their commits. The check prints the exact commands, and CONTRIBUTING.md explains them.
  • A sign-off is a statement, not proof of identity. The check confirms that a trailer matches the author email; it cannot confirm the person is who they say they are.
  • Without a CLA, the project cannot relicense contributions. Any future change of licence would need every contributor's consent, or the removal of their code.
  • The record for squash-merged changes lives in the pull request, not in main's history. If the hosting platform lost pull request history, the per-commit sign-offs would go with it.
  • The owner exemption puts the owner-opened pull requests' record in GitHub's account history rather than in a trailer, and it leaves a carried commit from someone else to the owner's manual check.
  • The Dependabot rule depends on the bot's current author and sign-off addresses. If they change, its pull requests fail DCO until the script is updated.
  • Changes introduced inside a merge commit, by conflict resolution or by editing the merge, carry no sign-off and are not checked. Squash merging puts them on main like any other change. The pull request's diff, which reviewers read, still shows them.

Security impact

The DCO is a provenance control for the source, not a runtime control. A sign-off ties each change to a named contributor who has certified their right to submit it, which helps trace and remove a tainted or disputed contribution that arrives through a pull request: the source-hosting boundary TB-12 in the threat model. It does not stop malicious code: a hostile contributor can sign off just as easily as an honest one, and it does nothing about a compromised third-party crate, build tool or action (actor AC-09), which the dependency policy covers. Review, CODEOWNERS and the required checks remain the controls against malicious changes.

The check has three known gaps, all closed by review rather than by the check:

  • Content added inside a merge commit is not checked (see Decision).
  • An owner-opened pull request is not checked at all, so a third party's commit carried in it passes without a sign-off unless the owner checks it (see Decision).
  • The workflow runs the script from the pull request's own branch, so a pull request can edit dco.yml or check-dco.sh to make its own check pass. Every change under .github/ needs the maintainer's review (CODEOWNERS), and the reviewer reads that diff before merging.

Choosing a script in the repository over a hosted app or third-party action adds no new code with access to pull requests, and the workflow needs only contents: read. The workflow uses the pull_request trigger, not pull_request_target, so fork pull requests run it without secrets or a write token. Every value taken from the event (the commit SHAs and the pull request author's login) reaches the script through environment variables, never through expression interpolation into the shell.

Links

  • Issue #28 (contributor docs, governance and licensing), which this ADR completes.
  • PR #244: adds the DCO workflow and script, and the sign-off section of CONTRIBUTING.md, the DCO section of docs/ci.md and the steps in docs/repo-settings.md for making the check required.
  • PR #249: the owner exemption in the DCO workflow.
  • Issue #21: required status checks on main, which DCO joins once this ADR is accepted.
  • ADR 0010: the licence, which left this decision to #28.

Tracking issue#219, under epic #18

Palisade is an educational, personal-development project and is in the design phase (see the README). Almost every component in this document is still to be built. The model describes the planned design, as fixed by the ADRs and the GitHub issues, so that each component can be checked against it while it is built. The status column says honestly what exists today.

This document is the reference that every child of epic #18 and every enforcement epic (#4, #6, #7, #8, #9) is checked against. It states what Palisade claims to resist, and just as plainly what it does not.

How to use this document

  • Threat IDs have the form T-<component>-<nn>, for example T-agent-03. They are stable: an ID is never renumbered or reused. A threat that no longer applies is marked retired in its row, with the reason, and stays in the table.
  • Code comments that implement a mitigation reference the threat: // threat: T-agent-03. Bypass scenarios in #230 list the threats they test in their threat_ids field. Coverage can then be found with git grep 'T-agent-03'.
  • Issue keys are GitHub issue numbers in this repository. A mitigation always names at least one issue that owns it.
  • Status has three values:
    • planned: the design exists (an ADR or an issue), but there is no code on main yet.
    • implemented: the code that enforces the mitigation is on main, and the verification column names an existing test, fuzz target or CI check that exercises it. When the component that will call that code is still to be built (often the agent), the row's residual-risk note says so.
    • verified: a #230 bypass scenario or a recorded red-team test shows the mitigation holding end to end on the Windows VM harness (#26). Nothing is verified yet, because the harness does not exist yet.
  • Impact and likelihood are L, M or H. Likelihood assumes the planned mitigation is absent, so it says how much the mitigation matters. Residual risk is in its own column.
  • When you change Palisade: if your change adds or moves a trust boundary, adds a parser of untrusted input, or changes how a listed mitigation works, update this document in the same pull request (see Process).

Scope

Modelled

Every Palisade component and the paths between them:

  • on the endpoint: the optional kernel driver, the agent service, the health and watchdog service, the tray notifier, the local CLI, local IPC, the protected local store (policy cache, anti-rollback record, hash cache, time state), the event buffer and the update client;
  • the OS-native policy layer that Palisade compiles and deploys (ADR 0002);
  • on the server: the agent endpoints, the REST API, the web console, the database, the signer, the certificate authorities, event ingest and outbound or inbound integrations;
  • the CI and release pipeline, from source to the agent's update client;
  • the shared policy engine and file-identity parsers, which every component relies on;
  • script and interpreter control (#7), which the interpreter bypass tree depends on.

Not modelled

  • Physical attacks that need special hardware: DMA attacks through external ports, cold-boot memory extraction, hardware implants and side channels such as speculative execution.
  • Firmware and boot-chain implants below the OS (UEFI implants, a compromised boot manager). Secure Boot is an assumption, not something Palisade enforces.
  • Vulnerabilities in Windows itself. An attacker who exploits a kernel bug is treated as the kernel-level actor in Actors and claims, and Palisade does not claim to resist them.
  • The security of the operator's own identity provider, directory, SIEM, ticketing system or hosting platform, beyond how Palisade authenticates to them.
  • High-volume denial of service against a deployment, and social engineering of the maintainer (both also out of scope in SECURITY.md).
  • Formal certification of any kind (#18 lists it as out of scope).

Assumed OS baseline

  • Endpoints: Windows 11, and Windows 10 22H2 only while it still receives security updates. Servers: Windows Server 2019 or later. x64 and ARM64.
  • Secure Boot is on. Disk encryption with the OS's built-in full-volume encryption and a TPM protector is recommended; where it is off, the residual-risk register applies.
  • The full list is in Assumptions.

Method

  • STRIDE per element. Every component has a table that considers Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. A category that does not apply is written as N/A with the reason.
  • Attack trees for the bypass techniques that are specific to application control. They use AND and OR nodes, and every leaf maps to a mitigation, an issue and a verification.
  • LINDDUN-lite for privacy threats. Its output is shared with #228 (privacy and data minimisation).
  • MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs are given for bypass trees where one fits (ATT&CK is an open framework). This answers the open question in #219: the mapping is included, at the level of attack-tree roots, and #230 scenarios may carry the same IDs in their technique field.

Three design decisions shape the whole model:

  1. The native layer keeps enforcing without the agent (ADR 0002, ADR 0012). Stopping or crashing the agent removes reporting and the driver-only rules, not the baseline policy.
  2. Everything the agent trusts is signed end to end (ADR 0005, ADR 0008): policy bundles, commands, unlock tokens, trust sets and updates. The transport is protected too, but trust never depends on it.
  3. Decisions never wait for the network (ADR 0009). Slowing or blocking the server cannot hang or loosen enforcement.

Assets

Ratings are for confidentiality (C), integrity (I) and availability (A): H (high), M (medium) or L (low).

IDAssetWhere it livesCIAWhy
A-01Enforcement correctness (the decision itself)Driver, native policy, agent evaluatorLHHA wrong allow is a bypass. A wrong deny stops work. The rules are not secret.
A-02Policy bundles: server-side source and the endpoint cacheDatabase, signer output, %ProgramData%\Palisade\MHHPolicy defines what may run. Read access reveals the gaps an attacker would look for, but Palisade does not depend on policy secrecy.
A-03Private keys: policy signing, update signing, root CA, issuing CA, unlock token, escrow, audit chainSigner back end, offline root machine, release signing tokenHHMA stolen key lets an attacker sign policy, updates, certificates or unlock tokens for the whole fleet.
A-04Device identity keys and certificatesCNG key store on the device (TPM where present); certificate in the agent storeHHMA copied key lets an attacker impersonate the device.
A-05Event and audit logs: the endpoint buffer and the server storeAgent store, database, external log sinkMHMThey are the evidence trail (ISM-1815, ISM-1985). Edits hide attacks.
A-06Exception, override and unlock secrets: device secrets, stop-code hashes, CLI password hashes, unredeemed tokens and codesDatabase (escrow), agent store, console sessionHHMThey switch protection off.
A-07Admin credentials, API tokens and SSO configurationDatabase (hashes, envelope-encrypted secrets), identity providerHHMThey control the management plane and so every endpoint.
A-08Collected user data: usernames, command lines, file pathsEvent buffer, database, SIEM exportsHMLPersonal data, sometimes with secrets in command lines (#228).
A-09Release artefacts and the build pipelineRepository, GitHub-hosted runners, release storage, update metadataLHMA tampered release runs as SYSTEM on every endpoint. Artefacts are public by design.

Actors and claims

This table is what "users cannot disable or bypass" means for Palisade (ISM-0846): the claim column says which actors Palisade resists and under which conditions, and the last column says what Palisade does where it does not resist.

IDActorCapabilitiesPalisade's claimGoal where not resisted
AC-01Standard userRuns programs as themselves; writes to their profile and to user-writable folders; uses the tray and unprivileged CLI verbs.Resists fully while the driver is enforcing. Cannot run code that policy blocks, or stop, reconfigure, uninstall or blind Palisade. Exception when driver-only conditions lapse: without the driver, or while it is disconnected or its requests time out under the default driver_failure_mode = fail_safe (which a standard user can provoke by flooding the agent, T-driver-07), owner and other driver-only conditions only audit. A path-plus-owner rule then falls back to the broader native path allow, so if ACL drift makes an allowed path user-writable, a standard user can run a payload from it (R-07, T-engine-11, AT-03.3). fail_secure closes the timeout case (ADR 0012).
AC-02Malware running as a standard userAs AC-01, plus automation, persistence in the user's profile, and injection into the user's own processes.Resists fully while the driver is enforcing, as for AC-01, with the same exception when driver-only conditions lapse: no driver, or a disconnect or timeout under the default fail_safe (R-07, T-driver-07, T-engine-11, AT-03.3). Phishing a user for a single-use, device-bound unlock token is limited by token scope (T-tray-01).
AC-03Local administrator (legitimate)Full control of the OS configuration; can load drivers, change services, debug processes and boot other media.Resists casual tampering without an unlock token: stopping the service, uninstalling, editing configuration or deleting the cache (#220, #222). A signed native policy on a Secure Boot device resists removal (#85). Does not resist a determined administrator, who can disable the driver and then the agent (ADR 0013).Detect and alert: tamper events, heartbeat gaps at the server, binary-integrity failures.
AC-04Malware with administrator or SYSTEM rightsAs AC-03, automated and hostile; can read anything a SYSTEM process can.Does not claim to resist. Listed as residual risk R-01.Detect and alert. The native layer, especially a signed one, keeps enforcing until the attacker takes further steps.
AC-05Kernel-level attacker, for example through a vulnerable signed driver (BYOVD)Arbitrary kernel read and write; can remove callbacks and kill protected processes.Does not claim to resist. The vulnerable driver blocklist (#87) and driver load control (#105) aim to stop the entry point. Residual risk R-02.Detect and alert where any user-mode or server-side signal survives.
AC-06Malicious or compromised console administratorAny action their RBAC role and scope permit, through the console or API.Partly resists. Limited by scoped RBAC (#131), optional four-eyes approval (#142, #229), the mandatory-deny tier no policy can override (ADR 0004), staged rollout (#135) and audit (#132, #229). An administrator with tenant-wide rights and no dual control can widen policy (R-08).Audit, alerting and immutable policy history make the change visible and reversible.
AC-07Network attacker: on-path, or a TLS-inspecting proxyReads, drops, delays and modifies traffic; presents certificates from its own CA.Resists for confidentiality and integrity: mTLS with server pinning (ADR 0005, #223) and end-to-end signatures. Does not resist blocking traffic, but enforcement continues offline (ADR 0009).Offline devices keep their policy; check-in gaps are reported.
AC-08Compromised management serverEverything the server process can do: use the signer, read the database as the runtime role, talk to every agent.Resists pushing binaries: update metadata is signed by keys not held on the server (#226). Resists cross-tenant reads caused by application bugs at the database layer (ADR 0006); NOBYPASSRLS and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY stop RLS from being disabled. Does not resist cross-tenant reads by a process that holds the runtime role, because the server sets the tenant scope itself. Does not resist pushing a permissive, validly signed policy unless dual control and hardware-backed signing are in place (R-08).Signing audit, agents reporting bundle kid and hash, dual control.
AC-09Compromised dependency or supply chainMalicious code in a crate, build tool or action.Partly resists: registry and source restrictions, lockfile, advisory scans and SHA-pinned actions (#21, #23). Does not resist a malicious release of a crate that is already trusted, before an advisory exists (R-15).Advisory scan daily; SBOM per release (#226).
AC-10Compromised CI runner or maintainer accountRun code in CI, push to branches, open and merge pull requests, start a release.Partly resists: ephemeral GitHub-hosted runners, protected tags and release environment, provenance attestations, and an offline threshold root for update metadata (#226). Does not resist a fully compromised sole maintainer account (R-14).Provenance and pal verify let anyone check what was built from which commit.
AC-11Insider with physical accessBoots other media, removes the disk, uses safe mode.Partly resists: safe-mode registration and tamper events (#220). With disk encryption and Secure Boot, offline tampering is impractical. Does not resist without disk encryption (R-05). DMA attacks are out of scope.Binary and cache integrity checks at the next boot.

Data-flow diagrams

In each data-flow diagram, every node sits in exactly one subgraph, every subgraph is one trust zone, and subgraphs are not nested. An arrow that leaves its subgraph crosses at least one trust boundary, and its row names each one: at level 0, which has no separate network zone, F-03 crosses both TB-04 and TB-05. Every arrow has a flow ID. A flow that stays inside one zone says "None (same zone)" in its Boundary column, and names the boundary that the zone's protection enforces, where there is one. The table under the diagram gives each flow's protocol, authentication, integrity protection, confidentiality protection and the boundary it crosses.
