T-engine-04TPath forms (ADS, 8.3 names, case, trailing dots and spaces, \\?\, UNC, volume GUID) make one file match a different path rule.Standard userHH#54, #32plannedNew path forms may appear (R-16). Rule matching already normalises separators, prefixes, device paths, case, streams and dot components, and treats an unexpanded short name as unknown; volume GUID mapping and the agent's final-path facts are still #54 and #4.
T-engine-05TA broad allow rule defeats a deliberate deny because of the precedence model.Policy author mistakeHM#35, #125implementedPolicies that select allow_wins accept this risk; validation warns (allow_wins_not_recommended).
T-engine-06RA decision cannot be explained or reproduced later.Any decisionMM#41plannedNone.
T-engine-07IA block message reveals policy internals (which paths are trusted).Standard userLM#147, #41plannedSome detail is intended so users can ask for help.
T-engine-08DCrafted input (PE tables, policy YAML) consumes excessive CPU or memory.Standard user (files), policy author (YAML)MM#45, #190, #42implementedPE parsing limits are per table; the full evaluation budget is #42.
T-engine-09EA memory-safety bug in a file parser gives code execution in the SYSTEM agent.Crafted file on the endpointHL#19, #45, #25, #230implementedLogic bugs and panics remain possible; panics are contained (T-agent-12). The fuzz targets run for 60 s each on every PR and for 30 minutes each weekly (docs/testing.md), and parsers still to come need their own targets (#230).
T-engine-10EA path rule allows a folder that has a user-writable descendant (%WINDIR%\Temp, %WINDIR%\Tasks, %WINDIR%\System32\spool\drivers\color), or a folder whose ACL is later loosened, so a user copies a payload there and runs it.Standard userHH#54, #212, #124, #87implementedACLs can change between checks; the drift report finds it later (#212). The engine and ACL evaluation are on main; the agent that computes the writability fact for each file is still to be built (#4).
T-engine-11SA user gains owner-based trust for a file: by owning it, by taking ownership of a file in a trusted location, or by overwriting in place an administrator-owned file whose ACL lets users write to it. NTFS keeps the existing owner on an in-place overwrite; the owner only changes when a new file is created.Standard userHM#117, #54, #220plannedOwner is a driver-only condition (ADR 0002): without the driver, or with it failing open, owner-based rules only audit and a path-plus-owner rule falls back to the broader native path allow (R-07). With the driver, the gap is a write made while the DACL was briefly permissive and tightened again before the trust was re-checked; the change journal and re-hash (#60, #46) record it.
T-engine-12EA trusted installer or updater writes or fetches an attacker file, which then inherits trust.Ability to influence an installer or updater (custom action, download source)HM#114, #116, #119plannedA trusted updater that is itself compromised passes its trust on until it is revoked.
T-engine-13EA parent-process trust rule is abused: a trusted parent spawns a shell or interpreter, or the attacker spoofs the reported parent process ID.Standard userHM#118, #175, #111plannedUntil the driver ships, parent conditions can only be audited (ADR 0002, R-07).
T-engine-14SA file whose signature does not hold (digest mismatch, tampered signer data, weak digest, a chain to an untrusted root, a signer not allowed to sign code, revoked before the signing time, or expired without a trusted timestamp) is treated as signed by a trusted publisher.Crafted or altered signed fileHM#48, #49, #50, #32implementedThe OS trust store cross-check (#48) and fetching revocation data online (#4) are still to be built; until then revocation is only what policy ships or the caller supplies. Parser differentials remain (R-16).
T-engine-15SA file is accepted as catalog-signed through a tampered or untrusted catalog, a digest looked up in the wrong slot, or a member entry for a different file.Ability to place a catalog file or alter a fileHL#51implementedThe OS catalog database cross-check (#51) and folding catalog matches into the file identity record (#55) are still to be built.
T-engine-16EAn administrator of a tenant, a group or a device layer weakens a control it inherits: suppresses an inherited mandatory deny or blocklist rule, lowers a locked mode or a locked setting, pins an older version of an inherited blocklist library, moves its rules ahead of global ones under first_match, or references another tenant's library.Rights over a node below the one that sets the controlHM#37, #125implementedWhoever can edit the ancestor node can still change the control there; who may edit which node is enforced by the server (#131, #10), and one administrator without dual control can widen policy for the nodes they manage (R-08).

Bypass attack trees

Each tree has a goal at the root. OR means any child achieves the parent. AND means every child is needed, so blocking any one of them defeats the parent. Each leaf ends with → and its mitigation, the owning issue, the threat ID and the verification.

Verification IDs:

  • BYP-* are bypass scenarios for the #230 suite (tests/bypass/);
  • FUZZ-* are #230 fuzz targets;
  • RT-* are entries in the #230 red-team checklist, for techniques that cannot be automated safely;
  • TEST-* are unit or integration tests owned by the named issue;
  • TEST: followed by a test name is a test that already exists on main;
  • fuzz: followed by a name is a cargo-fuzz target that already exists on main;
  • CI: followed by a command is a check that already runs in CI.

The BYP, FUZZ, RT and TEST-* names are proposals. #230 fixes the final names.

In the verification column, entries are separated by ;, and each entry that points at something on main starts with its tag:

  • TEST: then the crate in backticks and one or more test paths in backticks, for example TEST: `palisade-policy` `tests::allow_rules_need_a_strong_positive_identity` . A later crate name in backticks switches the crate. The last segment of a path is the test function's name.
  • fuzz: then one or more fuzz target names in backticks.
  • CI: then the command in backticks, as a workflow under .github/workflows/ runs it.

cargo xtask threat-coverage checks this document on every pull request (see Keeping it current).

AT-01 LOLBins: signed OS binaries that run arbitrary code

ATT&CK: T1218 (System Binary Proxy Execution), T1127.001, T1047, T1140. Epics #6 and #7.

  • OR: run attacker code through a signed OS binary
    • AT-01.1 mshta runs an HTML application or inline script → recommended block rules (#87), HTML application adapter (#93); T-native-07; BYP-lol-01
    • AT-01.2 msbuild compiles and runs an inline task → recommended block rules (#87), toolchains allowed only in developer profiles (#165); T-native-07; BYP-lol-02
    • AT-01.3 installutil runs installer classes from any assembly → recommended block rules (#87); T-native-07; BYP-lol-03
    • AT-01.4 regsvr32 loads a local or remote scriptlet → recommended block rules (#87), script-host child-process rules (#100), COM and scriptlet control (#107); T-native-07; BYP-lol-04
    • AT-01.5 rundll32 runs a javascript: URL or an export of an arbitrary DLL → DLL control (#104), recommended block rules (#87); T-native-07; BYP-lol-05
    • AT-01.6 cscript or wscript runs .js, .vbs or .wsf → script host adapters (#93), per-type script modes (#92); T-native-07; BYP-lol-06
    • AT-01.7 wmic runs an XSL stylesheet containing script → recommended block rules (#87), managed LOLBin hardening set (#100); T-native-07; BYP-lol-07
    • AT-01.8 AND: certutil decodes or downloads a payload, then the payload is run. Blocking either step defeats it.
      • AT-01.8a decode or download a payload with certutil → certutil network and decode use in the managed LOLBin hardening set (#100); T-native-07; BYP-lol-08
      • AT-01.8b run the decoded file from a user-writable path → implicit deny of unknown files (#39), path-rule ACL checks (#212); T-engine-10; BYP-lol-08
    • AT-01.9 any other proxy binary (developer hosts, interactive compilers, add-in hosts, the OS's application deployment engine, old versions of signed tools) → block-list ingestion and updates (#87); new ones are residual risk R-16; T-native-07; BYP-lol-09

AT-02 DLL search-order hijacking and side-loading

ATT&CK: T1574.001, T1574.002. Epic #8.

  • AND: an allowed executable loads an attacker DLL. Blocking either branch defeats it.
    • AT-02.1 OR: the attacker puts a DLL where an allowed executable's loader will find it
      • AT-02.1a side-loading: copy an allowed executable (a publisher or hash rule allows it wherever it is) to a writable folder, and put the DLL beside it → lint warning for publisher-only allow rules without a path or version condition (#191), writable-path report (#212); T-native-08; BYP-dll-01
      • AT-02.1b search-order hijack: an allowed executable in a protected folder searches the current directory, a user-writable PATH entry or a writable application folder, or looks for a DLL that does not exist → writable-path report (#212), path ACL checks (#54); T-native-08; BYP-dll-03
    • AT-02.2 the loader maps the attacker DLL → DLL enforcement: every image load is decided on its own, wherever the loader found it, so the DLL itself must be allowed (#104, #8, #111); T-native-08; BYP-dll-02

AT-03 User-writable subfolders inside allowed paths

ISM-1392 and ISM-1746. Epic #6.

  • AND: run a payload from inside an allowed folder. Blocking any branch defeats it.
    • AT-03.1 a path rule allows a folder such as %WINDIR%\* → path-rule ACL validation: a rule whose folder has a user-writable descendant is a lint error (#54, #212); T-engine-10; BYP-path-01
    • AT-03.2 OR: a user-writable subfolder exists under it
      • AT-03.2a a built-in writable subfolder (%WINDIR%\Temp, %WINDIR%\Tasks, %WINDIR%\System32\spool\drivers\color, %WINDIR%\tracing) → default deny exceptions for known writable subfolders in shipped templates (#124, #87), writable-path discovery scenario (#230); T-engine-10; BYP-path-02
      • AT-03.2b an installer later loosens a folder's ACL → ACL re-checks and drift reports (#212); T-engine-10; RT-path-01
    • AT-03.3 the user copies a payload there and the path rule trusts it → path-plus-owner rules: a file owned by a non-administrator, or writable by non-administrators, is not trusted by path alone (#117, #54). The owner condition needs the driver; without it the rule falls back to the native path allow (R-07); T-engine-11; BYP-path-03

AT-04 File-system tricks

ATT&CK: T1036, T1564.004. Epics #2 and #3.

  • OR: make a blocked file match an allow rule, or escape a deny rule
    • AT-04.1 rename after allow: replace an allowed-by-name file, or rename an untrusted file to an allowed name → hash and publisher identity over names, renamed-binary detection (#55), hash cache invalidated on write (#46); T-engine-01; BYP-fs-01
    • AT-04.2 hard link to an allowed file from a writable folder → decisions use file ID and the normalised path of the opened handle (#54); the driver denies hard links to protected files (#220); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-02
    • AT-04.3 junction or symbolic link redirects an allowed folder → path rules match the final path after reparse points are resolved (#54); T-agent-13; BYP-fs-03
    • AT-04.4 NTFS alternate data stream (file.txt:evil.exe) → the stream name is part of the normalised path, and path rules do not match named streams unless written to (#32, #54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-04
    • AT-04.5 8.3 short names → expanded to long names before matching (#54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-05
    • AT-04.6 case variations → case folding with the OS's upper-case table (#32, #54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-06
    • AT-04.7 trailing dots and spaces → normalised the way the Win32 layer does, and compared as NT paths (#54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-07
    • AT-04.8 \\?\ and device paths, including \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\... → converted to one canonical volume-relative form (#54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-08
    • AT-04.9 UNC paths versus mapped drives → mapped drives resolved to UNC; drive-type conditions (#54, #38); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-09
    • AT-04.10 volume GUID paths and mount points → canonical volume identity (#54); T-engine-04; BYP-fs-10
    • AT-04.11 copy to a new extension → content-based file type detection (#44); T-engine-01; BYP-fs-12

AT-05 TOCTOU: content changes between check and use

Epics #3 and #8. The two branches are independent attacks on different objects.

  • OR: get content run or enforced that differs from what was checked
    • AT-05.1 OR: executable image race: the code that is mapped is not the code that was checked. Each child is an independent path, so all three mitigations are needed.
      • AT-05.1a the file is swapped or rewritten after the agent's hashing handle closes and before the image section is created, so the decision is about content that is no longer there → decide on the file object that backs the image section, at section creation, not on a path re-opened later (#110, #111); T-driver-09; BYP-toctou-01
      • AT-05.1b the file is written while it is being hashed, pausing the agent's read with an opportunistic lock → concurrent-modification check: size, last-write time and USN change stamp are compared before and after the read, and a change means retry, then Unstable instead of a hash (#46); T-driver-09; BYP-toctou-01
      • AT-05.1c a stale hash-cache entry is reused after an in-place write → hash cache keyed by volume ID, file ID and USN change stamp, invalidated on write, with an HMAC per record (#46, #60, ADR 0007); T-cache-06; BYP-fs-11
    • AT-05.2 policy bundle race: the bundle changes between verification and parsing → verify-then-parse on a private copy (#61, ADR 0007); T-cache-04; BYP-toctou-02

AT-06 Policy tampering on the endpoint

Owned by #220 and #225. The two top-level branches need different access: Palisade's store is SYSTEM-only, while the deployed OS-native policy lives in OS policy locations that an administrator controls.

AT-07 Policy rollback

Owned by #225.

  • OR: get an older, more permissive policy enforced
    • AT-07.1 replay an older signed bundle captured from traffic or storage → anti-rollback record of the highest accepted version (#225); T-cache-03; BYP-policy-03
    • AT-07.2 reset the anti-rollback record → mirrored copies, mismatch raises tamper.policy.rollback_suspected (#225); T-cache-05; BYP-tamper-04
    • AT-07.3 corrupt the active bundle to force N-1 → bounded one-step exception with a critical event and a rapid check-in (ADR 0012, #225); R-09; T-cache-03; BYP-policy-02
    • AT-07.4 redeploy an older native policy → the agent compares the deployed native policy version with the expected one and re-deploys (#83, #85); T-native-02; BYP-policy-06
    • AT-07.5 get the server to re-sign old content → only through a new, higher, audited version (#133, #225); T-console-09; RT-console-01

AT-08 Clock rollback

ISM-0988. Owned by #220, #222 and #225; rules in ADR 0012.

  • OR: revive or extend an expired exception, token, window or rule
    • AT-08.1 set the wall clock back while the agent runs → anchored time and the floor are used, not the wall clock (#220); T-agent-15; BYP-clock-01
    • AT-08.2 set the clock while the agent is stopped, to start a scheduled grant early → offline-started rule: scheduled grants stay closed until check-in (#220); T-agent-15; BYP-clock-02
    • AT-08.3 spoof the time source at boot → as AT-08.2, plus the skew latch (#220); T-agent-15; BYP-clock-03
    • AT-08.4 redeem a genuine, unredeemed override code outside its window → accepted risk R-10: single use, floor check, monotonic session timer (#120, #222); T-agent-15; BYP-clock-04
    • AT-08.5 reset the protected time state (floor, redeemed-code list, skew latch) → protected storage that only moves in the closed direction (#220); T-cache-07; BYP-clock-05

AT-09 Stop, kill, suspend or debug the agent

ATT&CK: T1562.001. Owned by #220 and #221. Even when this succeeds, the native layer keeps enforcing (ADR 0012); residual risks R-01 and R-06.

  • OR: stop the agent enforcing driver-only rules and reporting
    • AT-09.1 stop the service through the service control manager → service DACL: administrators can only query (#220); T-agent-10; BYP-tamper-01
    • AT-09.2 terminate the process → driver strips PROCESS_TERMINATE from handles (#220); protected process light if adopted (#221); T-agent-10; BYP-tamper-01
    • AT-09.3 suspend its threads → driver strips suspend and resume rights (#220); T-agent-06; BYP-tamper-01
    • AT-09.4 attach a debugger or inject code → handle stripping, debugger detection, mitigation policies (#220); T-agent-06; RT-agent-01
    • AT-09.5 set the start type to disabled and reboot → registry protection, start type checked and reverted (#220); T-agent-05; BYP-tamper-03
    • AT-09.6 add a debugger redirect under image execution options so the agent cannot start → protected image-execution-option and silent-process-exit keys (#220); T-agent-05; BYP-tamper-06
    • AT-09.7 kill the agent and the watchdog together → recovery actions, mutual watchdog, heartbeat gap at the server (#220); T-health-06; BYP-tamper-01

AT-10 Unload the driver or change its filter order

Owned by #8 and #220.

  • OR: remove or blind the driver
    • AT-10.1 unload it with the filter manager's unload command → release builds refuse unload except on a signed command (#110); T-driver-02; BYP-tamper-02
    • AT-10.2 detach its instance from a volume → instance teardown is refused for protected volumes and raises an event (#110); T-driver-02; BYP-tamper-02
    • AT-10.3 change its service key, start type or altitude → registry callback; the agent checks presence, version and altitude (#110, #220); T-driver-02; BYP-tamper-03
    • AT-10.4 load another filter above it → driver load control and filter inventory (#105); T-driver-03; BYP-drv-01
    • AT-10.5 stop it loading at boot by editing the disk offline → residual risk R-05; the agent reports the missing driver and driver_failure_mode applies (#113); T-agent-16; RT-boot-01

AT-11 Safe mode or offline boot

ATT&CK: T1562.009. Owned by #220. Disk encryption guidance is in Assumptions.

  • OR: tamper while Palisade is not running
    • AT-11.1 boot into safe mode → services registered for safe boot, tamper.boot.safe_mode event (#220); T-agent-16; BYP-boot-01
    • AT-11.2 boot other media (a preinstallation environment or another OS) and edit the disk → disk encryption with a TPM protector, Secure Boot (Assumptions); residual risk R-05; binary and cache integrity checks at the next start (#220); T-agent-16; RT-boot-01
    • AT-11.3 change the boot configuration to allow test-signed or unsigned drivers → Secure Boot; the agent reports the boot configuration (#210); T-agent-16; RT-boot-02

AT-12 BYOVD: a vulnerable signed driver kills the agent from the kernel

ATT&CK: T1068. Owned by #87 and #105. Residual risk R-02.

  • AND: use kernel access to disable Palisade. Blocking any step defeats it.
    • AT-12.1 obtain administrator rights to load a driver → out of reach for AC-01 and AC-02 (#161 removes standing admin rights); T-driver-10; RT-drv-03
    • AT-12.2 load a known vulnerable signed driver → vulnerable driver blocklist (#87), driver load control (#105), hypervisor-enforced code integrity recommended; T-driver-10; BYP-drv-04
    • AT-12.3 use it to remove callbacks or kill the agent → not preventable (R-02); detected by heartbeat loss and server-side alerting (#62, #201); T-driver-10; RT-drv-03

AT-13 Token theft or impersonation to reach agent IPC

ATT&CK: T1134. Owned by #220.

  • OR: call a privileged IPC verb without authority
    • AT-13.1 connect with an unsigned client → image signature check against the pinned publisher (#220); T-agent-02; BYP-tamper-08
    • AT-13.2 inject into the signed tray or CLI → privileged verbs also need an unlock token or CLI password (#220, #222); T-agent-02; RT-ipc-01
    • AT-13.3 create the pipe first (pipe squatting) → first-instance flag at agent start; clients check the server process before writing (#220); T-tray-02; BYP-tamper-07
    • AT-13.4 steal an administrator's token and impersonate them → where policy requires an unlock token, an admin SID alone is not enough (#222); T-agent-02; RT-ipc-02
    • AT-13.5 connect from another machine → remote clients are rejected (#220); T-agent-02; BYP-tamper-19
    • AT-13.6 reuse a verified caller's PID → handle held for the connection, creation time checked (#220); T-agent-03; BYP-tamper-11

AT-14 Uninstall through the installer or the OS's installed-apps page

Owned by #222.

  • OR: remove the agent without authorisation
    • AT-14.1 run the installer's uninstall (msiexec /x) → a deferred custom action requires UNLOCK_TOKEN (#222); T-agent-17; BYP-tamper-20
    • AT-14.2 uninstall from the OS's installed-apps settings page → the same custom action; the entry can be hidden (#222); T-agent-17; BYP-tamper-20
    • AT-14.3 delete the services and files by hand → service DACL, file protection, watchdog repair (#220); T-agent-04; BYP-tamper-12
    • AT-14.4 install an older version over it → a downgrade needs a signed allow_downgrade entry and an unlock token (#222, #226); T-update-02; BYP-update-02

AT-15 Enrolment abuse

Owned by #223.

  • OR: get a device identity the attacker should not have
    • AT-15.1 a rogue device enrols with a leaked registration code → codes scoped to tenant and group, expiry, use limits, source-address allowlist, rate limits (#223); T-api-02; TEST-enrol-code
    • AT-15.2 clone a real device's identity from a golden image → reseal flag clears identity (#220); duplicate detection (#223); T-api-01; TEST-enrol-clone
    • AT-15.3 copy a device key → non-exportable, TPM-backed keys where present (#223); residual risk R-12; T-api-01; RT-enrol-01
    • AT-15.4 enrol into a group with weaker policy → a code only enrols into its own group; moves are audited (#223, #129); T-api-02; TEST-enrol-code

AT-16 A malicious server or console administrator pushes an allow-all policy

Owned by #10 (approvals and four-eyes, #142) and #229 (audit). Residual risk R-08.

  • OR: widen policy for many endpoints
    • AT-16.1 switch groups to audit or allow-all → four-eyes approval for high-impact changes (#142, #229), audit (#132), alerting (#201); T-console-09; RT-console-01
    • AT-16.2 delete blocklists → the mandatory-deny tier cannot be overridden by policy (#125); deletion is a four-eyes action (#229); T-console-09; RT-console-01
    • AT-16.3 add broad allow rules → lint (#191), staged rollout rings (#135), approvals; T-console-09; RT-console-01
    • AT-16.4 issue unlock tokens for many devices → agent.unlock.issue permission, mandatory reason, four-eyes for uninstall (#222); T-console-09; RT-console-02
    • AT-16.5 push malicious binaries as an update → not possible: update metadata keys are not on the server (#226); T-update-01; BYP-update-01
    • AT-16.6 change policy rows directly in the database → audit chain and dual control (#229); T-db-03; RT-db-01

AT-17 Update channel compromise

ATT&CK: T1195.002. Owned by #226.

  • OR: get attacker code installed by the update client
    • AT-17.1 serve a malicious package from a mirror or relay → TUF metadata chain and pinned publisher (#226); T-update-01; BYP-update-01
    • AT-17.2 roll back or freeze metadata → version monotonicity and expiry (#226); T-update-02, T-update-03; BYP-update-02, BYP-update-03
    • AT-17.3 AND: steal both the targets key and the code-signing key. Protecting either key defeats it.
      • AT-17.3a steal the targets metadata key → key held only in the release job, threshold root rotation on compromise (#226); T-update-01; RT-ci-02
      • AT-17.3b steal the code-signing key → key in hardware or a signing service, never a repository secret (#226, #224); T-ci-02; RT-ci-02
    • AT-17.4 compromise the build → GitHub-hosted runners only, provenance attestations (#21, #226); T-ci-07; RT-ci-01
    • AT-17.5 compromise a dependency → source and advisory checks (#23); residual risk R-15; T-ci-05; CI: cargo deny --locked check

AT-18 Interpreter abuse

ATT&CK: T1059.001, T1562.010, T1620. Epic #7.

  • OR: run unapproved code inside an allowed interpreter
    • AT-18.1 PowerShell version 2 downgrade → downgrade protection and removal of the old engine (#94); T-script-06; BYP-ps-01
    • AT-18.2 escape constrained language mode (type compilation, COM objects) → lockdown contract (#94), COM control (#107); T-script-06; BYP-ps-03
    • AT-18.3 use a script host that does not enforce code integrity → host adapters (#93), recommended block rules (#87); T-native-06; BYP-ps-04
    • AT-18.4 load code reflectively from memory (Assembly.Load(byte[])) → AMSI provider and dynamic-code control (#96, #109); T-script-07; BYP-ps-05
    • AT-18.5 run a user-installed interpreter (for example Python) → interpreter identification, per-type modes and argument rules (#92, #98, #99); T-script-08; BYP-int-01
    • AT-18.6 use encoded commands or -ExecutionPolicy Bypass → execution policy is never relied on; command-line rules (#94, #99); T-script-08; BYP-ps-06

AT-19 Trust-source abuse

ATT&CK: T1134.004, T1218.007. Epic #9.

  • OR: get an attacker file trusted through a trusted installer, updater or parent
    • AT-19.1 a trusted installer writes an attacker file (custom action) → direct versus chained inheritance, installer scope (#114, #116); T-engine-12; BYP-trust-01
    • AT-19.2 a trusted updater fetches an attacker payload → updater catalogue checks the updater's own signature rules (#119); T-engine-12; BYP-trust-02
    • AT-19.3 a trusted parent spawns a shell or interpreter → created-by rules exclude shells and interpreters by default; child-process control (#118, #175); T-engine-13; BYP-trust-03
    • AT-19.4 spoof the parent process ID → use the real creator from process-creation callbacks, not the reported parent (#111, #118); T-engine-13; BYP-trust-04
    • AT-19.5 OR: get owner-based trust for attacker content
      • AT-19.5a take ownership of a file → only administrator owners are trusted (#117); T-engine-11; BYP-trust-05
      • AT-19.5b overwrite in place an administrator-owned file whose ACL lets users write to it (NTFS keeps the owner) → owner-based trust also requires a DACL with no non-administrator write rights; with the driver, a non-administrator write revokes the trust (#117, #54, #220); T-engine-11; BYP-trust-07
    • AT-19.6 install from a URL (msiexec /i http://...) → installer rules (#98); T-script-08; BYP-trust-06

Privacy threats (LINDDUN-lite)

Shared with #228, which owns the mitigations and the data inventory.

IDLINDDUN categoryThreatMitigationIssue
PV-01LinkingEvents from one person on several devices can be joined into a profile of their work.Pseudonymised usernames with a per-tenant key; re-identification needs the privacy.reidentify permission and is audited.#228
PV-02IdentifyingUsernames and profile paths in events identify the user directly.collect.username and collect.file_paths_user_profile settings; generalised profile paths in uploads.#228
PV-03Non-repudiation (unwanted)Detailed command lines and allow events give a complete record of what a person ran, beyond what application control needs.Allow events summarised by default; command lines redacted by default; retention per data class.#228
PV-04DetectingA third party learns which files a device has from reputation lookups or blocked-file uploads.Integrations and blocked-binary archiving are off by default; the "data leaving your environment" page lists every field sent.#206, #228
PV-05Data disclosureSecrets typed on command lines (passwords, tokens, connection strings) are collected.Built-in and custom redaction patterns applied before storage and upload; rules still evaluate the unredacted line on the device.#228
PV-06UnawarenessUsers do not know what is collected about them.The tray "About this device" view shows the collection settings, the server and the organisation's notice.#228
PV-07Non-complianceData is kept longer than needed, or cannot be exported or deleted on request.Configurable retention with warnings below the ISM-1988 minimum; pal privacy export and delete; legal hold.#228
PV-08Data disclosureThe project itself collects data through update checks, crash upload or analytics.No phone-home: Palisade only contacts endpoints the operator configures, and a CI test checks it.#228

One row per threat, in the same order as the STRIDE tables. N/A rows are omitted.

Assumptions

  1. Secure Boot is on on every endpoint, and the boot configuration does not allow test-signed or unsigned drivers outside disposable lab VMs.
  2. Disk encryption with a TPM protector is recommended on every endpoint. Where it is off, R-05 applies in full.
  3. Administrative accounts are separate from everyday accounts and are not used for email or web browsing, in line with ISM-1175-style guidance. Standard users do not hold local administrator rights (#160, #161).
  4. The OS is supported and patched. Kernel vulnerabilities in the OS itself are not mitigated by Palisade.
  5. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity is recommended where hardware supports it. It reduces R-02 but is not required.
  6. Time: endpoints and the server use a reliable time source. The server keeps its offset under 1 s (#224).
  7. TLS inspection is bypassed for the agent endpoints. Palisade never disables verification to work with an inspecting proxy (ADR 0005).
  8. The server is run by trusted operators on a hardened host or container (#229), with the database owner role and signer credentials kept off the runtime host.
  9. Root keys stay offline: the root CA and the update metadata root are used only in documented ceremonies (#224, #226).
  10. GitHub-hosted runners are the only CI runners (docs/ci.md), and the hosting platform's own controls (branch rules, environments, attestations) work as documented.
  11. Testing happens on disposable VMs first (ADR 0014).

Process

Review cadence

The model is reviewed, and the header's "Last reviewed" date updated:

  • at every minor release;
  • whenever a new component or trust boundary is added;
  • whenever a mitigation's status changes from planned;
  • and at least every 6 months.

Each review is a changelog entry that says what changed and who reviewed it.

Keeping it current

  • A pull request that changes a trust boundary or adds a parser of untrusted input updates this document. The pull request template asks this question.
  • New threats get the next free number for their component. IDs are never reused.
  • A mitigation moves from planned to implemented in the pull request that lands it, with the test name in the verification column.
  • cargo xtask threat-coverage runs in the doc-checks CI job, behind the required ci-ok check, so it is blocking. It fails when:
    • a STRIDE row is malformed (cell count, ID form, category, status, impact or likelihood), an ID is reused, an N/A row has no reason, or a component does not consider all six categories;
    • the mitigation table lacks a row for a threat, has one twice or out of order, or names different issues from the STRIDE row;
    • a threat marked implemented or verified has no TEST:, fuzz: or CI: entry, or a verified threat has no BYP-* or RT-* entry;
    • any TEST:, fuzz: or CI: entry, on any row, names a test function, fuzz target or workflow command that does not exist;
    • the summary by status does not match the tables;
    • this document or a tracked .rs or .md file names a threat ID the tables do not define, such as a // threat: comment with a wrong number.
  • What it cannot check: that a cited test really exercises the mitigation. Reviewers check that, and #230 turns the proposed BYP-* and RT-* names into scenarios.

Disclosure

Vulnerability reports go through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, as described in SECURITY.md, which also has the supported-versions table. Private reporting is enabled on the repository (docs/repo-settings.md). A finding is in scope when it defeats a claim in Actors and claims. It is out of scope when it needs an actor this model says Palisade does not resist.

Hardening guide

Palisade is educational software and must not protect production systems. This page is about running a lab without making that lab, or the network it sits on, less safe. Product hardening (self-protection of the agent, signed policy, server and console hardening to ASVS L2) is designed in the threat model and epic #18; each item there says whether it exists yet.

The lab

  • Run the agent only on disposable virtual machines you own, never on a workstation you rely on. Snapshot before every test and revert after.
  • Keep lab VMs on an isolated virtual network. The server binds its admin, agent and metrics listeners separately; bind each to the lab interface only (server README: listeners).
  • Use test certificates made for the lab. Never reuse a real code-signing or TLS key.

The server

  • Run palisade-server check-config before serve. It checks the TLS chain, key, agent CA, file permissions on secret files, and that every public URL matches a certificate name, and reports every problem at once.
  • Keep secrets in files readable only by the server's account; the server refuses group- or world-readable secret files.
  • Give the server two database logins: a migration login that owns the schema, and a runtime login that does not. Row-level security isolates tenants (server README: database).

Policies

  • Start in audit; enforce by object type; keep a mandatory blocklist for known-dangerous tools (Modes).
  • Prefer hash and publisher rules. Use path rules only for locations users cannot write (ISM-1392), and let validation's weak-identity warnings guide you (Identities).
  • Time-box every override; it reverts on its own.

The supply chain

Every dependency is reviewed, audited or exempted with a reason (Dependencies), and CI runs on GitHub-hosted runners only, with SHA-pinned actions from an allowlist (CI).

Source: docs/book/src/security/hardening.md on GitHub.

Security policy

Palisade is an educational, personal-development project maintained by one person on a best-effort basis. It is not a replacement for commercial application control products, and it should not be relied on to protect production systems. Security reports are still welcome and are taken seriously. This page explains how to send one privately and what response to expect.

Supported versions

Palisade has no releases yet. Once it does, only the latest minor release receives security fixes. Older releases are not patched, so you must upgrade to get a fix. Until the first release, fixes land on main only.

VersionSecurity fixes
Latest minor releaseYes
Any older releaseNo
main (before the first release)Yes

Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue, discussion or pull request for a vulnerability.

Report it through GitHub private vulnerability reporting:

  1. Open the Security tab of this repository.
  2. Select Report a vulnerability, or go straight to the private reporting form.
  3. Describe the issue, the affected commit or version, and the steps to reproduce it.

Only you and the maintainer can see the report. It becomes a draft security advisory, so the discussion, any fix and the final advisory all happen in one private place.

GitHub private vulnerability reporting is the only private channel. The project does not offer an email address or an encryption key for reports. If you cannot use the form, start a discussion that asks the maintainer for a private channel and contains no details of the vulnerability.

A useful report includes:

  • the Palisade commit or version, the Windows build and the architecture (x64 or ARM64);
  • the policy or configuration needed to reproduce it, with secrets and enrolment tokens removed;
  • what you expected to happen and what happened instead;
  • the impact as you understand it.

Use benign test files only. Do not attach real malware.

What to expect

These are best-effort targets, not commitments. Palisade has one maintainer and no service level agreement.

StepTarget
Acknowledge your reportwithin 7 days
Triage it (confirmed or not, severity, next steps)within 14 days
Public disclosure90 days after the report, by default

If a target is missed, the maintainer will say so in the report thread, and the advisory will say so too.

Coordinated disclosure

The default disclosure window is 90 days from the report. Within that window the maintainer aims to release a fix and publish an advisory. The window can change by agreement:

  • shorter, if a fix ships early or the issue is already being exploited;
  • longer, if a fix needs more time and you agree to wait.

Please do not disclose the issue publicly before the advisory is published or the window ends.

Advisories are published as GitHub Security Advisories in this repository. A CVE is requested through GitHub when the issue affects released code. You are credited in the advisory unless you ask not to be.

Scope

In scope:

  • Agent bypasses: running code that policy should block, for example through a rule-matching flaw, path or file-identity confusion, a race between the check and the execution, or a script-host or interpreter gap.
  • Tamper: stopping, unloading or reconfiguring the agent or the optional driver, or editing its policy, its local store or its logs, without the rights the threat model requires.
  • Privilege escalation through any Palisade component, including the elevation features.
  • Server and API authentication and authorisation: getting access without credentials, crossing tenants, escalating roles, forging or replaying enrolment, or misusing override codes.
  • Supply chain: the build, the CI workflows, release signing, dependency handling and the update path.
  • Memory-safety bugs, panics and resource exhaustion in parsers of untrusted input (files, policy, network messages).

Out of scope:

  • Findings that need administrator-equivalent access on the endpoint, or any other access that the threat model already defines as a trust boundary Palisade does not defend. Its Actors and claims table says which actors Palisade resists. A finding is in scope when it defeats one of those claims, and out of scope when it needs an actor the table says Palisade does not resist, such as malware with administrator or SYSTEM rights, or a kernel-level attacker. The residual-risk register lists the accepted risks. If you are unsure, report it anyway and say why you think it is in scope.
  • Bugs in the operating system, in third-party dependencies (report those upstream; tell us if Palisade is affected) or in GitHub itself.
  • Missing hardening with no demonstrated impact, scanner output without a working proof of concept, and social engineering of the maintainer.
  • Denial of service that needs high traffic volumes against a deployment you do not own.

Safe harbour

If you research and report in good faith under this policy, the maintainer will not pursue or support any legal action against you, and will treat your work as authorised. Good faith means that you:

  • test only on systems and data you own or are explicitly allowed to test;
  • do not access, change or delete other people's data, and stop as soon as you reach it;
  • do not degrade services for other users;
  • use benign test files, never real malware;
  • give the maintainer a reasonable chance to fix the issue before you disclose it.

This statement covers the maintainer only. It cannot give permission on behalf of anyone else, including GitHub or the owners of any system you test against. If you are unsure whether something is covered, ask in your report first.

See also docs/responsible-use.md.

Source: SECURITY.md on GitHub.

Responsible use

Palisade is a defensive project. It exists to learn how application control stops unwanted code from running on Windows, and how to explain and evidence that control. It is educational, not a replacement for commercial application control products, and it should not be relied on to protect production systems.

Test files and scenarios are benign

Everything in this repository that is used to exercise a control is harmless:

  • Test executables, scripts, libraries and installers only prove that they ran, for example by writing a marker file or printing a line. They do nothing else.
  • Fixtures are built from source in this repository, or are well-known harmless files.
  • Scenarios run on disposable virtual machines that you control (#26), never on machines you do not own.

If a test needs something that looks like attacker behaviour, such as a file in a user-writable folder, an unsigned binary or an unusual parent process, it reproduces the shape of that behaviour with a benign file. It never uses the real thing.

Contributions that are rejected

Pull requests and issues that do any of the following are closed, and the content may be removed:

  • Offensive tooling: code whose purpose is to attack systems, such as exploit chains, credential theft, persistence or lateral movement.
  • Real malware samples, live or "defanged", including links to download them, and test signatures or hashes that only make sense for real samples.
  • Bypass weaponisation: turning a way around a control, in Palisade or in any other product, into a ready-to-use tool, payload or step-by-step guide.
  • Detection-evasion techniques presented as something to use, rather than as a gap to close.

Discussing classes of bypass in design documents and the threat model is fine and encouraged, as long as the aim is to defend against them.

Found a bypass?

If you find a way to run code that Palisade should block, tamper with it or escalate privileges through it, do not open a public issue or pull request. Report it privately as described in SECURITY.md. That page also covers scope and safe harbour for good-faith research.

Your responsibilities

  • Only test on systems you own or are explicitly allowed to test.
  • Follow the law and the policies of your organisation.
  • Treat Palisade as a learning project. Test it on disposable machines first, and do not make it the only control protecting a system you care about.

Contributors also follow the Code of Conduct.

Source: docs/responsible-use.md on GitHub.

Compliance

Evidence, not certification. These pages map Palisade's controls to the Australian Signals Directorate's Essential Eight and the Information Security Manual (ISM) to show what a lab deployment could evidence and where to look for it. They are not an assessment, an attestation or a claim of compliance. Palisade is educational software (ADR 0014), and no part of it has been assessed. Maturity is assessed for a whole environment by a qualified assessor, using ASD's Essential Eight Assessment Process Guide.

  • Essential Eight: application control at Maturity Levels One to Three.
  • ISM controls: every ISM control the code or docs cite, with where it is addressed.

Sources: the Essential Eight Maturity Model (November 2023) and the ISM (September 2026 release), both published by ASD at cyber.gov.au. Reporting and the control mapping engine are epic #17 (milestone M6).

Source: docs/book/src/compliance/README.md on GitHub.

Essential Eight: application control

Evidence, not certification. See Compliance. "Status" says what exists in the repository today; it is not an assessment of any deployment.

Status values: in place (implemented and tested), partial (some of it is implemented), planned (designed in the issue named, not built).

Maturity Level One

ISMRequirementPalisadeStatus
ISM-0843Application control is implemented on workstations.The endpoint agent (#4) and OS-native policy compilation (#6).planned
ISM-1870Applied to user profiles and temporary folders used by operating systems, web browsers and email clients.Path facts with ACL safety; allow rules only trust paths users cannot write. Default-deny covers these folders; unknown-application variants for user-writable locations in #39.partial
ISM-1657Restricts executables, libraries, scripts, installers, compiled HTML, HTML applications and control panel applets to an organisation-approved set.Every one is an object type in the policy model (ObjectType), with its own mode (mode_by_type) and protection status. Enforcement needs the agent.partial

Maturity Level Two

All of ML1, and:

ISMRequirementPalisadeStatus
ISM-1490Application control is implemented on internet-facing servers.Server editions are a platform target (#68); device.is_server is a context criterion today.planned
ISM-1871Applied to all locations other than user profiles and temporary folders.The same engine and default-deny apply everywhere; nothing is excluded by location unless an ignore rule says so, which needs a permission.partial
ISM-1544The OS vendor's recommended application blocklist is implemented.A mandatory blocklist tier that nothing overrides (ADR 0004); ingesting the published list is #87.partial
ISM-1582Application control rulesets are validated at least annually.Governance metadata and review-by dates, static analysis of rules (#40).planned
ISM-1660Allowed and blocked application control events are centrally logged.Deny, audit, elevation and trust-source rules must log every decision; the canonical event schema checks the ISM-0585 fields. Central storage is #202.partial

Maturity Level Three

All of ML2, and:

ISMRequirementPalisadeStatus
ISM-1656Application control is implemented on non-internet-facing servers.As ISM-1490.planned
ISM-1658Restricts the execution of drivers to an organisation-approved set.driver is an object type with its own mode; driver load control is #105.partial
ISM-1659The OS vendor's vulnerable driver blocklist is implemented.The mandatory blocklist tier; ingestion is #87.partial

How rules are written

These ISM controls are not tagged Essential Eight, but assessors use them to judge whether application control is effective. The ISM page lists them all.

ISMRequirementPalisade
ISM-0955Implemented using cryptographic hash rules, publisher certificate rules or path rules.All three are identity criteria; Identities.
ISM-1471Publisher rules use publisher names and product names.palisade-fileid records the publisher and product pair; validation warns on weak identities.
ISM-1392Path rules: only approved users can modify approved files and write to approved folders.Allow rules on paths only match where the path and its ancestors are not user-writable.
ISM-1746Path rules: only approved users can change permissions on approved files and folders.The same ACL check covers permission changes.
ISM-0846Users cannot disable or bypass application control.Agent self-protection in #18 and the threat model; overrides are time-boxed and logged.
