Contributing to Palisade

Thanks for your interest. Palisade is an educational, personal-development project with one maintainer. It is not a replacement for commercial application control products. Contributions are welcome, and are reviewed on a best-effort basis (see SUPPORT.md).

By taking part you agree to follow the Code of Conduct and the responsible-use statement.

Security vulnerabilities, including bypasses, are never reported in issues or pull requests. Use SECURITY.md.

Before you start

  • For anything larger than a small fix, comment on the issue first, or open one, so the work is not duplicated and the design is agreed before you write code.
  • Decisions that affect several crates, the security model, or what is blocked or allowed need an ADR (see Architecture decisions).

How issues are organised

  • Epics are issues labelled epic (#1 to #18). Each covers one area of the project.
  • Every other issue names its parent epic at the top (**Parent epic:** #N), and often the issues it depends on (**Depends on:** #N).
  • Every issue belongs to one milestone, from M0 Foundations to M6 Compliance & Advanced. Milestones are delivered roughly in order.
  • area:* labels say which part of the project an issue touches, and priority:p0 to priority:p2 give its priority within the milestone.
  • good first issue and help wanted mark issues that suit new contributors.
  • New issues get needs-triage. The maintainer replaces it with area and priority labels. blocked marks an issue that waits on another issue or a decision.
  • The label set and the milestone titles are kept in .github/labels.yml and .github/milestones.yml, and a workflow syncs them to GitHub. To add or change a label, edit the file in a pull request (docs/repo-settings.md).

A pull request says which issue it relates to: Closes #N if it completes the issue, or Part of #N if it delivers part of it. Say what is left and which issue it belongs to.

Development setup

You need rustup and Git. The toolchain is pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, so the first cargo command in the repository installs the right version, components and targets.

  • Windows: rustup's installer offers to install the Windows C++ build tools that the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-pc-windows-msvc targets need. Accept that.
  • Linux and other desktop OS: no extra system packages are needed today. Windows-only crates build as stubs, so the whole workspace builds and tests anywhere.
  • cargo-deny (for the dependency check): cargo install cargo-deny --version 0.22.0 --locked.

To check Windows-only code from Linux or another desktop OS:

rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
cargo check --workspace --all-targets --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu

Fuller guides: docs/dev/windows.md (build tools, running the agent in the foreground, tracing, test signing in a VM, and what to do if a policy locks you out) and docs/dev/unix.md (what builds where, the dev container, running the server, and the fake agent for server and console work without Windows).

Git hooks (opt-in)

.githooks/ has a pre-commit hook (formatting, spelling and banned terms) and a commit-msg hook (the Conventional Commit format below). They are off until you turn them on for your clone:

git config core.hooksPath .githooks

Nothing in the repository turns them on for you. git commit --no-verify skips them once; CI runs the same checks either way. See .githooks/README.md.

Before you push

Run the same checks CI runs. docs/ci.md explains each one, and how to install the few extra tools.

cargo xtask ci          # every check in ci.yml
cargo xtask ci --fast   # skips coverage, fuzz, docs, feature-powerset, msrv and the package builds

Coding standards

The lints live in [workspace.lints] in the root Cargo.toml, and every crate inherits them (cargo xtask check-manifests enforces that). CI runs clippy with -D warnings, so every warning fails CI, including the lints set to warn.

Errors and panics

  • No unwrap() or expect() in non-test code. clippy::unwrap_used is denied, and clippy::expect_used warns, which fails CI. Tests may use both (clippy.toml).
  • Return errors with enough context to act on. Do not panic on bad input: Palisade parses untrusted files, policy and network messages.
  • todo!(), unimplemented!() and dbg!() are denied.

Time, processes and the platform

  • Read the OS only through the palisade_core::platform traits (#29), so the logic can be tested on any OS with the mocks in palisade_core::test_util.
  • clippy.toml bans std::time::SystemTime::now everywhere: take time from a palisade_core::platform::Clock. The one implementation that reads the wall clock, and repository tooling, say so with #[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods, reason = "...")].
  • palisade-policy also bans std::process::Command::new, in its tests too (crates/palisade-policy/clippy.toml). Clippy reads the nearest clippy.toml, so a setting added to the root file must be added to that one as well.
  • Formatting is cargo fmt with the stable options in rustfmt.toml. .editorconfig sets the editor defaults that match it.
  • Silent numeric truncation is flagged (cast_possible_truncation and related lints). Use checked conversions.
  • Public items need doc comments (missing_docs).

Unsafe code

  • Today unsafe_code is forbid for the whole workspace, so no crate may contain unsafe.
  • When unsafe code is allowed is decided in ADR 0011. In short: unsafe only in a few named FFI modules and the driver, and every file that allows it listed in unsafe-allowlist.txt, which needs maintainer review. cargo xtask check-unsafe checks that the allowlist matches the code (docs/workspace.md).
  • Every unsafe block needs a // SAFETY: comment that explains why it is sound. Clippy's undocumented_unsafe_blocks lint is already denied.

Naming

Docs, code, comments, commit messages and PR text must not name commercial products, vendors or their trademarked feature names. Use the neutral terms in docs/NAMING.md. Operating system components and open standards are fine to name.

Licence headers

Source files do not carry licence headers. The licence is declared once, as the SPDX expression Apache-2.0 OR MIT, in [workspace.package], and every crate inherits it (cargo xtask check-manifests enforces that). Files copied from elsewhere keep their original notices.

Third-party notices

Release artefacts ship the licence texts of every third-party crate they contain, in a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md file generated from Cargo.lock at release time. It is not kept in the repository, because it would go stale with every dependency update. Generating it, and including it in the release archives and the installer, is part of the release pipeline (#24) and MSI packaging (#22). The licences it may contain are limited by the allowlist in deny.toml.

Testing expectations

  • Every change that affects behaviour comes with tests. Bug fixes include a test that fails without the fix.
  • New rule types or condition types need property tests (for example: a rule never matches a file it should not) and snapshot tests of their compiled or serialised form.
  • Every parser of untrusted input needs a fuzz target, listed in xtask/src/fuzz.rs so CI runs it (docs/testing.md). If a parser's target is not ready yet, say in your PR that it is still owed.
  • Test names, determinism (no sleeps, no network), platform gating and fixtures follow docs/testing.md.
  • Test files must be benign (responsible use). Never commit real malware.
  • Code that only runs on Windows is gated with #[cfg(windows)], so the workspace still builds and tests on other platforms.

Dependencies

Every third-party dependency becomes part of the code a privileged Windows service trusts, so new ones are added with care.

  • Add the version once, in [workspace.dependencies] in the root Cargo.toml, and use { workspace = true } in the crate. cargo xtask check-manifests enforces this.
  • Justify every new dependency in the PR description: why it is needed, what it pulls in, and its licence and maintenance status.
  • cargo deny --locked check must pass: allowed licences only, crates.io only, no known advisories (deny.toml).
  • The allowed dependency directions between workspace crates are enforced by cargo xtask check-deps.

The full admission policy, cargo-vet audits and the other supply-chain checks are in docs/dependencies.md.

Architecture decisions

Significant decisions are recorded as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) in docs/adr/. PROCESS.md says when a change needs an ADR, and how to write, number, accept and supersede one, starting from the template. If you are not sure whether your change needs one, ask in the issue. If a PR contradicts an accepted ADR, it must link a new ADR that supersedes it. cargo xtask adr new "<title>" starts one from the template, cargo xtask adr index updates the index, and cargo xtask adr lint checks the format, as CI does.

Commits and pull requests

Conventional Commits

Commit messages and PR titles follow Conventional Commits:

<type>(<optional scope>): <summary>
  • Types: feat, fix, security, docs, ci, build, refactor, test, chore, and revert for reverting an earlier change.
  • Scope: a crate name without the palisade- prefix (core, fileid, policy, agent, server, cli and so on) or an area (adr, deps, xtask). Lowercase letters, digits and -, . or _.
  • Add ! before the colon for a breaking change, for example feat(policy)!: ….
  • Examples: feat(policy): add publisher rule condition, fix(agent): handle renamed files, docs: explain rule precedence.

Pull requests are squash-merged, and the PR title becomes the commit message on main, which the release changelog is generated from (cargo xtask release prepare, docs/releasing.md). The PR title check (.github/workflows/pr-title.yml) fails a pull request whose title does not follow this format. Edit the title to fix it; the check reruns.

Sign-off and licensing of contributions

There is no Contributor Licence Agreement. Contributions are accepted under the project licence, inbound = outbound (ADR 0010): unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in Palisade, as defined in the Apache-2.0 licence, is dual-licensed as Apache-2.0 OR MIT, without any additional terms or conditions.

Sign-off

Sign off every commit with the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO). Signing off says that you wrote the change, or otherwise have the right to submit it under the project licence. Add the sign-off with git commit -s, which appends a trailer with the name and email from your Git configuration:

Signed-off-by: Ada Lovelace <ada@example.org>
  • The email in the trailer must match the commit's author email.
  • To sign off commits you have already made, run git rebase --signoff <base branch> and then git push --force-with-lease.
  • Never sign off on someone else's behalf.

Maintainer exemption. Pull requests opened by the repository owner's account do not need sign-off, and the DCO check passes them with a notice. The owner holds the copyright and the right to license their own changes, so a sign-off adds nothing. This also covers changes prepared by AI coding agents working for the owner: the owner authorises each one by opening and merging the pull request from their own account, and agents never add a Signed-off-by: line in the owner's name. The exemption is decided by GitHub's record of who opened the pull request (author_association is OWNER), not by anything in the commits, so it cannot be claimed by copying the owner's name or email. Everyone else, including collaborators, signs off as above. The exemption covers every commit in an owner-opened pull request, so if the owner carries someone else's commit, the owner checks that commit's sign-off by hand.

The DCO check (.github/workflows/dco.yml) reports every commit in a pull request that has no matching sign-off. It is informational for now. The decision to require sign-off, with no CLA, is recorded in a separate ADR under #28. Once that ADR is accepted, the maintainer makes DCO a required check (docs/repo-settings.md).

Squash merges turn a pull request into one commit on main. The DCO check covers the commits in the pull request, and the pull request keeps them on record, so the squashed commit on main is not checked again.

Pull request size

  • One concern per pull request. Refactoring, formatting and behaviour changes go in separate PRs.
  • Aim for under about 400 changed lines, not counting generated files, lockfiles and test fixtures. Split larger work into a series of PRs that each build, pass CI and make sense on their own.
  • Fill in the pull request template. It is the reviewer's checklist.

Review

  • The ci-ok check and the PR title check must pass. The main branch ruleset makes both required (docs/repo-settings.md). The DCO check must pass too, although it is not yet a required check. It passes pull requests opened by the repository owner (see Sign-off).
  • Changes to CI, supply-chain policy, unsafe code, the driver and signing need the maintainer's review (.github/CODEOWNERS).
  • Workflow changes must pass cargo xtask check-workflows: GitHub-hosted runners only, allowlisted actions pinned to a full commit SHA, and read-only default permissions. Self-hosted runners and cloud-managed build services are never allowed (docs/ci.md).

Source: CONTRIBUTING.md on GitHub.

Developing on Windows

The agent, the tray and the driver are Windows programs, and this guide sets up a Windows machine to build and run them. Most other work does not need Windows; see unix.md.

Never enforce a policy on the machine you develop on. Palisade is application control: a wrong policy in enforce mode can stop a machine from running its own tools. Run the agent in audit mode on a development machine. Test enforcement, drivers and test signing only in a virtual machine with a snapshot to roll back to.

Tools

  1. The C++ build tools for Windows (the MSVC toolchain and a Windows SDK). The Rust *-pc-windows-msvc targets link with them. In the build tools installer, select the C++ build tools workload, and add the ARM64 build tools component as well as x64, so you can build aarch64-pc-windows-msvc too. When rustup's installer offers to install the build tools for you, it installs only the x64 components; add ARM64 afterwards from the same installer.
  2. Rust, through rustup. The first cargo command in the repository installs the toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, with its components and the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-pc-windows-msvc targets.
  3. Git, which also provides the Bash the opt-in Git hooks use.
  4. WiX Toolset v4 or later, only to build the MSI. The packaging work (#22) pins the version and its install command; cargo xtask dist --msi will say what is missing.
  5. The Windows Driver Kit (optional), only for the kernel driver (#8, #110). Today the driver crate is a placeholder that builds anywhere, and cargo build leaves it out. Install the Driver Kit that matches your SDK version when driver work starts.

Then, from the repository root:

cargo build
cargo test --workspace
cargo xtask ci --fast        # the CI checks; see docs/ci.md for the extra tools

Build for ARM64 from an x64 machine with cargo build --target aarch64-pc-windows-msvc. Tests for that target only run on an ARM64 machine; CI runs them natively on an ARM64 runner.

Running the agent without installing it

The agent runs as a console program, in the foreground, without being installed as a service:

cargo run -p palisade-agent -- --console --config dev.toml

(#29 calls this palisade-agent run --foreground; the flag is --console, as the agent README describes.) It runs until Ctrl-C and logs to standard error. A minimal dev.toml for a development machine:

# dev.toml: never enforce on a development machine.
fail_mode = "fail_open"
safe_mode_behaviour = "audit_only"

[log]
level = "debug"

The agent reads %ProgramData%\Palisade\agent.toml only when --config is not given, so an explicit --config keeps your development settings separate from any installed agent.

Run the terminal as a standard user unless the code you are testing needs administrator rights. Code that reads process tokens or other users' files will need them (#59), and the console reports what it could not read.

The service mode, --service, only works when the service control manager starts the agent. The installer registers it (#57); until then, test the service code in a VM.

Tracing

The agent writes structured logs to standard error in console mode. Raise the level with [log] level = "trace" in the configuration file.

The agent will observe process starts through Event Tracing for Windows (ETW, #59). To see the events it will consume, record the kernel process provider yourself, from an elevated terminal:

# Start a session for the kernel process provider (keyword 0x10: process start and stop).
logman create trace palisade-dev -p "{22FB2CD6-0E7B-422B-A0C7-2FAD1FD0E716}" 0x10 -o "$env:TEMP\palisade-dev.etl" -ets
# ... start some programs ...
logman stop palisade-dev -ets
tracerpt "$env:TEMP\palisade-dev.etl" -o "$env:TEMP\palisade-dev.xml" -of XML

Always stop the session when you are done: an ETW session keeps running, and writing, until it is stopped or the machine restarts. logman query -ets lists the sessions that are running.

The OS's own application control logs (code integrity and the legacy rule collections) are read by the agent in #58, which lists their exact channel names. Event Viewer shows them under the OS application logs.

Test signing in a VM

Loading a driver you built yourself needs test signing. Turn it on only in a VM, never on your main machine: test signing lets any test-signed driver load, which weakens the machine.

  1. Make a VM with Secure Boot off (test signing cannot be turned on while it is on), and take a snapshot.
  2. In the VM, from an elevated terminal: bcdedit /set testsigning on, then restart. The desktop shows a "Test Mode" watermark.
  3. Sign the driver with a test certificate that only the VM trusts. The driver build (#22) and signing (#24) work describes this when the driver exists.
  4. When you are done, bcdedit /set testsigning off and restart, or roll back to the snapshot.

The VM test harness (#26) automates VMs for end-to-end tests.

If you lock yourself out

Today nothing in Palisade blocks a program: the agent is audit-only (milestone M1), and enforcement arrives in M2. These rules keep it that way on a development machine as enforcement lands:

  • Audit mode only on a development machine. Every policy you deploy there uses mode audit (or monitor), never enforce (#36). An audit policy reports what it would block and blocks nothing.
  • Enforce only in a VM with a snapshot. If an enforce test goes wrong, roll back the snapshot.

If a policy does block what you need, the emergency procedure, from least to most drastic:

  1. Stop the agent. In console mode, press Ctrl-C; nothing it did persists. An installed agent is stopped with sc stop PalisadeAgent from an elevated terminal. (Stop protection and its break-glass unlock come later, in #222, and offline override codes in #120.)
  2. Remove an OS-native policy. A policy that Palisade compiled for the OS's own code integrity enforcement (#6) keeps enforcing when the agent is stopped (ADR 0012). Remove it with the OS's code integrity policy command-line tool, from an elevated terminal: list the active policies, remove the one with Palisade's policy ID, and restart. The OS documentation for the tool gives the exact options for your build.
  3. If no terminal will start, restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (hold Shift while choosing Restart), open a command prompt, delete the policy file named after the policy ID from the code integrity policies folder under \Windows\System32\CodeIntegrity, and restart.
  4. Roll back the VM, if this happened in one.

Git hooks

Opt-in hooks check formatting, spelling, banned terms and the commit message before each commit. They run under Git's Bash. Turn them on with git config core.hooksPath .githooks; see .githooks/README.md.

Source: docs/dev/windows.md on GitHub.

Developing on Linux and other desktop OS

Most of Palisade does not need Windows. The policy engine, file identity parsers, event schema, server and CLI build and test on any OS, and so does the agent's service host. This guide covers working on those from Linux or another desktop OS. For Windows, see windows.md.

What builds where

The whole workspace builds and tests everywhere: cargo test --workspace works on Linux and other desktop OS. Code that only means something on Windows is behind #[cfg(windows)], so elsewhere it is left out or replaced by a stub:

CrateOn Linux and other desktop OS
palisade-core, -fileid, -policy, -protoEverything. The file identity crate parses Windows files from bytes; only its optional os-trust backend (OS trust and file-system APIs) is Windows only
palisade-server, -cli, -consoleEverything
palisade-agentThe service host, configuration, supervisor and --console mode; the platform backends that the standard library covers; and the fake agent (--simulate). --service and the Windows registry backend are Windows only
palisade-tray, -driverPlaceholders that build anywhere

To check the Windows-only code without Windows:

rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu -- -D warnings

That needs a MinGW-w64 C cross-compiler on PATH for the build scripts (gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64 on Debian and Ubuntu). The dev container has it. CI checks the real MSVC targets on Windows runners, so this is a quick local check, not a replacement.

The dev container

.devcontainer/ defines a Linux image with:

  • the toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, its components and targets, plus the Windows GNU target, the MSRV toolchain and the pinned nightly for fuzzing;
  • the tools CI uses, at the versions CI installs: cargo-nextest, cargo-deny, cargo-audit, cargo-vet, cargo-hack, cargo-llvm-cov, cargo-insta, cargo-fuzz, zizmor and actionlint (the release archive, checked against its SHA-256, as the CI job does);
  • the documentation tools: mdBook, mdbook-mermaid-ssr, lychee and typos (not the headless browser that mdbook-mermaid-ssr renders diagrams with, so cargo xtask docs build names it as missing);
  • a Postgres 17 service (the image and digest the CI postgres job uses), with PALISADE_TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL set, so the server's database tests run instead of skipping.

Open the repository in any editor that supports dev containers, or run it with the dev container CLI. The cargo tools are built from source with cargo install --locked, so the first build takes a while; actionlint is the one prebuilt binary, checked against its published SHA-256. xtask tests check that the image's toolchain and tool versions match rust-toolchain.toml and CI.

cargo xtask ci runs every CI check inside the container, and --fast skips the slow ones. The image has every tool it checks for, and an xtask test fails if a CI step needs one the image lacks. Two exceptions: the Windows-only package and signing steps never run on Linux, and the server-image steps need podman, a container runtime the image does not nest; run those on the host, or use --fast, which skips them. The Postgres step runs because the container sets PALISADE_TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL.

Optional: building the image with --build-arg WITH_XWIN=1 adds cargo-xwin, which can check the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc target from Linux (cargo xwin check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc). On first use it downloads the Windows SDK and C runtime headers, under their own licence terms, which you have to accept; that is why it is off by default.

The container never turns on the Git hooks. See Git hooks.

Running the server

The server needs a TLS certificate and an agent CA even for local work: it has no plaintext listener (its README). For a throwaway local setup, make a development CA and a certificate for localhost with OpenSSL. These are for your machine only; never use them anywhere else.

mkdir -p dev/tls && cd dev
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -days 30 \
  -subj /CN=palisade-dev-ca -keyout tls/ca.key -out tls/agent-ca.crt
openssl req -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -subj /CN=localhost \
  -keyout tls/server.key -out tls/server.csr
printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,IP:127.0.0.1\nextendedKeyUsage=serverAuth\n' > tls/ext.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in tls/server.csr -CA tls/agent-ca.crt -CAkey tls/ca.key \
  -CAcreateserial -days 30 -extfile tls/ext.cnf -out tls/server.crt
chmod 600 tls/*.key
cat > server.toml <<'EOF'
[tls]
cert_file = "tls/server.crt"
key_file = "tls/server.key"

[listen.admin]
bind = "127.0.0.1"
port = 8443
public_url = "https://localhost:8443"

[listen.agent]
bind = "127.0.0.1"
port = 8444
public_url = "https://localhost:8444"
client_ca_file = "tls/agent-ca.crt"
EOF
cd ..
cargo run -p palisade-server -- check-config --config dev/server.toml
cargo run -p palisade-server -- serve --config dev/server.toml

In another terminal:

curl --cacert dev/tls/agent-ca.crt https://localhost:8443/healthz   # {"status":"alive"}
curl --cacert dev/tls/agent-ca.crt https://localhost:8443/readyz    # {"status":"ready"}

dev/ is not ignored by Git; keep it outside the repository, or never git add it. Keys must not be committed (.gitignore already drops *.pem and *.pfx).

To run the server with Postgres, add a [database] section (server README). In the dev container the database is at host postgres, port 5432. Outside it, any disposable Postgres 16 or later works; docs/ci.md describes how the tests use one.

The web console is still a skeleton (#136); there is nothing to run yet.

The fake agent

Server, console and event-pipeline work needs agent events, and the real agent's sources (ETW, the OS event logs) only exist on Windows. The fake agent produces the same events on any OS:

cargo run -p palisade-agent --features test-util -- --simulate
cargo run -p palisade-agent --features test-util -- --simulate --scenario my-scenario.toml

It replays a scripted scenario on the mock platform (palisade_core::test_util) and writes one canonical event per line to standard output: agent.started, an exec.decision per process start, then agent.stopped. Every event passes the schema's validation, carries a sequence number and a chain link, and is the same on every run. The built-in scenario is crates/palisade-agent/scenarios/default.toml, and the agent README documents the format.

cargo run -q -p palisade-agent --features test-util -- --simulate | jq -c '{seq, event_type, outcome}'

The fake agent cannot send its events to a server yet: the server has no agent endpoints, and devices cannot enrol. Both come with server communication (#62), enrolment (#223) and the server's agent endpoints (#126). The simulator will then post the same events. Until then, pipe its output into whatever you are building.

--simulate only exists in builds with the test-util feature, which release builds never turn on (workspace.md). A normal build rejects it.

Testing against the platform mocks

Agent logic reads the OS only through the traits in palisade_core::platform: the clock, files, signatures, identity, processes, the environment, the registry and the event sink. palisade_core::test_util (feature test-util) has an in-memory mock of each, and MockPlatform bundles them:

use palisade_core::platform::{Clock, UtcTime};
use palisade_core::test_util::{MockFile, MockPlatform};

let mut p = MockPlatform::new();
p.clock.set_utc(UtcTime(1_764_000_000_000_000));
p.fs.insert(r"C:\Tools\tool.exe", MockFile::new(b"MZ...".to_vec()).owner("S-1-5-32-544"));
p.clock.advance(30 * 60 * 1_000_000); // let 30 minutes pass

Add it as a dev-dependency: palisade-core = { workspace = true, features = ["test-util"] }.

palisade_core::test_util::contract holds the behaviour every implementation must have. The mocks pass it in palisade-core's tests, and the agent's real implementations pass it in crates/palisade-agent/tests/platform.rs, on every CI runner, Windows included. If you change a mock, change the contract with it, so mocks and real behaviour cannot drift apart.

The VM test harness

End-to-end tests on real Windows run in VMs. The harness, and how to drive it from a Linux host, is #26 (milestone M1). It is not built yet; this section will describe it when it lands.

Git hooks

Opt-in hooks run the quick checks before each commit: formatting, spelling and the banned-terms check, and the Conventional Commit format of the message. Nothing turns them on for you:

git config core.hooksPath .githooks      # on
git config --unset core.hooksPath        # off

See .githooks/README.md.

Source: docs/dev/unix.md on GitHub.

Testing

How Palisade is tested, which tests run where, and the conventions new tests follow. CONTRIBUTING.md says what a change must come with, and ci.md lists every CI job.

Kinds of test

KindWhereRuns
Unit tests#[cfg(test)] mod tests next to the code, or a tests.rs sibling moduleEvery cargo test / cargo nextest run, on every CI test runner
Integration testscrates/<crate>/tests/*.rs, using only the crate's public APISame
Property testsproptest, in either of the aboveSame
Golden-file testsExpected output committed next to the test, regenerated on requestSame
DoctestsExamples in /// commentscargo test --doc, because nextest does not run them
Fuzz targetscrates/<crate>/fuzz/, cargo-fuzz (libFuzzer)60 s per target on every PR; 30 min per target weekly
Benchmarkscrates/<crate>/benches/*.rs, criterionBuilt and run once in test mode on every PR; measured locally
CoverageUnit, integration, property and golden-file tests, instrumented (not doctests, fuzzing or benchmarks)Every PR, on Linux and Windows x64

Running tests

cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --locked   # the `default` profile
cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --locked --profile ci
cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked --doc
cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked           # also works, without the JUnit report

.config/nextest.toml has two profiles:

  • default: for local runs. No retries, and a test is reported as slow after 60 s.
  • ci: the same, plus fail-fast = false, so one run reports every failure, and a JUnit report at target/nextest/ci/junit.xml. cargo xtask test-summary turns that report into the job summary (ci.md).

Neither profile retries. A test that passes only on a retry is flaky, and a flaky test in a security product hides real failures, so it is fixed rather than retried. Do not add retries to a profile or a per-test override.

The postgres test group holds palisade-server's database tests (tests/postgres.rs). Each test creates its own database and roles, so they run in parallel, at most four at a time so the server's connection limit never fails a test. Outside the postgres CI job they skip themselves, because PALISADE_TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL is not set. A new test binary that needs Postgres joins the group by adding its binary(...) to the filter in .config/nextest.toml.

The slowest tests are the 10,000-case property tests in palisade-policy, which take tens of seconds in a debug build. Set PROPTEST_CASES to run fewer cases locally.

Conventions

Names

A test name says what is expected, as a sentence in snake case: what holds, or what happens in which case. For example hostile_descriptors_are_errors, every_truncation_of_a_rich_image and huge_counts_do_not_overflow. A reader of a failure should know what broke from the name alone. Do not prefix names with test_.

Determinism

  • No sleeps. A test that waits for something uses a channel, a barrier or a mock clock. A Clock trait for code that reads the time arrives with the platform abstraction (#29). Until then, pass times in as values.
  • No network. Unit and integration tests do not open sockets to anything outside the test, resolve names or download anything. Tests that need a real service, such as Postgres for the server (#126, #127), are marked and run only where that service is provided.
  • No dependence on the machine. Tests do not read the user's home directory, environment or locale, or the system clock's time zone. Temporary files go in a fresh directory under std::env::temp_dir() or the target directory, and are removed afterwards.
  • Randomness comes only from proptest, which reports a seed for every failure.

Platforms

  • Code and tests that only work on Windows are gated with #[cfg(windows)], so the workspace builds and tests on every platform. CI runs the tests on Linux, macOS, Windows x64 and Windows ARM64.
  • Tests that need administrator rights or a test VM are #[ignore]d, with a reason, and run in the VM harness (#26).
  • Ignored tests that write files on request, such as the fuzz seed writers below, say so in their #[ignore = "..."] reason.

Fixtures

  • Fixtures are synthetic and built at test time where possible. palisade-fileid builds its PE images byte by byte (crates/palisade-fileid/tests/common), so no binaries are committed.
  • Small committed fixtures (policy documents, PKCS#7 signatures) live in the crate's tests/fixtures/, each set with a note, or a script, that says how it was made.
  • Never commit malware, antivirus test strings or third-party signed binaries (responsible-use.md). The one exception is the content tagger's built-in rule for the standard anti-malware test file (#44): its rule and test fixture hold the string as hex only, assembled in memory at test time and never written to disk, and source_files_do_not_carry_the_test_string (crates/palisade-fileid/tests/tags.rs) fails if the string appears verbatim in the crate's sources. cargo xtask check-testdata (the fixtures CI job) fails if any file in the repository starts like an executable (MZ) and its SHA-256 is not in testdata/manifest.txt with a reason. Generated fixtures are never committed, so that list is normally empty, and a dropped-in PE, anywhere, fails the check.

The fixture corpus

palisade-fileid builds a whole corpus from Rust at test time, on any OS, in crates/palisade-fileid/tests/corpus/:

KindFixtures
PEPE32+ x64 and ARM64, PE32 x86, each as an .exe and a .dll, with a version resource (original file name, product, company, file version)
Test PKIA root CA, an intermediate and RSA-3072 leaves; an ECDSA P-256 leaf; expired, revoked-in-CRL, wrong-EKU (TLS server only) and self-signed leaves; a CRL
Signed PEEmbedded Authenticode, dual signed (nested), tampered after signing, a truncated certificate table, a page-hash-bearing signature, and one per bad leaf above
CatalogA signed catalog (.cat) and the unsigned PE it lists by SHA-256 Authenticode digest (catalog-signed)
MalformedZero length, MZ only, truncated headers, overlapping sections, NumberOfSections 0xffff, a recursive resource directory, SizeOfImage near 4 GiB
Script.ps1, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js, .wsf, .hta, each only printing PALISADE-FIXTURE
  • Signing is pure Rust (tests/corpus/sign.rs): PKCS#7 SignedData over SpcIndirectDataContent (or a catalog's trust list), as code signers write it, so no OS signing tools are needed.
  • Deterministic. The RSA test keys come from an RNG seeded by the key's name, and the signing time is fixed, so every run on every OS makes the same bytes. The one exception is the ECDSA fixture, whose signature is random by nature.
  • Checked by the crate itself. tests/fixture_corpus.rs parses every fixture and asserts the property it was built to have: machine, format and version info; signatures that verify and chain to the test root (and the nested one); the tampered fixture a digest mismatch; the wrong-EKU leaf refused because code signing is not permitted, the self-signed one because it reaches no anchor; the CRL listing the revoked leaf; the page hash table matching; malformed inputs never panicking. This runs in the test job on every OS.
  • On disk: cargo xtask fixtures writes the corpus and a MANIFEST to target/fixtures/.
  • Golden hashes: cargo xtask golden rebuilds the corpus and compares every fixture's SHA-256 with testdata/golden/fixtures.txt; cargo xtask golden --update rewrites it. A changed hash is a changed fixture, reviewed in the PR. Provenance: testdata/golden/README.md.
  • Fuzz seeds: write_corpus_fuzz_seeds adds the corpus to the seed corpora of the PE, PKCS#7 and X.509 fuzz targets.

Not in the corpus: MSI/MSP/MST fixtures, which arrive with installer identity (#53; its compound-file builder is on main since #279), and CHM and CPL fixtures, which arrive with compiled HTML and control panel item enforcement (#98, M2).

  • Builders. Policy tests in other crates build their inputs with palisade-policy's test-util feature (palisade_policy::test_util) rather than hand-written JSON:

    [dev-dependencies]
palisade-policy = { workspace = true, features = ["test-util"] }

    let policy = PolicyBuilder::new()
    .rule_set(RuleSetBuilder::allowlist(1).rule(RuleBuilder::allow(1, hash('a'))))
    .validate();
let decision = subject(&facts().sha256('a')).decide(&policy);

Unwrap in tests

clippy.toml allows unwrap and expect inside #[test] functions. Helpers outside them need #![allow(clippy::unwrap_used)] at the top of the test file, with a comment that says why.

Property tests

Property tests use proptest. Use them for invariants that must hold for every input: parsers never panic and respect their limits, serialisation round-trips, and matching agrees with a simpler reference.

  • Failing cases are saved and replayed first on every run, so a fixed bug stays fixed: for unit tests in proptest-regressions/ next to the crate's sources, and for integration tests in tests/<name>.proptest-regressions. Commit those files.
  • Check that a property can fail: plant a bug (an off-by-one at a bound, say), run it, and revert. tests/version_properties.rs in palisade-policy says which bugs it was checked against.
  • Prefer mutating valid inputs (flip, truncate, overwrite) over purely random bytes: they reach much deeper into a parser.
  • The default case count is 256. Expensive properties set a smaller count with ProptestConfig::with_cases; important cheap ones set a larger one.

Golden-file tests

A golden-file test compares generated output with a committed file. The convention is the one palisade-policy's JSON Schema test uses (crates/palisade-policy/tests/schema.rs):

  • The test fails with a message that says how to regenerate the file.
  • Setting PALISADE_BLESS=1 makes the test rewrite the file instead of failing: PALISADE_BLESS=1 cargo test -p palisade-policy --test schema.
  • A change to a golden file is reviewed in the PR like code. The diff shows what changed in the output.

Snapshot tests

Structured output that people and other systems rely on is checked with insta snapshots: the test serialises the value, and insta compares it with a reviewed .snap file next to the test.

CrateTestWhat is snapshotted
palisade-policytests/decision_snapshots.rsWhole-pipeline decisions (outcome, deciding rule, overridden rules, annotations, directives, effects, reason code), for policies built with test_util
palisade-prototests/event_snapshots.rsEvent JSON: the canonical bytes, and a readable pretty-printed copy

Conventions:

  • One directory per test file, set with Settings::set_snapshot_path (for example tests/snapshots/pipeline/), and named snapshots (assert_json_snapshot!("name", value)), so file names say what they hold and do not depend on test function names.

  • Deterministic input. Fixed IDs (the test_util builders make them), fixed times, fixed trace IDs. Never snapshot a random or time-dependent value; redact it or set it.

  • .gitattributes with * -text in each snapshot directory, so Windows checkouts keep LF and the byte comparison holds on every runner.

  • Review like code. A snapshot diff in a PR is a change to output. After a deliberate change:

    cargo insta test -p palisade-policy --all-features   # writes .snap.new files for changes
cargo insta review                                   # accept or reject each one

    INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test ... writes them directly; read the diff before committing.

  • CI (the snapshots job) runs cargo insta test --check --unreferenced reject, offline after cargo fetch --locked: it fails if any snapshot differs, is missing, or is no longer referenced by a test. The normal test job also fails on a differing snapshot, because insta does not write files when CI is set.

The older golden-file convention above (PALISADE_BLESS=1) stays for committed artefacts that are not snapshots of a test value: the JSON Schemas and the event registry. Snapshots of the compiled OS-native policy XML and of CLI output arrive with that code (#84, #15), using the same conventions.

Fuzzing

Every parser of untrusted input has a coverage-guided fuzz target. The targets live in a separate cargo-fuzz workspace per crate (crates/<crate>/fuzz/), so normal builds never compile them, and only they need a nightly toolchain. There are three projects:

  • crates/palisade-fileid/fuzz, with thirteen targets: pe_parse, version_info_parse, authenticode_ranges, authenticode_pkcs7, fsctx_parse, x509_chain, timestamp_crl, fuzz_ctl, fuzz_classify, fuzz_msi_tables, legacy_parse, fuzz_tags and script_sig. The project builds palisade-fileid with its content-rules feature, for fuzz_tags.
  • crates/palisade-proto/fuzz, with one target: trust_set_decode.
  • crates/palisade-policy/fuzz, with three targets: fuzz_policy_json (the strict JSON reader, validation and the evaluator build), fuzz_policy_yaml (the YAML reader) and fuzz_wildcard_regex_compile (compiling and matching wildcards, regular expressions and text values).

Target names are unique across projects, so --target names one without its project. Each fuzz workspace has its own committed Cargo.lock. Dependabot keeps it up to date, cargo-deny checks it against the root deny.toml on every PR and daily, and cargo xtask audit runs cargo-audit over it. cargo-vet covers only the root workspace, so a fuzz-only dependency is reviewed in its PR instead (dependencies.md). The fuzz crates are never shipped.

One command builds every target of every project, seeds its corpus from the synthetic test fixtures, and runs it:

rustup toolchain install nightly-2026-11-20 --profile minimal
cargo install --locked cargo-fuzz@0.13.2
cargo xtask fuzz                         # 60 s per target, every target, as a PR runs them
cargo xtask fuzz --shard 2/6             # only the targets of one of CI's 6 shards
cargo xtask fuzz --seconds 1800 --target pe_parse

The nightly is pinned by date in xtask/src/fuzz.rs, so a new nightly cannot break CI. The lockfile is checked with cargo fetch --locked on that nightly, and the build and runs are then offline, so they cannot download anything or re-resolve the lockfile. The corpus and any findings go to target/fuzz-smoke/<target>/. Each target runs with a 10 s limit per input and a 2 GiB memory limit, so hangs and runaway allocation count as findings too.

  • On every PR, the fuzz job in ci.yml runs every target for 60 s, split across 6 parallel shards: shard I runs cargo xtask fuzz --shard I/6, the targets whose position in PROJECTS (counted from 0 across all projects) is I modulo 6, and builds only the projects those targets are in. Together the shards run every target exactly once, and cargo xtask ci runs them all in one go.
  • Every week, fuzz.yml runs each target for 30 minutes, as one job per target. If any fails, it opens an area:security issue, or comments on the open one.

A finding fails the job. The job summary lists each target's result and, for each failing input up to 64 KiB, the input itself as base64 with the command that reproduces it. That stands in for an artefact upload, which would need an action outside the allowlist (ci.md). To fix a finding:

  1. Reproduce it locally with the command from the job summary.
  2. Fix the parser.
  3. Add the input as a regression test in the crate's normal tests, so it runs on every platform on every PR, not only under the fuzzer.

xtask/src/fuzz.rs lists every fuzz project and target. Its tests fail if a target is missing from the list, from a project's Cargo.toml or from fuzz.yml's matrix, if two projects use the same target name, if a crates/*/fuzz project is not listed, or if a project has no committed lockfile. To add a target:

  1. Add the target to fuzz_targets/ and as a [[bin]] in the project's Cargo.toml.
  2. Add it to PROJECTS in xtask/src/fuzz.rs, with its dictionary and the ignored tests that write its seed inputs (they read the output directory from PALISADE_FUZZ_SEED_DIR).
  3. Add it to the matrix in .github/workflows/fuzz.yml.

A test also fails if the PR fuzz job's shards would have more than 5 targets each. Then add shards: extend the shard list in the job's matrix in .github/workflows/ci.yml, and change the /6 in its SHARD to the new count, so no shard nears its 30-minute limit.

For a new crate's fuzz project, also add it to PROJECTS with the package whose tests write its seeds, commit its Cargo.lock (and keep Cargo.lock out of its .gitignore), add it to .github/dependabot.yml, and add its cargo-deny step to the deps job in ci.yml, to audit.yml and to xtask/src/ci.rs. The tests in xtask/src/fuzz.rs fail until all of these are in place. A seed writer that writes nothing fails the run, because libtest passes when --exact matches no test.

Coverage

The coverage job in ci.yml runs the nextest suite under cargo-llvm-cov, on ubuntu-latest and windows-latest. cargo xtask coverage-summary then writes a table to the job summary page: line, function and region coverage for each crate, and the total. The instrumentation needs llvm-tools-preview, which rust-toolchain.toml installs.

Coverage is reported, not enforced, with one exception. The initial targets are 80% line coverage for palisade-policy and palisade-fileid (#25). A crate below its target gets a warning annotation on the run, and the job still passes.

The exception: palisade-policy line coverage must not decrease. On every pull request the coverage-gate job measures the crate's own tests at the base commit and at the PR, in the same job, and fails if the share of covered lines went down. New code needs tests in the same PR; new code at the same ratio passes. PROPTEST_RNG_SEED is fixed for both runs, so property tests generate the same cases and the number is reproducible. To check before pushing:

cargo xtask coverage-gate --base origin/main

The full line-by-line report is not uploaded as an artefact, because that needs an action outside the CI allowlist (ci.md); generate it locally with cargo llvm-cov report --html (below). For the same reason the table goes to the job summary, not a PR comment, which would also need a write token on pull requests.

To see the report locally:

cargo install --locked cargo-llvm-cov@0.9.2
cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --all-features --locked --profile ci \
  --json --summary-only --output-path target/llvm-cov-summary.json
cargo xtask coverage-summary local target/llvm-cov-summary.json
cargo llvm-cov report --html --open      # line-by-line, from the same run

Benchmarks

Benchmarks use criterion, in crates/<crate>/benches/:

CrateBenchWhat it measures
palisade-policycriterion_evalOne compiled criterion against an object's facts: hash, 25-value text, path wildcard, regex and version range
palisade-fileidhash_and_parseFlat hashing of 1 MiB with each algorithm set, streamed hashing, PE parsing (full and metadata-only) and the Authenticode hash

Run them locally, on a quiet machine:

cargo bench -p palisade-policy --bench criterion_eval
cargo bench -p palisade-fileid --bench hash_and_parse
cargo bench -p palisade-policy --bench criterion_eval -- --save-baseline before   # then, after a change:
cargo bench -p palisade-policy --bench criterion_eval -- --baseline before

The bench job in CI builds every bench and runs each benchmark once in test mode (cargo test --bench <name>). That catches benches that no longer build or that panic, but it measures nothing. Shared hosted runners vary too much from run to run for their timings to be compared. A test in xtask/src/ci.rs fails if a benches/*.rs file is missing from the job.

criterion 0.7 was chosen because later releases needed a newer Rust than the MSRV of the time (1.85), and the msrv job builds every target, including benches. The MSRV is now 1.94 (workspace.md); moving to a newer criterion is a separate change. Its plotting and parallel features are off.

Regression gate

.github/workflows/bench.yml runs cargo xtask bench-compare --base <commit> weekly (main against main a week earlier) and on demand for any branch. It measures every bench at the base commit and at the head, in one job on one runner, twice each, alternating (base, head, base, head), keeps each side's faster median, and compares them. A benchmark regresses when its median is more than 10% slower and the 95% confidence intervals of the two medians do not overlap. The table is in the job summary.

How it copes with noise on shared hosted runners, which vary by tens of percent between runs and machines:

  • Same job, back to back. A stored baseline from another run would not be comparable, so the base is measured again every time.
  • Iteration counts. criterion runs many iterations per sample and 100 samples per benchmark, which gives the confidence intervals.
  • Alternating rounds, best of two. Noise on a shared machine almost only ever slows a run down, and alternating means a slow patch hits both sides alike.
  • Two conditions. Over the threshold and outside the noise.

Small changes still show up as noise, so treat a regression as a prompt to measure locally, where a quiet machine gives sharper numbers:

cargo xtask bench-compare --base origin/main    # the same comparison, locally

The gate was checked by slowing one benchmark (hash_1mib/sha256) by 20% on purpose. The comparison measured it at +19.7%, reported it as regressed and failed, and reported the other eleven benchmarks within ±5% as unchanged.

Benchmarks over whole policies (100 to 100k rules), the decision cache and bundle loading, and the absolute performance budget of evaluation, arrive with the code they measure (#42, #43). The gate covers them as soon as they are added, because it runs every crates/*/benches/*.rs. The 100 MB and 1 GB file hashing runs stay local and on demand.

Source: docs/testing.md on GitHub.

Continuous integration

CI is defined in .github/workflows/. It runs on GitHub-hosted runners only. Self-hosted runners, third-party runner services and cloud-managed build or pipeline services are permanently prohibited: self-hosted runners on a public repository can be taken over by pull requests from forks, and paid build services have caused surprise bills. The runner-guard job enforces this on every PR (see below). If a job cannot run on a hosted runner, it becomes a documented local-only step; it is never moved to another runner type.

Workflows

JobRunnersWhat it runs

workflow-lintubuntu-latestactionlint (checksum-verified release) and zizmor --offline

sign-testwindows-latestCode signing end to end with throwaway certificates made on the runner and deleted: cargo xtask dist --msi --sign test-ca, cargo xtask release verify of every signature including inside the packages, then packaging/sign/ci-test.ps1 (the pfx signer with a canary password that must not appear in the output, and a signed package of unsigned executables that verification must reject). No secrets (releasing.md)

ci-okubuntu-latestPasses only if every job above succeeded

Branch protection requires ci-ok (and the PR title check below). It depends on every other job and fails if any of them failed, was cancelled or was skipped, so new jobs are covered without changing the branch rules. The ruleset is in repo-settings.md. Requiring the one aggregate check, instead of each job by name, is how the required set in #21 (fmt, both clippy runs, the tests, msrv, deps, docs and runner-guard), and the coverage, fuzz and bench jobs from #25, is enforced: a matrix job's check names change whenever the matrix does, and the aggregate cannot be left out of date.

The test matrix runs the whole workspace on every runner. On Linux and the other desktop OS that means the portable crates, plus the Windows-only crates as stubs; Windows x64 and Windows ARM64 run everything natively. The issue's test-portable, test-windows-x64 and test-windows-arm64 are the four entries of this one matrix.

Test reports

nextest writes a JUnit report (.config/nextest.toml, profile ci) to target/nextest/ci/junit.xml. The Test summary step runs even when the tests fail, and cargo xtask test-summary turns the report into a table on the job's summary page and one error annotation per failed test. Failure names are escaped, so a test name cannot inject a workflow command. If the tests did not build, there is no report, and the step only warns.

Coverage, fuzzing and benchmarks

Details and local commands are in testing.md.

  • coverage runs the same nextest suite instrumented by cargo-llvm-cov, and cargo xtask coverage-summary writes line, function and region coverage per crate to the job summary. It is reported, not enforced: a crate below its target (80% lines for palisade-policy and palisade-fileid) gets a warning annotation and the job still passes.

  • coverage-gate is the one coverage rule that is enforced (#25): palisade-policy line coverage must not decrease. On a pull request, cargo xtask coverage-gate runs cargo llvm-cov nextest -p palisade-policy at the PR's base commit (in a temporary git worktree) and at the PR, with PROPTEST_RNG_SEED fixed so property tests cover the same cases each time, and fails if the share of covered lines went down. Adding code at the same coverage ratio passes. Both numbers are in the job summary. Nothing is stored between runs: a baseline from main would need an artefact or a cache write from a pull request, and measuring the base again in the same job needs neither.

  • fuzz-locks runs cargo metadata --locked on each fuzz workspace (found on disk, so a new one is checked before it is listed anywhere). A pull request that changes a dependency of a crate a fuzz workspace builds, even indirectly, must re-lock that workspace; this job says so in seconds, with the minimal re-lock command (cargo metadata --manifest-path <dir>/Cargo.toml, which upgrades nothing). The fuzz job waits for it.

  • fuzz runs cargo xtask fuzz, split across a matrix of 6 shards that run in parallel. Shard I runs cargo xtask fuzz --shard I/6: the targets whose position in the list in xtask/src/fuzz.rs (in project order, counted from 0 across all projects) is I modulo 6. Together the shards run every target exactly once. Each shard builds only the projects it has a target in, each from its fuzz workspace's committed Cargo.lock, seeds each corpus from the crate's synthetic fixtures, and runs each of its targets for 60 s. A crash, hang, leak or out-of-memory input fails that shard, and so ci-ok; the shards do not cancel each other (fail-fast: false), and each shard's summary shows each failing input up to 64 KiB as base64, with the command that reproduces it.

    Shards keep each job well under its 30-minute limit as targets are added. As one job, the 17 targets took 26 minutes (1,581 s) on main: about 7 minutes building the three projects (fileid about 70 s, proto about 175 s, policy about 155 s on a hosted runner), and 60 to 85 s per target with its seeding. With 6 shards each runs at most 3 targets (18 with the bundle decoder) and builds at most two projects, about 8 minutes in all. A unit test in xtask/src/fuzz.rs reads the shard count from ci.yml and fails once a shard would get more than 5 targets; then add shards: extend the shard list and change the /6 in the job's SHARD to match (a test in xtask/src/ci.rs checks the two agree).

    The nightly toolchain is pinned by date. cargo-fuzz has no prebuilt binary in the install action, so it is built from crates.io with cargo install --locked (fallback: cargo-install, which passes no token).

  • bench builds every criterion bench and runs each benchmark once in test mode, so a bench that no longer builds or panics fails. Timings are not measured on shared runners. A unit test fails if a benches/*.rs file is not named in the job.

main-snapshot

Every push to main whose CI passed replaces the files of one rolling pre-release, tagged main-snapshot, with that commit's unsigned packages (<commit>.Palisade-<version>-x64.msi and -arm64.msi, where <commit> is the first 12 characters of the commit) and their .msi.sha256 checksums (#22). The release is marked as a pre-release, never as the latest release, and its notes say the builds are unsigned, untested snapshots and not for production use, and name the commit and the run. Every file name starts with its commit, so an upload never replaces another commit's file: the previous set stays published until the new one is complete, and is then removed, so there is only ever one set.

Only the three snapshot jobs have a write scope (contents: write, to edit the release and move the tag), and they run only on push to main, never on pull requests, so fork code never runs with it. snapshot-prepare creates the release on first use and marks it as being updated, snapshot builds and uploads each architecture's package on its own runner, and snapshot-finish checks that main still points at the commit (a re-run of an older run's job keeps that run's commit, and must not publish over a newer snapshot) and that all four files are there, then points the tag at the commit, removes older files and writes the notes. snapshot-prepare stops on any release lookup failure other than "not found", so an API error never creates a release or moves the tag. The commands are in .github/scripts/main-snapshot.sh, which uses the preinstalled gh CLI; its tests (main-snapshot.test.sh, a fake gh) run in runner-guard. Pushes to main queue rather than cancel each other (concurrency), so two snapshots never interleave.

The snapshot job builds the packages again instead of reusing the package job's: passing files between jobs needs an artefact action, and only three actions are allowed (see below). The packages are built from the same commit with the same command. Pull requests build and test the packages in package and publish nothing.

release.yml (pushed v* tags; pull requests that change release tooling)

The release pipeline: check-tag, build (x64 and ARM64, natively), server, sign (the approval-gated release-signing environment), verify, provenance and publish. Files move between jobs through a draft release, using the preinstalled gh, because no artefact action is allowed; the draft is published only after verify passes. Pull requests that change release.yml, xtask/src/dist/, xtask/src/release/ or packaging/ run only dry-run: the same build, signing with a throwaway test CA, packaging and verification, with no secrets, no write access and no upload. Details: releasing.md.

fuzz.yml (weekly on Sunday at 04:41 UTC, and on demand)

JobRunnersWhat it runs
fuzzubuntu-latestcargo xtask fuzz --seconds 1800 --target <name>, one job per target of every fuzz project (target names are unique, so the name selects the project)
reportubuntu-latestOn failure, opens an issue titled "Scheduled fuzzing found a failure" with the area:security label, or comments on the open one

Longer runs find what the 60 s PR run cannot. A unit test in xtask/src/fuzz.rs keeps the matrix in step with the target list. Only report has issues: write, and it runs no repository code. The failing input is in the failed job's summary.

bench.yml (weekly on Monday at 05:23 UTC, and on demand)

JobRunnersWhat it runs
compareubuntu-latestcargo xtask bench-compare --base <commit>: every criterion bench at the base commit and at the head, in the same job, twice each, alternating, keeping each side's faster median; fails if any median is more than 10% slower with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals

The weekly run compares main with main a week earlier. Run it on demand from the Actions tab for any branch, with base (default main) to compare against. It is not part of PR CI: two full benchmark runs take longer than a PR check should, and the result is only meaningful when both runs share a runner, which is why the base is measured again each time instead of being stored. The comparison table is in the job summary. See testing.md.

pr-title.yml (pull requests, including title edits)

JobRunnersWhat it runs
PR titleubuntu-latestbash .github/scripts/check-pr-title.test.sh, then .github/scripts/check-pr-title.sh on the pull request title

Pull requests are squash-merged with the PR title as the commit message, so the title must be a Conventional Commit (CONTRIBUTING.md). This is a separate workflow because it reruns when the title is edited, which should not rerun the whole build. The title reaches the script through an environment variable, never by expression interpolation into the shell. It is also a required check.

dco.yml (pull requests)

JobRunnersWhat it runs
DCOubuntu-latestbash .github/scripts/check-dco.test.sh, then .github/scripts/check-dco.sh on the pull request's base and head commits

Fails if a commit in the pull request has no Signed-off-by: trailer from its author (CONTRIBUTING.md). It is not a required check yet (repo-settings.md). The commit SHAs reach the script through environment variables. It reruns when a pull request's base branch changes (edited).

Dependabot authors its commits at a noreply address but signs them off as dependabot[bot] <support@github.com>. When GitHub reports that Dependabot opened the pull request, the workflow passes --dependabot, and the script accepts that sign-off for commits authored at the bot's noreply address only. The pull request author comes from GitHub, not from the commits, so a commit that copies the bot's address gains nothing.

Pull requests opened by the repository owner pass with a notice and are not checked (CONTRIBUTING.md). The workflow reads GitHub's author_association for the pull request, which commits cannot change. The checker's own tests still run on those pull requests.

syncubuntu-latest.github/scripts/sync-labels.sh --apply on a push to main; --check (a dry run) on a manual run unless apply is ticked

Runs on pull requests and pushes to main that change .github/labels.yml, .github/milestones.yml, the issue templates, dependabot.yml, the sync script or the workflow. sync never runs on a pull request, and is the only job here with a write scope (issues: write, plus contents: read for the checkout). Details: repo-settings.md.

JobRunnersWhat it runs

reportubuntu-latestOn failure, opens an issue titled "Documentation site has broken external links" with the area:infra label, or comments on the open one

audit.yml (daily at 03:17 UTC, and on demand)

Runs cargo deny check advisories and cargo xtask audit (cargo-audit with the same ignores) against main, for the root workspace and every fuzz workspace's lockfile. Both also run on every PR (the deps job). A new advisory can affect main without any change here, which is why this is also scheduled. On failure, a second job opens an issue titled "Scheduled advisory audit is failing" with the area:security label, or comments on the open one. That job, the report jobs in fuzz.yml and links.yml, and the sync job in labels.yml are the only places with issues: write.

Dependabot (.github/dependabot.yml)

Weekly updates for Cargo dependencies (the workspace, and each fuzz workspace's own lockfile) and for the pinned action SHAs, with minor and patch bumps grouped into one PR per manifest. Security updates are opened as soon as an advisory is published. Dependabot PRs run the full CI like any other PR, including DCO, cargo-deny, cargo-audit and cargo-vet, so a bump of the root workspace merges only once the new version is audited or exempted with a note (dependencies.md). cargo-deny and cargo-audit also check each fuzz workspace's lockfile; cargo-vet covers only the root workspace, so a fuzz-only bump is reviewed in its PR. The fuzz crates are never shipped (testing.md). They are labelled area:security (Cargo) or area:infra (actions), because the label sync deletes Dependabot's default labels.

Documentation site

The book at https://jusso-dev.github.io/palisade/ is built from the repository's own Markdown (docs/, the root policy files and every crate README) by cargo xtask docs. docs/book/ holds only the book's configuration, theme, the pages that are new, and the generated reference.

CommandWhat it does
cargo xtask docs generateRegenerates docs/book/src/reference/generated/: the policy and event reference from schemas/*/v1.json, the CLI reference from each binary's --help, the crate map from the crate READMEs and xtask/src/deps.rs, and the reference and ADR lists in SUMMARY.md. Commit the result
cargo xtask docs checkFails if a generated page or list is stale; if a docs/**/*.md, crate README or root Markdown file is not in the book; if a page has no single title, skips a heading level or has an image without alt text; if a policy example is inline instead of included from docs/examples/policies/ (where palisade-policy's tests/yaml.rs validates it), or an example there is not shown; if a rust block is untested and not marked ignore; or if the disclaimer is missing from the README or the theme
cargo xtask docs buildStages the sources into target/book-src (repository links that are not chapters become links to GitHub; a broken one fails), runs mdbook build with every warning an error, renders every Mermaid diagram (a diagram that does not parse fails), checks every internal link and anchor with lychee --offline, and checks every page has the disclaimer banner. The site is in target/book
cargo xtask docs assemble <dir> --version <name>Assembles the GitHub Pages tree: the book and the cargo doc API docs under <dir>/<name>/ and <dir>/<name>/api/rust/, versions.json for the version switcher, and a root redirect to latest/

docs build needs mdBook 0.5.2, mdbook-mermaid-ssr 0.3.0 with the headless browser its README names (GitHub's Ubuntu runner image has one), and lychee 0.24.2; it names any that is missing. Search is mdBook's built-in search.

Spelling is checked with typos 1.52.2 over the whole repository; _typos.toml lists the accepted words (British spellings, test vectors and abbreviations). cargo xtask check-banned-terms fails on any commercial vendor or product name in any file or path, matched as whole words in any letter case; the list is docs/banned-terms.txt, which holds only SHA-256 digests (NAMING.md).

Publishing

pages.yml builds the site on every push to main (as latest) and on every release tag vX.Y.Z (as vX.Y), and pushes it to the gh-pages branch. A push made with the workflow's token does not start a Pages build, so the job then requests one through the REST API. Its write permissions, contents: write for the push and pages: write for the build request, are on that job only. It does not use the Pages deployment actions, which are not on the action allowlist; GitHub Pages serves the branch instead. One-time setting for the maintainer, in repo-settings.md.

links.yml checks every external link in the built book once a week, and opens or updates an issue when one is broken. Pull requests check internal links only (offline), so a third-party site being down never fails a PR.

Runner and action policy

cargo xtask check-workflows (the runner-guard job) checks every workflow file against allowlists in xtask/src/workflows.rs:

  • runs-on must be one of ubuntu-latest, ubuntu-24.04, windows-latest, windows-2025, windows-11-arm, macos-latest, macos-15. The only expression allowed is ${{ matrix.<key> }}, and every value of that key must be an allowed label. Matrix keys are matched case-insensitively, as GitHub does, and a matrix or include: entry built from an expression fails. Label lists, runner groups, and labels read from inputs or variables fail.
  • Every action is on the allowlist (actions/checkout, Swatinem/rust-cache, taiki-e/install-action) and pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA, with the version in a trailing comment. Container actions fail.
  • No job calls a reusable workflow (jobs.<id>.uses), local or remote. None are needed yet.
  • The workflow has a top-level permissions: block that is read-only: read-all, {}, or scopes set only to read or none. Jobs that need more ask for it themselves.
  • pull_request_target is never used, so fork PRs never run with secrets or a write token.
  • actions/checkout sets persist-credentials: false.
  • Swatinem/rust-cache sets save-if exactly once (in any letter case, as the runner matches input names), to false or to the main-branch expression, so only main writes the cache (threat model T-ci-06).
  • No file under .github/ (workflows, scripts, issue templates, anything) names a cloud-managed build or pipeline service, in any letter case, anywhere in its text or its file name. The names are kept out of this repository (NAMING.md), so the check stores only their SHA-256 digests and compares the digest of every substring of the same length.

Because the check allowlists runners and actions rather than blocklisting services, an unapproved build service fails by default. Adding a runner label or an action is a reviewed change to xtask/src/workflows.rs.

Other hardening:

  • Rust caches are written only from main (save-if, checked above), so PR builds, including forks, cannot poison them.
  • Superseded PR runs are cancelled; pushes to main always finish.
  • Every job has a timeout-minutes (30, or 60 for the test and coverage matrices and the weekly fuzz jobs).
  • CI sets CARGO_TERM_COLOR=always, CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 and RUST_BACKTRACE=1.
  • Every Cargo command uses --locked, so CI builds exactly Cargo.lock. Tools that run Cargo themselves and have no --locked (cargo-fuzz, cargo-insta) run offline after a cargo fetch --locked, which has the same effect: the lockfile cannot be re-resolved and nothing new is downloaded.

The workspace rules the deps and feature-powerset jobs enforce are described in workspace.md.

Running the checks locally

The toolchain is pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, so rustup picks it up automatically. One command runs every check in ci.yml, with the same command lines:

cargo xtask ci          # everything, including coverage, fuzz, docs, the book, feature-powerset and msrv
cargo xtask ci --fast   # skips those slow steps, and the package, signing and server-image builds

It runs every step even after one fails, and lists the failed ones at the end. Before it starts, it checks that the extra tools are installed (cargo-nextest, cargo-deny, cargo-audit, cargo-vet, cargo-hack, typos, actionlint, zizmor and, without --fast, cargo-llvm-cov, the fuzzing nightly with cargo-fuzz, mdBook, and the MSRV toolchain), and prints the install command for each one that is missing, at the version CI uses. Jobs that differ only by runner run once, on your machine, and the fuzz job's shards run as one cargo xtask fuzz, every target once. Steps whose job runs only on one OS run only there: on Windows, ci builds both packages (the package job, without its smoke test, which installs a service); on Linux, it builds the server binary and image (the server-image job, with podman). Elsewhere they are skipped with a note, and --fast skips them. A unit test in xtask/src/ci.rs compares its steps with ci.yml, so the two cannot drift.

The same checks, one by one:

cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
cargo clippy -p palisade-core -p palisade-driver --no-default-features --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo clippy -p palisade-core --no-default-features --features schema --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --locked --profile ci   # needs cargo-nextest 0.9
PALISADE_TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL=postgres://postgres:<pw>@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres \
  cargo nextest run -p palisade-server --test postgres --locked --profile ci  # needs a disposable Postgres 16+
cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked --doc
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features --locked
cargo xtask check-deps
cargo xtask check-manifests
cargo xtask check-unsafe
cargo xtask check-workflows
cargo xtask adr lint
cargo xtask threat-coverage
cargo xtask check-banned-terms
cargo xtask docs check
cargo xtask docs build             # needs mdbook 0.5.2, mdbook-mermaid-ssr 0.3.0, lychee 0.24.2

cargo deny --locked --manifest-path crates/palisade-fileid/fuzz/Cargo.toml --config deny.toml check
