To check Windows-only code from Linux or another desktop OS:

rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
cargo check --workspace --all-targets --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu

cargo test --workspace --all-features --locked still works and runs the same tests, without the JUnit report.

Not run in CI yet

Each of these arrives with the work it depends on, and runs on GitHub-hosted runners like everything else:

  • Uploading reports as artefacts (the JUnit XML, the lcov coverage report, fuzz crash inputs, the dependency report) and posting summaries as PR comments. These are not done, by policy, not by omission. Artefacts need an action outside the allowlist, and comments need a write token on pull requests, which no workflow here is given. Every one of these is in the job summary instead: test results, the coverage table and the coverage gate, fuzz findings as base64 with a reproducer, the dependency report, and the benchmark comparison.
  • The absolute performance budget of policy evaluation, with the benchmarks it is measured on (#42).
  • The vm-smoke subset of the Windows VM harness (#26).

Source: docs/ci.md on GitHub.

Packaging

How Palisade's release binaries, Windows Installer packages, symbols and server image are built (#22). Everything here runs on GitHub-hosted runners or on a developer machine with the same command: cargo xtask dist. Signing and publishing releases is the release pipeline (#24).

Artefacts

ArtefactBuilt onContents
Palisade-<version>-x64.msiwindows-latestpalisade-agent.exe, palisade-tray.exe, pal.exe for x64
Palisade-<version>-arm64.msiwindows-11-armThe same, built natively for ARM64
Palisade-<version>-<arch>.msi.sha256with each packageIts SHA-256, in sha256sum format
palisade-<version>-<arch>-symbols.zipwith each packageThe PDBs, in symbol-server layout
palisade-serverubuntu-latestThe server for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
palisade-server OCI imageubuntu-latestThat binary on a minimal base (Server image)
sizes-<arch>.jsonwith each buildThe size of every file above, for size tracking

The ARM64 package is built and tested natively on the ARM64 runner, with an ARM64 notifier, so it never relies on x64 emulation.

Building locally

# On Windows x64 or ARM64: binaries, symbols, and with --msi the package.
cargo xtask dist --msi
# On Linux x64: the server binary.
cargo xtask dist
# Then the image (podman or any OCI builder):
podman build -f packaging/server/Containerfile -t palisade-server:dev target/dist/linux-x64-0.1.0

--target <triple> picks the target explicitly (x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc or x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu). Windows targets build on Windows and the server on Linux, each with the platform's own linker. Output goes to target/dist/<arch>-<version>/, or to --out <dir>. --sign <signer> signs every executable before it is packaged, then the package, with any cargo xtask sign signer (none only logs); see releasing.md. --from <dir> packages executables built and signed elsewhere, after checking they are this version's; the release pipeline uses it. --bump-patch builds as the next patch version, which CI uses to test upgrades. --compare-sizes <sizes.json> warns about every binary that grew by more than 10% against an earlier build's size report. Everything dist builds and downloads goes under Cargo's target directory, wherever CARGO_TARGET_DIR or build.target-dir puts it.

A Windows build needs the MSVC build tools and, for --msi, the .NET runtime. dist downloads the WiX toolset itself (see WiX). Nothing else is installed.

What dist does

For each Windows executable it:

  1. writes the version resource and the application manifest straight to a compiled resource file (.res), with no resource compiler and no build script (xtask/src/dist/res.rs);
  2. builds it with cargo rustc --release --locked, adding the static C runtime (+crt-static), --remap-path-prefix for the workspace and Cargo home, and the linker options /Brepro (reproducible timestamps), /PDBALTPATH:%_PDB% (only the PDB's file name is recorded), /MANIFEST:NO and the .res file;
  3. checks the result and fails the build if anything is off: the PE machine type matches the target (0x8664 or 0xAA64), there is a PDB record holding a file name and no path, a reproducible-build marker, no C runtime DLL is imported, and the version resource and manifest are byte for byte the ones step 1 wrote;
  4. copies the PDB into the symbols archive.

Then, with --msi, it builds the package from those executables and validates it.

Version stamping

FieldValue
FileVersionMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.0 from workspace.package.version
ProductVersionThe SemVer and the commit: 0.1.0+g1a2b3c4d5e6f (.dirty for uncommitted changes)
CompanyNamePalisade Project
ProductNamePalisade
OriginalFilename, InternalNameThe file name, with and without .exe
FileDescriptionPer binary
LegalCopyrightThe dual licence
Pre-release flagSet for -alpha, -beta and -rc versions

The package's ProductVersion is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: Windows Installer compares only three numeric parts, and the first two must be at most 255.

Application manifest

Every executable has the same embedded manifest: requestedExecutionLevel asInvoker, longPathAware, and supportedOS for Windows 10 and 11. The service gets its rights from its service account, not from elevation, and the notifier and CLI never ask for elevation.

The manifest schema only works with the operating system's fixed XML namespaces, which contain the OS vendor's name. They, and the autostart registry path, are kept in one file, xtask/src/dist/os_ids.rs, as NAMING.md allows for identifiers the OS requires.

C runtime

The Windows executables link the C runtime statically, so no VC++ redistributable is needed. The choice is documented per target in .cargo/config.toml. That file may only define aliases (ADR 0011), so dist passes the flags with --config for the one target it builds; a plain cargo build is unaffected. The server uses the default dynamic glibc, which its image provides.

Symbols

The release profile writes split debug info (PDBs). The PDBs are never packaged. They go to palisade-<version>-<arch>-symbols.zip in the symbol-server layout, <name>.pdb/<GUID><age>/<name>.pdb, where <GUID> is the 32 hex digits of the CodeView signature and <age> its age in hex, read from each executable. Unzipped into a symbol store directory, it serves debuggers as is.

Reproducibility

The linker runs with /Brepro, so the COFF timestamp is a hash of the output rather than a time, and --remap-path-prefix keeps local paths out of the binaries and PDBs. The symbols archive uses one fixed timestamp, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH or the commit time of HEAD.

To compare two builds of one commit:

cargo xtask dist --msi --out a
cargo clean
cargo xtask dist --msi --out b
fc /b a\palisade-0.1.0-x64\pal.exe b\palisade-0.1.0-x64\pal.exe

The executables are expected to match; CI does not compare two builds yet. The packages are not: each build gets a new product code (see below), and the package database records its build time. Exact reproducibility of the package is a stretch goal.

Installer package

The package is built from packaging/wix/ with WiX and uses only standard Windows Installer 5 tables: no WiX extension and no custom action code. The custom actions set properties, and one runs the operating system's service-control tool, sc.exe, to set the service's recovery actions: the installer's own failure-actions table opens the service without the right a restart action needs and fails with access denied. It runs deferred, as SYSTEM, right after the service is installed.

  • Per machine only. Files go to %ProgramFiles%\Palisade\.
  • Upgrades. One upgrade code per architecture (xtask/src/dist/msi.rs) and a new product code every build. Installing a newer package replaces the older one in place, inside the same transaction, so a failed upgrade rolls back to the old version; installing an older one is refused with a message. Packages of the same version replace each other, so snapshot builds of main can be installed in turn. The service is stopped before files change and started again afterwards.
  • Service. PalisadeAgent ("Palisade Agent"), started automatically with a delayed start, as LocalSystem, with the command line palisade-agent.exe --service. Recovery restarts it after 0, 5 and 30 seconds, and the failure count resets after a day. Its service SID type is unrestricted. Splitting privileges is evaluated in #18.
  • Data. %ProgramData%\Palisade\ with policy, queue and logs below it. Each of the four folders gets the same protected DACL and SYSTEM as owner, not only by inheritance: SYSTEM and Administrators have full control and nobody else has access, even if a user created one of the folders before the install (CI tests that case). Hardening is extended in #18. The agent's own files there are not the package's, so upgrades, repairs and removal leave them alone.
  • Settings. The properties below, except the two hidden ones, are written to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Palisade\Agent, readable by SYSTEM and Administrators only, for the agent's enrolment bootstrap (#57). An upgrade or repair keeps their earlier values unless they are given again. The earlier values are read in the elevated part of the install only: the user-interface part of an interactive install runs unelevated and cannot read the key.
  • Notifier. palisade-tray.exe is started in every user's session at sign-in, from the per-machine Run key, unless NO_TRAY=1. The conditional parts (this entry, ADD_TO_PATH and each stored setting) are re-evaluated on a repair or reinstall, so msiexec /i <package> REINSTALL=ALL REINSTALLMODE=amus NO_TRAY=1 removes the entry, and NO_TRAY=0 puts it back.
  • CLI. pal.exe is installed next to the agent. ADD_TO_PATH=1 adds the folder to the system PATH.
  • Logging. Windows Installer records every install, upgrade and removal in the Windows Application log (source MsiInstaller). msiexec /l*v <file> writes a full log.
  • Licence dialog. An interactive first install shows the educational-project notice and the licence; a silent install (/qn) shows nothing. The dialogs are written out in packaging/wix/UI.wxs instead of using a WiX UI extension, whose print button needs a native custom action.

Properties

All are optional. SERVER_URL must start with https://, and MODE must be one of the values below; otherwise the install, or a repair or reinstall that passes them, is refused before anything changes. Removal never checks them, so a damaged stored value cannot block it.

PropertyMeaning
SERVER_URLHTTPS base URL of the management server
ENROLL_TOKENEnrolment token. Hidden: never written to installer logs or the registry; taken over by enrolment (#57)
GROUP_KEYPolicy group to join at enrolment
PROXYProxy for agent traffic
MODEInitial mode: audit (default), monitor, learning, enforce or disabled
NO_TRAY1: do not start the notifier at sign-in
SKIP_ENROLL1: offline install, no server
ALLOW_UNINSTALLUninstall authorisation, for uninstall protection (#18). Hidden like the token
ADD_TO_PATH1: add the install folder (and pal.exe) to the system PATH
 
msiexec /i Palisade-0.1.0-arm64.msi /qn SERVER_URL=https://palisade.example ENROLL_TOKEN=... GROUP_KEY=lab
msiexec /i Palisade-0.1.0-x64.msi /qn SKIP_ENROLL=1 MODE=audit
msiexec /x Palisade-0.1.0-x64.msi /qn

ENROLL_TOKEN and ALLOW_UNINSTALL are hidden properties (MsiHiddenProperties), so the installer does not log their values. The package also never writes either one anywhere: a verbose log records every registry value and command line the installer writes, hidden property or not. Taking the token over into the agent's protected store at install (machine-scoped data protection) is part of enrolment, #57; until then the property is accepted and validated for logging only, and SKIP_ENROLL=1 installs are unaffected. CI checks that a random token is in none of the verbose logs. One exception is outside the package's control: when the machine's installer logging policy is set to its most verbose debug level, Windows Installer writes command-line properties to the log regardless.

Tests in CI

The package job in ci.yml runs on windows-latest and windows-11-arm. It builds the package twice, the second time with --bump-patch, and runs packaging/wix/smoke-test.ps1 on the runner, which:

  • checks the package tables: shared upgrade code, distinct product codes, both hidden properties, no PDBs, three files, no custom action code, that the only custom actions set properties, stop with an error, or run the sc.exe recovery command, that the unelevated user-interface sequence never reads the settings key or defaults MODE, and that the old version is removed inside the install transaction;
  • refuses an unknown MODE and a plain-HTTP SERVER_URL;
  • installs silently with every property set, then checks the service (state, start type, delayed start, account, command line, recovery actions, SID type), every binary's version resource and machine type, that the agent runs natively, the %ProgramData%\Palisade and settings-key ACLs, the stored settings (and that the token is not among them), the notifier entry, and the verbose log for the token;
  • upgrades and checks that agent state in %ProgramData%\Palisade and the settings survive and the service runs the new binaries;
  • tries a downgrade and checks it is refused and changes nothing;
  • deletes a binary, repairs, and checks it is back;
  • uninstalls and checks the service, files, settings and autostart entry are gone;
  • plants a data folder with a permissive, non-inheriting ACL, as a standard user could, then installs offline with SKIP_ENROLL, NO_TRAY, ADD_TO_PATH and MODE=enforce and checks the planted folder's ACL was replaced; upgrades it; repairs it with the basic user interface and checks the settings and MODE are kept; damages the stored MODE and checks it can still be removed. Windows Installer runs the user-interface sequence only with reduced or full UI, which need a person, so that sequence is checked through the package tables above;
  • checks the Application log has the install and removal events.

wix msi validate runs the standard ICE suite on every package; any ICE error fails the build. Three warnings are expected and left in place: ICE61, because same-version packages replace each other on purpose (snapshot builds); WiX's note that the installer's service configuration table is documented as unreliable, which the smoke test checks directly on every run; and WiX's note that the property search is suppressed in the user-interface sequence, which is intended (see Settings above). cargo xtask ci on Windows builds both packages but does not run the smoke test, which installs a service on the machine.

Snapshot builds

Every push to main whose CI passed publishes its unsigned packages and their checksums to the rolling main-snapshot pre-release. See ci.md.

Binary size

Each build writes sizes-<arch>.json. dist --compare-sizes <file> prints a warning annotation for every executable or server binary more than 10% larger than in that file. The release pipeline (#24) compares each release with the previous one.

Server image

packaging/server/Containerfile copies the server binary onto a minimal base image that has glibc, the C++ runtime and CA certificates and no shell or package manager, pinned by digest. It runs as an unprivileged user and starts palisade-server serve --config /etc/palisade/server.toml; the configuration and TLS files are mounted in (see the server README). The server-image job builds it with the runner's preinstalled podman and runs palisade-server version in it. Image signing is #18.

WiX

WiX 5.0.2 is pinned in xtask/src/dist/msi.rs. dist downloads the package from the NuGet registry into target/wix/, checks its SHA-256 before anything in it runs, and runs it with the .NET runtime preinstalled on the hosted Windows images. No WiX installation and no dotnet tool install is needed.

WiX 5 is the last major version under its plain open-source licence (MS-RL). Version 6 and later require each user to accept an additional maintenance-fee licence agreement before use, and CI must not accept a licence agreement on the maintainer's behalf. Moving to a later version is the maintainer's decision.

Kernel driver

The optional kernel driver (#8) is not implemented yet. When it is, its package will be built on a developer machine with the Windows Driver Kit, with cargo xtask dist driver, and its files signed with a test certificate. It is local-only: the Driver Kit is not part of every hosted image and installing it exceeds job limits, and no other runner type is ever used (ci.md). Until then, cargo xtask dist driver explains this and fails.

Not covered here

  • Signing binaries and packages, and publishing releases: releasing.md.
  • Testing on clean x64 and ARM64 virtual machines, including the notifier in a real user session: the VM harness (#26).
  • Image signing, uninstall protection and further ACL hardening: #18.
  • Enrolment itself, including storing ENROLL_TOKEN protected for the agent, CONFIGFILE, tags, relays and the other installer properties of the full installer: #57.

Source: docs/packaging.md on GitHub.

Releasing

How a Palisade release is cut, signed, checked and published (#24). Everything runs on GitHub-hosted runners, from .github/workflows/release.yml, with the steps in cargo xtask release and cargo xtask sign. Building the artefacts themselves is described in packaging.md.

Until the maintainer has done the one-time setup in Code signing, pushing a release tag fails at its first job. A release never produces unsigned packages. Pull requests and main produce unsigned builds only, clearly marked as such: the package job's packages and the main-snapshot pre-release.

Versioning

  • SemVer for the whole workspace, one version for every binary: workspace.package.version in the root Cargo.toml.
  • Pre-releases are -alpha.N, -beta.N and -rc.N, and are published as GitHub pre-releases.
  • Tags are vX.Y.Z or vX.Y.Z-rc.N (and so on), annotated and signed with SSH or GPG (git tag -s). cargo xtask release check-tag refuses a lightweight or unsigned tag, a name that is not a release version, and a tag whose commit's Cargo.toml has another version. In the release workflow it then verifies the signature cryptographically with git tag -v against the maintainer keys committed in packaging/sign/allowed_tag_signers (SSH, in allowed_signers format) and packaging/sign/tag-signers.asc (GPG), and fails if neither file is there.

The pipeline

A pushed v* tag runs these jobs. Files move between jobs through a draft GitHub Release, because only three actions are allowed and none of them carries artefacts between jobs (ci.md). Nobody sees a draft but maintainers, and it is published only after verify passes.

JobRunnerSecretsWhat it does
check-tagubuntu-latestnoneChecks the tag (above) and that CHANGELOG.md has its section, fails unless signing is configured, creates the draft
buildwindows-latest (x64), windows-11-arm (ARM64)nonecargo xtask dist --locked release builds, natively; uploads the unsigned executables, the symbols archive and the size report, warning about binaries more than 10% larger than in the previous release
serverubuntu-latestnoneThe Linux server binary
signwindows-latestrelease-signing environmentAfter a reviewer approves: signs every executable, builds each architecture's package from the signed executables (dist --from, which first checks they are this version's), signs each package, writes SHA256SUMS over the final files and signs it; replaces the unsigned files in the draft
verifywindows-latest (x64), windows-11-arm (ARM64)noneChecks SHA256SUMS, then each architecture's package, on its own architecture's runner, and every executable inside it (unpacked with an administrative install) with the OS signing tool's default policy, every signature, SHA-256, and an RFC 3161 timestamp. Any unsigned, invalid or untimestamped file fails the release
provenanceubuntu-latestnoneThe hook for the SBOM, build provenance and signed update manifest (#18, #226); see Provenance
publishubuntu-latestnoneThe CHANGELOG.md section as release notes, the pre-release flag for -alpha, -beta and -rc, and publishes the draft

Only check-tag, build, server, sign and publish can write to releases (contents: write), only sign sees a secret, and nothing in this workflow uses a cache. A test in xtask/src/release/mod.rs keeps these rules: secrets only in the environment job, pull requests run only the dry run, releases are always timestamped, and publishing needs verify.

A release contains:

  • Palisade-<version>-x64.msi and Palisade-<version>-arm64.msi, signed, with signed executables inside;
  • palisade-<version>-x64-symbols.zip and palisade-<version>-arm64-symbols.zip;
  • palisade-server-<version>-linux-x64;
  • sizes-x64.json, sizes-arm64.json and sizes-linux-x64.json, for the next release's size comparison;
  • SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.sig.

Dry run on pull requests

A pull request that changes release.yml, xtask/src/dist/, xtask/src/release/ or packaging/ runs the dry-run job instead: the same build, signed with a throwaway test CA created on the runner, packaged, signed again, every signature verified (timestamps aside, as there is no timestamp server in a test), and the checksums written and checked. It has no secrets, no environment, no write access and uploads nothing.

In addition, CI's sign-test job (ci.md) runs on every pull request: the test-CA build and verification, the pfx signer with a throwaway PFX whose password is a canary that must not appear in the output, and a signed package of unsigned executables, which release verify must reject.

Code signing

Signing is pluggable (cargo xtask sign --signer <kind>, xtask/src/release/sign.rs). Every signer signs PE files and packages in place with a SHA-256 file digest and an RFC 3161 timestamp, and verifies them.

SignerUsed byKey material
nonePull request and main buildsNone: logs what it would sign
test-caCI tests and the release dry runA throwaway root CA and leaf made on the runner and deleted; its signatures are trusted only where its root was installed
pfxReleasesA PKCS#12 file with its password, from the release-signing environment
cloud-hsmReleasesA remote signing service, through a command template; the key never leaves the service

There is no publicly trusted code-signing certificate yet. That is the one step only the maintainer can do; everything else is in place.

What the maintainer sets up

  1. A code-signing certificate. Either:

    • an Authenticode code-signing certificate (the "code signing" extended key usage, 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.3) from a publicly trusted certificate authority, with its private key, as a password-protected PKCS#12 (.pfx) file, for the pfx signer. Current CA rules require such keys to be generated and kept on hardware, so a PFX export is often only possible for an internal enterprise CA; or
    • a remote signing service or HSM that signs files through a command-line client, for the cloud-hsm signer.

    An educational project may not have either. Without a publicly trusted certificate, the OS download-reputation check warns when the package is downloaded. That is an accepted limitation; it does not change what verify checks.

  2. The release-signing environment (Settings → Environments → New environment):

    • Required reviewers: the maintainer (and any co-maintainer). Prevent self-review if there is more than one.
    • Wait timer: for example 5 minutes, so a mistaken tag can be cancelled.
    • Deployment branches and tags: Selected branches and tags, with the tag rule v* only. No branch can deploy to it.

    With gh:

    gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/environments/release-signing --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "wait_timer": 5,
  "prevent_self_review": false,
  "reviewers": [{ "type": "User", "id": <maintainer user id> }],
  "deployment_branch_policy": { "protected_branches": false, "custom_branch_policies": true }
}
EOF
gh api -X POST repos/jusso-dev/palisade/environments/release-signing/deployment-branch-policies \
  -f name='v*' -f type=tag

  3. Environment secrets (in release-signing, never repository secrets):

    SecretSignerValue
    PALISADE_SIGN_PFX_BASE64pfxThe .pfx file, base64-encoded (base64 -w0 signing.pfx)
    PALISADE_SIGN_PFX_PASSWORDpfxIts password
    PALISADE_SIGN_COMMANDcloud-hsmThe client command that signs one file in place, with {file} where the path goes, for example remote-sign --profile palisade --digest sha256 --timestamp {file}. It is split on spaces and run without a shell. The client reads its own credentials from further environment secrets, which the maintainer adds to the sign job's env
    RELEASE_CHECKSUM_KEYallThe Ed25519 SSH private key that signs SHA256SUMS (below)

  4. Repository variables (Settings → Variables; not secret):

    VariableValue
    RELEASE_SIGNERpfx or cloud-hsm. Until it is set, check-tag fails every release tag with "Signing not configured"
    RELEASE_TSA_URLSOne or more RFC 3161 timestamp server URLs, separated by spaces, tried in order. Use the certificate authority's own server first
    RELEASE_PROVENANCELeave unset until #226 lands (Provenance)

  5. Protect v* tags with a tag ruleset, so only the maintainer can create, move or delete release tags:

    gh api -X POST repos/jusso-dev/palisade/rulesets --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "release tags",
  "target": "tag",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "conditions": { "ref_name": { "include": ["refs/tags/v*"], "exclude": [] } },
  "rules": [{ "type": "creation" }, { "type": "update" }, { "type": "deletion" }, { "type": "required_signatures" }],
  "bypass_actors": [{ "actor_id": 5, "actor_type": "RepositoryRole", "bypass_mode": "always" }]
}
EOF

    This stops anyone but the maintainer creating, moving or deleting a v* tag. It does not check tag signatures (the signatures rule covers commits, and the maintainer bypasses creation); the release workflow does that against the committed keys (below).

  6. Commit the keys that may sign release tags and checksums, in a pull request:

    • packaging/sign/allowed_tag_signers: one line per SSH key that may sign tags, <email> namespaces="git" <public key> (git config gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile format); or packaging/sign/tag-signers.asc: the armoured public GPG keys that may sign tags.
    • packaging/sign/release-checksum.pub: the public half of RELEASE_CHECKSUM_KEY (below). verify checks SHA256SUMS.sig against it and fails if it is missing.

How secrets are handled

  • They exist only in the release-signing environment, which only v* tags can use and a reviewer must approve. Pull request workflows never see them (pull_request runs get no secrets from environments they cannot deploy to, and this one has a tag-only policy).
  • They are passed to cargo xtask sign in the environment, never on a command line. The PFX is written to a temporary folder only the job's user can read, imported into that user's certificate store for one signature, then removed from the store and deleted in a finally block, whatever happens. The signing tool only ever gets the certificate thumbprint.
  • cargo xtask sign replaces any secret value in the signing tool's output with *** before printing it, on top of GitHub's own masking of secrets. No signing step uses set -x.
  • The checksum key is written to a mode-600 file under the runner's temporary folder and removed by a trap on exit. A final always() step removes the signing work folders.
  • The sign-test job proves this with a canary: it signs with a throwaway PFX whose password is a random value, and fails if that value, or the PFX, appears in the output.

Key rotation

  1. Obtain the new certificate (or service key) before the old one expires.
  2. Replace the environment secrets. Releases signed with the old certificate stay valid: every signature is timestamped, so it outlives the certificate.
  3. If a key may have been exposed, revoke the certificate with the CA first, then rotate, then follow Yanking for any release signed after the possible exposure.
  4. Rotate RELEASE_CHECKSUM_KEY the same way and publish the new public key in this file. Pinning the publisher certificate in the agent, and dual-signing during rollover, are #226; key management as a whole is #18.

Checksum signing key

SHA256SUMS.sig is an SSH signature (ssh-keygen -Y sign, namespace palisade-release) made with an Ed25519 key held as RELEASE_CHECKSUM_KEY. Create it once:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C 'palisade-release' -f palisade-release
# Secret: the contents of palisade-release.
# Public key: commit palisade-release.pub as packaging/sign/release-checksum.pub.

To check a download, here Palisade-0.2.0-x64.msi: the signature first, and only then that exact file's line in the checksums, compared as a literal name (grep . fails if the file is not listed).

file=Palisade-0.2.0-x64.msi
echo "palisade-release $(cat release-checksum.pub)" > allowed_signers
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I palisade-release -n palisade-release \
  -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS \
  && FILE="$file" awk 'substr($0, 65, 2) == "  " && substr($0, 67) == ENVIRON["FILE"]' SHA256SUMS \
     | grep . | sha256sum --check --strict - \
  && echo "$file is verified"

Install it only if the last line prints. release-checksum.pub is packaging/sign/release-checksum.pub in the repository, once the maintainer has committed it.

Release checklist

Pre-flight

  1. main is green, and nothing is waiting that must be in the release.

  2. Check open security advisories (Security → Advisories). A fix under embargo is released as in Security fixes, not as an ordinary release.

  3. Prepare the release on a branch:

    git switch -c release/v0.2.0 origin/main
RELEASE_DATE=2026-12-01 cargo xtask release prepare 0.2.0

    This sets workspace.package.version, updates Cargo.lock and each fuzz workspace's lock file to match (the release builds with --locked), and adds a CHANGELOG.md section generated from the Conventional Commit titles merged since the last release tag, under Breaking, Security, Features, Fixes, Docs and Internal. Edit the wording if needed, commit every changed file, then open a pull request titled chore(release): 0.2.0 and merge it once CI passes.

  4. Tag the merge commit and push the tag:

    git switch main && git pull
git tag -s v0.2.0 -m "Palisade 0.2.0"
git push origin v0.2.0

  5. Approve the sign job when it asks (Actions → the run → Review deployments), after checking the run is for the tag you pushed.

Security fixes

Under the coordinated disclosure process, a fix is prepared in the advisory's private fork, merged and released at the agreed time. Keep the changelog entry vague (security: fix a policy bypass) until the advisory is published, then publish the advisory, which links the release, the same day. Do not tag before the fix is ready to ship: tags are public.

Post-release verification

  1. Download the release files and check the checksums and their signature as in Checksum signing key.
  2. On a Windows machine, check a package: Get-AuthenticodeSignature Palisade-0.2.0-x64.msi. It should be valid and timestamped.
  3. Install it on a test machine or VM, silently, and check the service runs (packaging.md). The VM harness automates this (#26).
  4. Check the release is marked as a pre-release exactly when its version has -alpha, -beta or -rc.

Yanking

A published release is never deleted or replaced: someone may already have it, and a deleted release cannot be audited. To withdraw one:

  1. Edit the release: put **Withdrawn: <reason>. Use <version> instead.** at the top of its notes, and mark it as a pre-release so it is no longer latest.
  2. Publish a security advisory if the reason is a vulnerability.
  3. Release the fixed version as usual.
  4. The update channel's signed metadata (#18, #226) stops offering the withdrawn version. Until that exists, the release notes are the notice.

The tag stays. A tag that was pushed but whose release failed before publishing leaves only a draft. Delete the draft, fix the problem, then release a new patch version rather than moving the tag: run cargo xtask release prepare <next version>, merge that pull request, and tag its merge commit as in the checklist. check-tag refuses a tag whose Cargo.toml still has the old version.

Provenance

The provenance job is the slot for the SBOM, build provenance attestation and signed update manifest (#18, #226). It runs cargo xtask release provenance, which does nothing while the RELEASE_PROVENANCE variable is unset. Once #226 adds cargo xtask sbom, set the variable to on: from then on the job runs it and fails the release if it is missing or fails, so a release can never silently ship without provenance again.

Not covered here

  • Publishing the SBOM, provenance and the signed update manifest: #226 (hook above).
  • Signing the server's container image: #18.
  • Installing a release on clean VMs as part of the release: #26.
  • Driver catalog signing: #8.

Source: docs/releasing.md on GitHub.

Dependencies and supply chain

Third-party crates make up most of the code that Palisade's privileged Windows service trusts. A compromised or careless dependency can do anything the service can do. This page says how a dependency gets in, and what checks it on every pull request. CI runs all of them (ci.md), and cargo xtask ci runs them locally.

Admitting a new dependency

Every new top-level dependency is justified in the pull request description. Say why it is needed, and cover each of these:

CriterionWhat to check
NeedIs it worth it? A small piece of code may be better written in the crate that needs it.
MaintenanceRecent releases, open issues and pull requests, more than one maintainer, a security policy.
UseDownloads and reverse dependencies. Widely used crates are reviewed more, by more people.
unsafeHow much it has, and whether it is documented. cargo xtask deps-report counts it.
FootprintHow many crates it pulls in, on every platform. cargo tree -p <crate> --target all -e normal.
LicenceOne of the licences allowed in deny.toml.
Build-time codeBuild scripts and proc-macros run on the build machine. They must not use the network; prefer crates with none.
FeaturesUse default-features = false and turn on only the features needed, so less code is compiled.

Add the version once, in [workspace.dependencies] in the root Cargo.toml, and use { workspace = true } in the crate (cargo xtask check-manifests). The allowed directions between workspace crates are in workspace.md.

Keep the agent's tree small. The agent runs as a privileged service and should pull in much less than the server. The dependency report lists each crate's tree size separately. In the agent, prefer windows-sys to windows: it is bindings only, so it compiles faster and ships less.

What runs on every pull request

CheckToolEnforces
LockfileCargoCargo.lock is committed, and every Cargo command uses --locked.
Licencescargo deny check licensesOnly the licences in deny.toml (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC, Unicode-3.0, Zlib, CC0-1.0, MPL-2.0), plus the exceptions listed there with a reason. GPL, AGPL and LGPL fail unless an exception with a reason is added. confidence-threshold = 0.9.
Sourcescargo deny check sourcescrates.io only. Git dependencies and other registries fail.
Banscargo deny check bansNo wildcard versions. openssl and openssl-sys are denied (use rustls). Duplicate versions warn.
Advisoriescargo deny check advisories, cargo xtask audit (cargo-audit with the same ignores)No known vulnerability, unsound or yanked crate. Unmaintained crates fail when a workspace crate depends on them directly.
Auditscargo vet --lockedEvery crate is audited, covered by an imported audit, or exempted with a note (below).
Repository rulescargo xtask check-supply-chainAt most 10 crates in more than one version. Every advisory ignore has an ID, a reason and an expiry date that has not passed, and no audit.toml exists. Every skip has a reason, and every licence exception a # reason: comment. The cargo-vet criteria for each workspace crate, no [policy] entry that lowers what dependencies need, and a note on every exemption.
Reportcargo xtask deps-reportOn a PR that changes Cargo.lock, the job summary shows duplicates, cargo tree -d, third-party crates per workspace crate, every third-party crate's unsafe count with the change against the base branch, and the build scripts and proc-macros. A new crate with more than 100 unsafe keywords, or a version that adds more than 100 compared with the version it replaces, raises a warning on the run. The old counts come from the base commit: the report checks it out in a temporary git worktree and runs cargo metadata --locked there, which downloads and unpacks its locked crates.io packages (checksum-verified; nothing is built). If that fails, the change is shown without a warning rather than raising a false one.

The fuzz targets (crates/*/fuzz) are separate workspaces with their own Cargo.lock. The licence, source, ban and advisory checks run on them too, with this same deny.toml, and cargo xtask audit scans their lockfiles. Their one licence exception is NCSA for libfuzzer-sys (LLVM's permissive licence), which the root workspace does not use, so cargo deny check there warns that the exception is unused. cargo-vet covers only the root workspace; fuzz crates are never shipped, and a fuzz-only dependency is reviewed in its PR (testing.md).

Advisories are also scanned daily (audit.yml), because a new advisory can affect main without any change here. A failure opens or updates an issue labelled area:security.

To see the checks fail, add a GPL-licensed crate, a git = "..." dependency, or a crate from another registry: cargo deny check rejects each one.

Ignoring an advisory

Only when the vulnerable code cannot be reached, and only for a limited time. Add a table to [advisories] ignore in deny.toml:

ignore = [
    { id = "RUSTSEC-2026-0001", reason = "only the parser is used, not the affected writer", expiry = "2027-01-31" },
]

expiry is cargo-deny's own key: it fails the advisory check once the date has passed. cargo xtask check-supply-chain also fails then, and requires the ID, the reason and the date on every entry. Review the advisory again, and renew the date with a new reason or remove the ignore.

deny.toml is the only place an advisory is ignored. CI runs cargo-audit as cargo xtask audit, which passes the same IDs as --ignore, so both tools agree. A cargo-audit audit.toml anywhere in the repository fails check-supply-chain, because it would bypass these rules.

An ignore has exactly these three keys. cargo-deny also accepts allow, which limits an ignore to some dependents, but cargo-audit cannot scope an ignore, so allow is rejected to keep the two tools in step. cargo xtask audit runs these checks before cargo-audit, so an expired or incomplete ignore also fails the daily audit.

A licence exception works the same way, except that cargo-deny has no reason key for it: write a # reason: ... comment on the line directly above each entry in [licenses] exceptions, in the inline-array or the [[licenses.exceptions]] form. Each entry needs its own comment.

cargo-vet

supply-chain/ holds the cargo-vet files:

  • config.toml: the criteria and exemptions. Product crates, which are shipped, require safe-to-deploy for their whole tree. xtask and dev-dependencies require safe-to-run.
  • audits.toml: audits done for this project.
  • imports.lock: the audits imported from trusted public audit sets, pinned.

Audits are imported from two public sets run by non-profit open-source organisations. When cargo-vet was adopted, 6 crates were covered by imported audits, and the other 93 were recorded as exemptions with the note "Baseline when cargo-vet was adopted". The 17 crates that the Authenticode verifier (#247) brought in while cargo-vet was in review (ring and its build and platform dependencies) are exempted the same way, with a note that names #247. Identity matching (#251) added 2 more (unicode-normalization and tinyvec), exempted with a note that names #251. It also made regex-automata, regex-syntax and aho-corasick normal dependencies of palisade-policy, so their baseline exemptions were raised from safe-to-run to safe-to-deploy, with a note saying so. The agent service host (#252) added 16 more (the async runtime, logging and the Windows service crates), exempted with a note that names #252, and made bitflags and once_cell normal dependencies of a shipped crate, so their baseline exemptions were raised to safe-to-deploy the same way. The server's Postgres layer (#127) added 72 more (sqlx with its Postgres driver, migration support and the rustls-based TLS with the OS trust store), exempted with a note that names #127, and raised 31 baseline exemptions (syn, url, the Unicode and ICU crates and their helpers) to safe-to-deploy the same way. The exemptions are the backlog. Each one is removed when the crate is audited, or when an imported audit covers it (cargo vet prune removes exemptions that are no longer needed).

A new crate, or a version bump, fails cargo vet until one of these is done:

  1. An imported audit covers it. Run cargo vet to see.
  2. You audit it. Run cargo vet diff <crate> <old> <new> (or cargo vet inspect for a new crate), read the code against the criteria, then run cargo vet certify.
  3. It is exempted. Only with a reason. Run cargo vet add-exemption <crate> <version>, then add a notes field to the entry in config.toml saying why it was not audited. check-supply-chain fails on an exemption without notes.

cargo vet suggest lists the cheapest audits to do next.

Code that runs at build time

Build scripts (build.rs) and proc-macros run on the developer's or CI machine during the build, with that machine's permissions. cargo xtask deps-report lists every one. Review the list when a pull request adds one. The aim for the agent's tree is that no build script touches the network.

Not done yet

  • SBOM and provenance. cargo xtask sbom is reserved: it will write CycloneDX files to target/dist/sbom/<crate>.cdx.json. Generating them, attesting provenance, and deciding on cargo-auditable are in #226. The release pipeline that publishes them is #24.
  • Dependabot for npm (the console) and for the server's container image. These are added when those files exist: #136 and #126.

Source: docs/dependencies.md on GitHub.

Repository settings

Some of Palisade's security depends on GitHub repository settings, not on files in the repository. This page lists every setting the project relies on, why it matters, and how to apply it. Only a repository administrator can change these, so they are documented here and reviewed like code. When a setting changes, update this page in the same change.

The gh api commands below use the GitHub REST API. Run them as a repository administrator. The same settings are also available under Settings in the web UI.

Summary

SettingRequired valueWhy
Private vulnerability reportingOnThe only private channel in SECURITY.md
Secret scanningOnCatches leaked credentials in commits
Push protectionOnBlocks pushes that contain a detected secret
Dependabot alertsOnWarns about vulnerable dependencies between scheduled audits
Dependabot security updatesOnOpens fix PRs for those alerts (docs/ci.md)
Allowed actionsSelected: the allowlist in xtask/src/workflows.rs only, pinned to a full SHAA second layer behind cargo xtask check-workflows
Default GITHUB_TOKEN permissionsReadLeast privilege; jobs ask for more themselves
Actions can approve pull requestsOffA workflow must never approve its own change
Fork pull request workflowsNeed approval for first-time contributorsStops drive-by workflow runs from new accounts
main rulesetPull requests only, required checks, linear history, no force pushes or deletionSee Branch protection
Merge methodsSquash only, commit title from the PR titleThe PR title is the changelog entry (CONTRIBUTING.md)
DiscussionsOn, with a Q&A categoryThe support channel in SUPPORT.md
Labels and milestonesExactly the lists in .github/labels.yml and .github/milestones.ymlSynced by labels.yml; see Labels and milestones
DCO checkRuns on every pull request; not yet requiredSee DCO check
GitHub PagesDeploy from the gh-pages branch, root folderServes the documentation site; see GitHub Pages

Code security

# Private vulnerability reporting.
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/private-vulnerability-reporting

# Dependabot alerts, then Dependabot security updates (alerts must be on first).
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/vulnerability-alerts
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/automated-security-fixes

# Secret scanning and push protection.
gh api -X PATCH repos/jusso-dev/palisade --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "security_and_analysis": {
    "secret_scanning": { "status": "enabled" },
    "secret_scanning_push_protection": { "status": "enabled" }
  }
}
EOF

To check them:

gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/private-vulnerability-reporting   # {"enabled":true}
gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/vulnerability-alerts               # HTTP 204 when on, 404 when off
gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade -q .security_and_analysis

After enabling private vulnerability reporting, file a test report from a second account through the private reporting form, check that it arrives as a draft advisory, then close it.

GitHub Actions

CI policy is enforced in two places: cargo xtask check-workflows checks the workflow files on every pull request (docs/ci.md), and these settings stop GitHub from running anything outside the same allowlist, even if a workflow file got past the check.

# Only selected actions, and only when pinned to a full commit SHA.
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions \
  -F enabled=true -f allowed_actions=selected -F sha_pinning_required=true

# The allowlist. Keep it identical to ALLOWED_ACTIONS in xtask/src/workflows.rs.
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/selected-actions --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "github_owned_allowed": false,
  "verified_allowed": false,
  "patterns_allowed": [
    "actions/checkout@*",
    "Swatinem/rust-cache@*",
    "taiki-e/install-action@*"
  ]
}
EOF

# Read-only GITHUB_TOKEN by default, and workflows may not approve pull requests.
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/workflow \
  -f default_workflow_permissions=read -F can_approve_pull_request_reviews=false

# Fork pull requests from first-time contributors wait for approval before workflows run.
gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/fork-pr-contributor-approval \
  -f approval_policy=first_time_contributors

To check them:

gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions                   # allowed_actions "selected", sha_pinning_required true
gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/selected-actions
gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/workflow          # "read", false
gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/actions/permissions/fork-pr-contributor-approval

When an action is added to ALLOWED_ACTIONS, add it to patterns_allowed too, or its workflow will not run.

Dependabot's own update jobs run as GitHub-managed workflows that bypass these Actions policies, so the allowlist does not stop Dependabot from opening pull requests.

Runners are not a setting: every job runs on a GitHub-hosted runner, and the runner-guard check rejects anything else. Self-hosted runners must never be registered for this repository, and cloud-managed build services are never used (docs/ci.md).

GitHub Pages

The documentation site is published by .github/workflows/pages.yml, which pushes the built site to the gh-pages branch (docs/ci.md). The Pages deployment actions are not on the action allowlist, so Pages serves that branch directly. This is a one-time setting, made after the first run of pages.yml has created the branch:

# Serve the gh-pages branch, root folder.
gh api -X POST repos/jusso-dev/palisade/pages \
  -f build_type=legacy -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/'

Or in the web UI: Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). Then check it:

gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/pages    # "build_type": "legacy", source gh-pages and /

The site is then at https://jusso-dev.github.io/palisade/, which redirects to latest/. The first deployment needs this setting before Pages serves anything: after making it, rerun pages.yml once (Actions → Pages → Run workflow on main).

A push made with a workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN does not start a Pages build, so pages.yml's push alone would update gh-pages but not the site. After each push it therefore requests the build itself (POST repos/jusso-dev/palisade/pages/builds), with the same token and only the job's pages: write permission, even when the site is unchanged, so rerunning pages.yml also retries a build request that failed. No personal token or deployment action is needed. A push to gh-pages made by hand, by someone with admin rights, still starts a build as usual.

Serving a branch still runs GitHub's own pages-build-deployment workflow. If the Actions allowlist above stops that workflow, its run shows a startup failure naming the blocked action, and the site is not updated. The fix widens the allowlist, so it is a maintainer decision: add the action it names to patterns_allowed, or allow actions created by GitHub, and record the change on this page. pages.yml itself needs neither.

Branch protection for main

main is protected by a repository ruleset named main. It:

  • requires a pull request for every change, so nothing is pushed to main directly;
  • allows squash merges only;
  • requires two status checks to pass on the latest commit:
    • ci-ok, which passes only when every job in ci.yml passed (docs/ci.md);
    • PR title, the Conventional Commits check on the pull request title (pr-title.yml);
  • requires review threads to be resolved before merging;
  • requires linear history, and blocks force pushes and deletion of main.

Both checks are pinned to the GitHub Actions app (integration_id 15368), so a status with the same name posted by anything else does not count.

Required approvals are 0 while Palisade has one maintainer. GitHub does not let a pull request author approve their own pull request, so requiring an approval would block every change the maintainer makes. Pull requests from anyone else are still reviewed, because only the maintainer can merge, and CODEOWNERS requests the maintainer's review on every pull request. When a second maintainer joins, set required_approving_review_count to 1 and require_code_owner_review to true.

Signed commits are recommended but not required.

gh api -X POST repos/jusso-dev/palisade/rulesets --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "main",
  "target": "branch",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "conditions": { "ref_name": { "include": ["~DEFAULT_BRANCH"], "exclude": [] } },
  "rules": [
    { "type": "deletion" },
    { "type": "non_fast_forward" },
    { "type": "required_linear_history" },
    {
      "type": "pull_request",
      "parameters": {
        "allowed_merge_methods": ["squash"],
        "required_approving_review_count": 0,
        "require_code_owner_review": false,
        "dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push": true,
        "require_last_push_approval": false,
        "required_review_thread_resolution": true
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "required_status_checks",
      "parameters": {
        "strict_required_status_checks_policy": false,
        "required_status_checks": [
          { "context": "ci-ok", "integration_id": 15368 },
          { "context": "PR title", "integration_id": 15368 }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
EOF

strict_required_status_checks_policy is false, so a pull request does not have to be updated with the latest main before it merges. That keeps a single maintainer's queue moving. The cost is that a branch can merge without rerunning checks that changed on main since it was last tested. main runs the full CI again after every merge, so a failure shows up there at once.

To check the ruleset, and to change it later, list it with gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade/rulesets, then update it with gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/rulesets/<id> --input <file>.

Merging and general settings

gh api -X PATCH repos/jusso-dev/palisade --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "allow_squash_merge": true,
  "allow_merge_commit": false,
  "allow_rebase_merge": false,
  "squash_merge_commit_title": "PR_TITLE",
  "squash_merge_commit_message": "PR_BODY",
  "delete_branch_on_merge": true,
  "has_issues": true,
  "has_discussions": true
}
EOF

To check them:

gh api repos/jusso-dev/palisade \
  -q '{allow_squash_merge, allow_merge_commit, allow_rebase_merge, squash_merge_commit_title, delete_branch_on_merge, has_discussions}'

squash_merge_commit_title must be PR_TITLE. The default uses the commit title instead when a pull request has a single commit, which would bypass the PR title check.

Labels and milestones

The label set and the milestone titles live in two files, so they are reviewed like code:

  • .github/labels.yml: every label, with its colour and description;
  • .github/milestones.yml: the seven milestones, M0 Foundations to M6 Compliance & Advanced, with their exact titles and descriptions.

The Label sync workflow (.github/workflows/labels.yml) runs .github/scripts/sync-labels.sh:

  • On a pull request that touches either file, the issue templates, dependabot.yml or the script, it runs the script's tests and validates the files. Validation also fails if an issue template or Dependabot applies a label that is not listed, because the sync would delete it.
  • On a push to main it applies the files. Missing labels are created, colours and descriptions are updated, and labels that are not listed are deleted, which removes them from every issue. Missing milestones are created and their descriptions updated. An open milestone that is not listed is reported and the run fails, but it is never deleted or closed; close it by hand, or add it to the file. Closed milestones that are not listed are ignored.
  • Run it by hand from the Actions tab for a dry run that prints every change and writes nothing. Tick apply to make the changes. Changes are only ever applied from main; a manual run on any other branch is always a dry run.

Only the sync job has a write scope, issues: write, which covers labels and milestones, plus contents: read for the checkout. It never runs on a pull request.

To dry-run locally, with the GitHub CLI signed in to an account that can read the repository:

bash .github/scripts/sync-labels.sh --validate
bash .github/scripts/sync-labels.sh --check --repo jusso-dev/palisade   # exit 1 means drift; nothing is written
bash .github/scripts/sync-labels.test.sh

Review the DELETE lines before the first apply. The first sync removes the default labels that GitHub creates with a repository (bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, invalid, question, wontfix) and accessibility, none of which is in the list. The issue templates apply needs-triage instead, and Dependabot applies area:security or area:infra.

DCO check

The DCO workflow (.github/workflows/dco.yml) runs .github/scripts/check-dco.sh on every pull request. It fails if any non-merge commit lacks a Signed-off-by: trailer whose email matches the commit author (CONTRIBUTING.md). It needs no token scope beyond contents: read. Dependabot's pull requests pass it with the bot's own sign-off (docs/ci.md). Pull requests opened by the repository owner pass without sign-off (CONTRIBUTING.md). The exemption follows GitHub's author_association, which is OWNER only on a repository owned by a personal account. Transferring the repository to another personal account moves the exemption to that account. Transferring it to an organisation ends it, because organisation owners and members are reported as MEMBER, so the check then applies to everyone (it fails closed).

The check is informational: the main ruleset does not require it yet. Requiring sign-off is decided by an ADR under #28. Once that ADR is accepted, add the check to the ruleset's required status checks:

{ "context": "DCO", "integration_id": 15368 }

in the required_status_checks list of the ruleset in Branch protection, then update the ruleset with gh api -X PUT repos/jusso-dev/palisade/rulesets/<id> --input <file>, and update the summary table above.

Source: docs/repo-settings.md on GitHub.

Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at the repository's private reporting form, with a title that starts with "Code of Conduct:". Only the maintainer (@jusso-dev) and the reporter can see a report filed there. Please do not report conduct concerns in a public issue or discussion. Content that breaks GitHub's own rules can also be reported to GitHub (how to report abuse). All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

1. Correction

Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

2. Warning

Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

3. Temporary Ban

Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

4. Permanent Ban

Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html.

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder.

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations.

Support

Palisade is an educational, personal-development project. Support is community best effort.

  • There is no service level agreement. Questions, bugs and pull requests are answered when the maintainer has time, and some may not be answered.
  • There is no commercial support, and none is planned. Nobody sells support, consulting or a hosted version of Palisade on the project's behalf.
  • Palisade is not a replacement for commercial application control products. Do not rely on it to protect production systems.

Report a Code of Conduct concernPrivately, as described in CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

Before you ask, please search existing issues and discussions, and check the README and the docs.

When you post logs or policy excerpts, remove secrets, enrolment tokens, override codes, host names and user names first.

Glossary

Allowlist. A rule set of things that may run. Under default-deny, everything not on it is blocked.

Application control. Allowing only approved code to run. ASD's definition covers executables, libraries, scripts, installers, compiled HTML, HTML applications, control panel applets and drivers.

Authenticode. The code-signing format for Windows files. Palisade parses the signature, the certificate chain and the image hash itself (palisade-fileid).

Audit mode. Decisions are evaluated and logged but not enforced. See Modes.

Blocklist. A rule set of things that may not run. A mandatory blocklist is decided before every other rule and is never overridden.

Catalog. A signed file that lists the hashes of other files, so unsigned files can be trusted through it.

Condition tree. A rule's match: all, any and not over criteria. See Rules and conditions.

Criterion. One test of one fact: field operator values.

Decision. The engine's answer for one object: the outcome, the deciding rule, the rules it overrode, and why. See Decision trace.

Effective policy. The single policy a device evaluates, after the group hierarchy is merged.

Essential Eight. ASD's eight baseline mitigation strategies, with Maturity Levels One to Three. See Compliance.

Identity criterion. A criterion about the file itself: hash, signer, path or metadata. See Identities.

Implicit deny. The decision when no rule decides: blocked, or reported in non-enforcing modes.

ISM. ASD's Information Security Manual.

Learning mode. Audit mode that also marks objects only the implicit deny would block as candidates for new rules.

Mode. disabled, monitor, audit, learning or enforce. See Modes.

OS-native policy. The operating system's own code integrity and rule-collection policy formats, which Palisade compiles to (ADR 0002).

Override session. A time-boxed, audited relaxation of ordinary rules on one device. See Exceptions and offline overrides.

Precedence model. How the matching rules are combined into one decision. See Precedence models.

Rule set. A named, reusable, ordered collection of rules, referenced by policies.

Trust source. A process whose output is trusted, such as an installer or updater.

Source: docs/book/src/glossary.md on GitHub.
